articles.title: Ukraine’s Drone Offensive Gives Kyiv a 3-to-1 Edge Over Russia
articles.body:
Ukraine has conducted approximately three times more long-range drone strikes against targets in Russia than the Kremlin has launched in the opposite direction over the past 100 days, according to a Kyiv Post analysis of open-source strike data.
The analysis found that even when Russia’s cruise, ballistic, hypersonic, and anti-ship missiles are included, the cumulative explosive payload delivered by Ukraine’s long-range drone campaign often matches, and at times exceeds, the total weight of warheads launched by Russia against Ukraine on a given night.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The study was based on open-source data tracking long-range strikes from the Ukrainian Air Force documenting Russian drones and missiles detected in Ukrainian airspace, alongside daily statements from Russia’s defense ministry reporting Ukrainian drones and missiles it claimed to have intercepted.
Those databases, to some degree, undercount strike-weapon totals for Russia as not all launched weapons are detected by Ukrainian air defenses. For Ukraine, even if all Russian shootdown claims are accurate, some Ukrainian drones and missiles are not stopped and go on to hit targets in Russia.
One problem with the Russian official data is that it is incomplete. On some days, Russia’s defense ministry publishes shootdown claims covering a full 24-hour period, while on others it reports figures for only 12 hours or less. Another challenge is the tendency to overcount. By the Kremlin’s own figures, Russia has destroyed 17,936 Ukrainian unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), yet an independent Western analysis estimates that Ukraine has likely launched only about 4,620 UAVs at Russian.
Serbia Hopes for Gas Deal Extension After Vucic-Putin Call
Still, based on that imperfect but extensive dataset, one figure stands out. During the 100-day period from June 17 to Sept. 24, official Ukrainian data recorded the launch of around 16,000 Russian drones of various types against Ukraine. Kyiv Post estimates, assisted by AI analysis, suggest the actual number was likely closer to 16,200, though an exact total is impossible to determine.
Over the same three-month period, Russian defense ministry claims, compiled from daily reports published by state-run news agency RIA Novosti, indicated that Russian forces had shot down or otherwise neutralized between 48,000-55,000 Ukrainian long-range drones. Those figures suggest Ukraine was launching more than three times as many explosives-toting robot aircraft at targets in Russia compared to what Moscow was sending the other direction.
Records of peak long-range strike activity also point to a roughly 3-to-1 Ukrainian advantage in large-scale aerial attacks. During the past 100 days, Russia launched more than 400 drones against Ukraine on two occasions, July 2 and Sept. 12, and more than 250 drones on five occasions: Sept. 24, Sept. 23, Sept. 12, Aug. 29, and Aug. 27. Three of those attacks were directed at Kyiv, striking civilian homes and infrastructure in the capital, while two others hit railway, logistics, energy, and industrial targets across the country.
Based on Kremlin shootdown claims, Ukraine carried out drone attacks involving more than 1,000 aircraft on at least three occasions. The largest came on Aug. 19-20, when Russian authorities claimed to have destroyed 1,164 Ukrainian drones, the highest figure recorded during the period. Russia also reported intercepting that same amount during attacks on Aug. 17-18 and Aug. 15-16, with two additional large-scale strikes, on Aug. 18-19 and Sept. 22-23, involving more than 900 Ukrainian drones, per Russian claims.
Major Ukrainian drone raids have generally been broader in scope and less focused on harming civilians, as compared to Russian attacks. Instead, Ukrainian long-range strike aircraft have typically targeted Russian energy infrastructure, military manufacturing, military headquarters, and ammunition storage sites.
Direct comparisons of Russian and Ukrainian drone strike totals do not provide a complete picture of their impact or the damage inflicted. Russia, a nuclear power with one of the world’s oldest missile industries, regularly supplements its drone attacks with ballistic, cruise, hypersonic, and even anti-ship missiles launched against targets across Ukraine.
Ukraine, while owning a fairly advanced aerospace industry capable of building ballistic and cruise missiles throughout the war, has been unable to conduct large-scale missile strikes against Russia due to high costs and sustained attacks. Worse for the Ukrainians, stopping Russian ballistic missiles depends heavily on interceptor missiles controlled by the White House.
On July 2, Russia launched 496 drones and 74 missiles at Ukraine. Ukrainian air defenses shot down nearly 90% of the drones, but a number of missiles penetrated the defense shield, killing at least 30 people and damaging around 130 buildings in Kyiv. On July 6, Russia launched 23 ballistic missiles. None were intercepted, and at least 20 Ukrainians were killed, most of them when a ballistic missile strike caused the collapse of the apartment building where they lived.
During the first three weeks of September, Ukraine reported detecting 2,100 jet-powered drones and 136 missiles launched by Russian forces. Over the same period, civilian authorities recorded 288 deaths, most caused by weapons that Ukrainian air defenses had little or no ability to stop.That death and destruction notwithstanding, measured by the raw weight of warheads, the amount of explosives carried by Ukrainian drones into Russia is, on average, at least in part and probably greater than the amount of destructive force carried by Russian drones and missiles heading the other way.
Based on open-source descriptions of the types of drones spotted over Russia, and statements by Ukrainian military sources, a typical mix in a major Ukrainian one-night attack involving more than 1,000 aircraft would probably include 550-600 workhorse FP-1-type drones, each carrying a warhead of around 100 kilograms (220 pounds), 100-150 longer-range Sichen or Morok drones armed with lighter 30-40 kilogram (66-88 pound) warheads, and a similar number of jet-powered drones carrying similar payloads.
The total warhead weight of such a strike force, while hypothetical, would closely approximate that of actual large-scale Ukrainian drone attacks. Depending on the exact mix of aircraft and payloads, it could deliver between 55 and 75 tons of explosive warheads against targets in Russia. Actual components and warheads are not publicly disclosed.
In a maximum-effort Russian strike against Ukraine, there is better data and a number of well-documented examples. The Russian attack of July 29-30 included 74 missiles, among them 61 cruise missiles, nine ballistic missiles, and four anti-ship missiles, all carrying warheads in the 450-kilogram (992-pound) range. The missiles were accompanied by 284 drones, some armed with warheads weighing around 100 kilograms (220 pounds) and others operating as unarmed decoys designed to complicate Ukrainian air defenses.
A reasonable estimate of the total warhead weight delivered by those Russian missiles, in what was one of the largest missile attacks of the war, is around 38-40 tons of high explosives. Even if every accompanying Russian drone had also been armed with a warhead, and Russian strike tactics always employ decoys, the maximum additional warhead weight in the drones would have been 25-30 tons.
The outcome of that notional arithmetic is that, if total explosive payload delivered in a single maximum-effort raid is used as the benchmark, then Ukraine, despite lacking the capacity to manufacture cruise and ballistic missiles in large numbers, probably delivers more explosives to its targets in a peak attack than Russia does in a comparable strike, thanks to a 3-to-1 advantage in the number of drones Ukraine is typically able to launch.
A major qualification to that Ukrainian numerical advantage is that a single 450-kg (992-pound) missile warhead detonation will cause significantly more damage than three or four 100 kg (220 pound) drone warhead detonations. Because of its high speed, a ballistic missile can penetrate a target more deeply, with the explosion of its warhead taking place in a single location. This is a partial answer to the begged question of why Russian strikes against Ukraine seem so destructive: the missiles Russia is using, when and where they hit, are far more destructive individually.
However, quantity matters as well as quality in a large conventional war. Over the past three months, practically every Ukrainian strike has, according to open-source imagery and Kyiv Post’s daily tracking of those attacks, achieved at least some useful hits on Russian targets – roughly three times more often than Russia has managed against targets in Ukraine during the same period.

articles.title: To Secure Arctic, NORTHCOM Builds Closer Ties to Pacific, European Commands
articles.body:
U.S. Airmen assigned to the 115th Fighter Wing, Wisconsin Air National Guard, marshal an F-35A Lightning II aircraft at Pituffik Space Base, Greenland, Sept. 10, 2026. U.S. Air National Guard photo by Master Sgt. Mary Greenwood
Audio of this article is brought to you by the Air & Space Forces Association, honoring and supporting our Airmen, Guardians, and their families. Find out more at afa.org
U.S. Northern Command plans to sign an agreement with its European and Pacific counterparts to enhance coordination and close security seams in the Arctic, a strategically vital region where all three commands converge, U.S. officials told Air & Space Forces Magazine.
NORTHCOM’s Gen. Gregory M. Guillot, U.S. European Command’s Gen. Alexus G. Grynkewich, and U.S. Pacific Command’s Adm. Samuel Paparo will finalize the agreement, which aims to strengthen information sharing and ensure that adversaries cannot exploit the geographic boundaries among the commands.
U.S. Northern Command’s long-standing motto, “We have the watch,” has taken on greater urgency in recent years as the potential means to attack the U.S. Arctic region have grown. Today, the command’s geographic focus stretches across Canada, Greenland, and south to Mexico and parts of the Caribbean, and the potential dangers have expanded to include a range of emerging threats, from intelligence-gathering balloons to ballistic missiles, cruise missiles, and drones.
Guillot, in a September interview with Air & Space Forces Magazine, said the command has managed the growth well. “Over the last couple of years, we’ve received a few new missions with Greenland, the Southern Border, Golden Dome, and the counter-UAS mission, and we’ve been able to evolve and incorporate those into our daily homeland defense operations, I think, seamlessly,” said Guillot, whose responsibilities also include heading the binational U.S.-Canadian North American Aerospace Defense Command, known as NORAD.
“The command is growing as the number of threats and the number of avenues of approach that they can use to threaten us increase,” he added of NORTHCOM.
The Arctic’s strategic importance has grown as melting polar ice has opened up the region for greater commercial traffic and resource exploitation.
Russia, which owns more than half the Arctic coastline, has long projected its military might in the region.
More recently, China has sought to assert itself as an Arctic nation, not because it controls territory there but because of its value as a transit venue, shortening the trade routes between China and Europe. China operates research vessels there, including submersibles.
“They’re seeking to move themselves forward militarily and become global power projectors, not regional power projectors, and part of that will involve holding us at risk through the Arctic and ensuring that policy in the Arctic reflects their interests,” retired Gen. Glen D. VanHerck, Guillot’s predecessor at NORTHCOM and NORAD, said in an interview.
A joint China-Russia bomber patrol in the region, which took off in 2024 from a Russian base, demonstrated closer ties between the two and raised concerns across North America and Europe about their growing cooperation.
“When you see Russia and China cooperating militarily in the Arctic, with a greater capacity arguably than anywhere else on Earth, I think that should give some signals that we should be paying attention to what’s going on in the region,” said Iris Ferguson, who served as deputy assistant secretary of defense for Arctic and global resilience from 2022-2025.
Ferguson sees closing the gaps between U.S. military commands that converge in the Arctic region as essential to enhanced security.
“There are multiple seams in the Arctic for the United States,” she said. “The one between NORTHCOM and EUCOM is a significant one and is one area that deserves more attention.”
NORTHCOM led the drive to formalize an agreement with its fellow combatant commands, working closely with EUCOM and its boss, Grynkewich, who is also NATO’s Supreme Allied Commander Europe, with critical ties to NATO’s Nordic allies. Through NATO, Grynkewich is responsible for defending what NATO dubs the High North, comprising Canada, Finland, Norway, Sweden, Denmark, Iceland, and the U.S. The alliance held multiple large-scale Arctic exercises this past summer, some of which Air & Space Forces Magazine experienced firsthand. NATO’s Arctic Sentry “enhanced vigilance activity” operates in cooperation with NORAD and NORTHCOM, and alliance officials describe that cooperation as at a level not seen in decades.
Guillot said the potential threats aren’t limited to America’s largest potential adversaries.
“I see the threat to our continent changing not just from Russia and China, but from multiple adversaries,” Guillot said. “The biggest change is that it’s from all avenues of approach instead of just from the north, and it’s with systems that could affect us from further away. So therefore our defense capabilities need to be expanded further from our borders to make sure that we’re defending at the appropriate range.”
“What that necessitates is cooperation with EUCOM, PACOM, and SOUTHCOM, where we can exchange information, pictures, intelligence, and even resources to defend further away,” Guillot said.
VanHerck applauded efforts to strengthen Arctic security and stop threats before they reach North America.
“Homeland defense doesn’t start in the homeland,” VanHerck said. “It starts forward with allies and partners and fellow combat commanders forward. Ideally, you have a posture and a presence and enough domain awareness that you deter those activities before they ever start. And if they’re going to attack, you can defeat those adversaries or capabilities further forward.”
The Trump administration has made Arctic security a centerpiece of its foreign policy, pressing to win new concessions for American basing in Greenland, expanding beyond a single Space Force installation to establish two new bases. Demonstrating the critical nature of Greenland to North American security, the administration transferred responsibility for Greenland, a territory of Denmark, to U.S. Northern Command, removing it from U.S. European Command’s area of responsibility.
That transfer is far from symbolic. “A lot of exercises and operations that we would normally conduct either unilaterally, or perhaps with Canada through NORAD, we’re now doing with other countries to include Denmark,” Guillot said.
A recent exercise with the U.S. and allied nations marked the first time Danish F-35s landed in Greenland.
U.S., Canadian, and Danish forces conducted joint Operation Arctic Vanguard and NATO exercises in Greenland this month that drew F-35As from continental U.S. bases, U.S. F-16s from Alaska, Canadian CF-18s, and Danish F-35As. French air-to-air refueling aircraft and NATO-operated E-3 AWACS command-and-control jets also joined the operations as part of NATO’s Arctic Sentry.
Referencing the recent exercises, Guillot said allies were “fully integrated” and “operating in multiple lanes at the same time,” a shift from a few years ago when the U.S. may have conducted unilateral training instead. Operating as an integrated whole creates dilemmas for adversaries and acts as a force multiplier for the allies.
“That is possible due to the great relationship and partnering by the Danish forces,” Guillot said.
On the other side of North America, near Alaska, the U.S. and Canada recently conducted a joint exercise practicing striking maritime targets in the Bering Sea, using aircraft, surface vessels, and a submarine. The U.S. has also conducted joint naval operations with Canada that involve the U.S. Coast Guard alongside the U.S. military. Those exercises fall under Operation Tundra Merlin, which focuses on deterrence near Alaska, including the western Arctic and Northern Pacific. Pacific Air Forces aircraft stationed in Alaska also supported Arctic Vanguard on the other side of NORTHCOM’s region.
Alaska’s geographic size and placement at the nexus of the NORTHCOM and PACOM areas of responsibility places it in proximity to potential threats from China, Russia, and North Korea.
“I don’t think people appreciate the role that Alaska plays for our homeland defense mission, but also for our Indo-Pacific mission,” said Ferguson, who also served as a senior advisor to the Air Force on the Arctic. “Alaska is critical as a place of power projection to be able to project power not only into the Indo-Pacific in the event of a contingency, but also into the European theater.”
The exercises underscore Guillot’s broader Nordic Bridge initiative, launched earlier this year to better integrate allied operations across the Arctic. It includes coordination among the various U.S. combatant commands that touch on the region, as well as Canada, Sweden, Finland, Denmark, Norway, and Iceland, all NATO allies. Working together, they aim to enhance domain awareness and interoperability.
“We’re working with other friendly Arctic nations to increase our presence,” Guillot said, “to increase and expand the deterrence, and make sure that every exercise we do up there is multinational and along multiple avenues of approach.”

The Anduril-built Barracuda cruise missile recently received certification as the Air Force’s first large-scale production munition compliant with open systems architecture.
The Air Force has invested $87.4 million to upgrade the F-16 Fighting Falcon's electronic warfare capabilities, bolstering the fighter's self-protection against increasingly advanced threats. Bringing the total program value to $1.92 billion, the move is expected to jump-start fielding by funding low-rate initial production of the AN/ALQ-257 Integrated Viper Electronic…
One of the Air Force and Navy’s most common air-to-air missiles is falling short of a key readiness metric, and the services are ramping up stocks of a vital air-to-ground missile, according to recent Pentagon reports.
Nellis Air Force Base, Nev.—a longtime hub for A-10 Thunderbolt II tactical training, operational testing and maintenance—ended nearly a half-century of flying the venerable Warthog on Sept. 22.
Chinese President Xi Jinping’s state visit to Washington D.C. has been filled with signs of American airpower: U.S. Air Force B-1 and B-2 bombers and F-22 fighters have all performed flyovers Sept. 23-24.
The Air Force’s HH-60G Pave Hawk helicopter made its final flight earlier this month. The 129th Rescue Wing retired its last HH-60G with a final flight and ceremony on Sept. 10 at Moffett Air National Guard Base, Calif. The Pave Hawk is being replaced by an updated model, HH-60W Jolly…
The Air Force is slashing all civilian positions at its premier research institute for Chinese military aviation, prompting concern among experts who say it will dilute the service’s focus on the Pentagon’s most significant long-term adversary.
General Atomics Aeronautical Systems Inc. and Anduril Industries both say they’re ready to produce Collaborative Combat Aircraft at a rapid clip and even expand that production, as they wait for a fiscal 2027 budget to fund that work.
A new think tank report calls for a buildup of U.S. drones and munitions needed for a potential fight against the Chinese military over Taiwan, thought other experts argue the report is missing some nuance in the munitions equation.

articles.title: Iran submits seven-day Hormuz plan; Yemen forces advance in Taiz
articles.body:
This live blog has now ended. Make sure to follow us for the latest news on Facebook, X, and Instagram.
Breadcrumb
Hello and welcome to today's coverage of the Middle East and beyond. Here is the latest:
US President Donald Trump on Saturday rejected Iran's latest proposal put forward by Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi during a visit to New York, which outlined a seven-day proposal to end the war and reopen the Strait of Hormuz.
In Yemen, government forces advance towards the Taiz and Lahaj governorates, coinciding with a call for "mobilisation" to confront Houthi troops. At least 13 Houthi militants have been killed and dozens others injured in the past 24 hours of fighting, according to Aden-based government figures.
Meanwhile, Israeli strikes have continued in southern Lebanon, with attacks reported in Mansouri, Majdal Zoun and Wadi Hassan overnight.
The natural springs and ancient pools of the occupied West Bank have long provided a respite from the oppressive summer heat. They also have been a lifeline for Palestinian communities, which rely on them for tourism and irrigation for their farmland.
But for the 2.8 million Palestinians who live in the territory, those springs and the stone reservoirs they fill are increasingly out of reach as Israeli settlers — encouraged by a hard-line government facing reelection — have stepped up efforts both to seize the springs and other heritage sites.
In one case this summer, water from a natural spring to the Palestinian village of Fasayil was illegally diverted to an ancient pool nearby. Whoever siphoned the water used it to fill up that pool, declaring it a new tourist attraction named after Herod, the Roman-appointed king of Judea.
Read the full story here.
Oscar-nominated actor Florence Pugh has said she was never "scared" to speak up for Palestine, while promoting her new movie East of Eden.
In an exclusive interview with Variety, the actor said no one ever advised her to keep quiet on the issue, and she was confused about why so many weren't voicing their support.
"I don't know why it took so long for people to start talking and for people to actually feel sympathy," Pugh told Vanity Fair.
ussian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said at the UN Saturday that Moscow is ready to help stabilize the situation in the Strait of Hormuz and the wider Gulf region, as the US-Iran conflict drags on.
"We need trust in the relationships between the Gulf states, the Arab states, and Iran. We need stable regional architecture," Lavrov told leaders at the UN General Assembly.
"Russia, together with other responsible states, stands ready to constructively contribute to stabilizing this strategically important region."
Attacks targeting Libya's energy infrastructure, or any actions that could undermine it, may constitute grounds for sanctions under relevant UN Security Council resolutions, the UN Support Mission in Libya said on Saturday.
The warning comes as the Sharara-Zawiya oil pipeline remains closed, causing losses in crude production and public revenues and raising risks to fuel supplies and electricity generation, the mission said in a statement.
US intelligence agencies have assessed that Saudi Arabia has not ruled out developing a nuclear weapons programme, according to classified documents provided to Congress and described to The Washington Post by US officials.
The assessment is raising fresh questions about US President Donald Trump’s agreement to help Riyadh establish a civilian nuclear industry. Some US lawmakers fear the deal could give Saudi Arabia the means to produce nuclear material that might eventually be used as a weapon, although the intelligence finding does not say the kingdom has decided to build one.
The agreement, announced in July, would allow US companies to pursue nuclear energy projects in Saudi Arabia. The Trump administration says the partnership will strengthen ties with Riyadh, uphold non-proliferation standards, and reduce the prospect of the kingdom turning to Russia or China for nuclear technology.
The University of Southern California (USC) ended the sale of human cadavers for Israeli military training on Thursday, closing a programme that ran for over five years.
A report by Annenberg Media in 2024 revealed that the University of California San Diego (UCSD) supplied bodies to the University of California (USC), which were then sold to the US Navy and used for training Israeli army medics.
The revelation sparked public outcry, with protests demanding an end to the programme.
USC's medical school said it would not renew its cadaver contracts because it would no longer supply bodies for the US Navy programme.
Israeli drone strike inside the so-called "ceasefire" zone in west Nuseirat, Gaza, kills at least one Palestinian and injured multiple others, according to local media.
US President Donald Trump said Saturday that he had rejected a plan proposed by Iran on the strategic Strait of Hormuz, which Tehran says would have opened the waterway within seven days.
"I reject their proposal," Trump told reporters outside the White House.
"They want to make a deal where they open the Strait immediately because they're losing so badly," he said. "They want to make a deal and I think that's fine. I like making a deal too."
Players from Ireland's football team voted on Saturday to fulfil a Nations League tie with Israel despite player unease over the war in Gaza.
"We carried out a vote amongst the squad to establish their sentiment on fulfilling the (Israel) fixtures," Football Association of Ireland head David Courell told reporters in Debrecen, Hungary, where the game will take place on Sunday.
"It was a significant majority that was returned with the intention to continue," he said.
Egypt’s then-intelligence chief travelled to Israel 11 days before Hamas’s 7 October 2023 attack and warned that the group appeared to be preparing a major assault, according to an investigation by The Atlantic.
The report comes amid intensifying pressure on Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to allow an independent inquiry into Israel’s failures ahead of the attack, as the country approaches an election next month.
Abbas Kamel arrived in Israel on 26 September 2023 aboard a plane linked to Egyptian intelligence, The Atlantic reported on Friday, citing an Israeli airport flight log and officials from Israel, Egypt and other countries who were briefed on the visit after the attack. The plane spent 67 minutes on the ground before returning to Cairo.
Saudi Arabia's Grand Mufti Saleh bin Fawzan al-Fawzan has exhorted the coalition forces fighting against Yemen's Houthis to be ready to sacrifice their lives in the conflict, the Saudi Press Agency reported on Friday.
Addressing soldiers on the frontlines of the conflict and in stationed along the country's borders, the mufti's statement comes as Yemen slides further back into civil war, with the Houthis advancing on government-held territory.
Ireland cancelled their pre-match press conference ahead of Sunday's Nations League game against Israel in Hungary, and their training session has also been delayed, the Israeli FA press officer said on Saturday.
The game has been under the spotlight since the sides were drawn together in February, with Ireland one of Europe's most outspoken critics of Israel's genocidal war in Gaza. There have been numerous protests in Ireland asking for the team not to fulfil the fixtures with Israel.
Ireland were due to hold the press conference on Saturday but shortly before the scheduled start at 10:15 a.m. local time (0815 GMT), reporters were informed that this would now take place following the team's training session at the stadium in Debrecen.
Iran's top security body denies that Iran is planning for military moves over bans on Iranian flights, according to state media.
Thousands of people rallied in Madrid on Saturday to protest the Spanish government's handling of a recent migrant influx into Ceuta, accusing it of failing to protect the country's borders and calling for an early general election.
Demonstrators, many waving red and yellow Spanish flags, chanted "Ceuta is not for sale, Ceuta must be defended" as they marched through the centre of the Spanish capital.
Ceuta, a Spanish territory located in North Africa, has been embroiled in a humanitarian crisis since more than 70,000 migrants arrived from neighbouring Morocco on July 30 and 31.
Most returned in the following hours, but thousands have remained for weeks, many sleeping on the streets, straining the small city's resources and creating a political crisis for Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez.
The protest was organised by right-leaning civil society platform Sociedad Civil Espanola and backed by the conservative People's Party (PP) and far-right Vox.
US actor Adam Brody said he wants a "free Palestine" on Friday while promoting his show Nobody Wants This, after several Hollywood actors were arrested during a protest against the arrival of Israel's ICC fugitive Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
In an interview with GQ, Brody, known for his breakout role in the series The O.C., said he wants to noted as being among those who believe a genocide is occurring in Gaza.
“Put me down as thinking it’s a genocide. Put me down as wanting a free Palestine,” Brody said when asked if he would like to speak about the topic.
One person injured following reported Israeli fire in the Beit Lahia area of northern Gaza, according to Palestinian media.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said Tehran's new plan to reopen the strategic Strait of Hormuz was coordinated with supreme leader Mojtaba Khamenei, state media reported Saturday, quoting an interview with US media.
Pezeshkian also told broadcaster CBS that the Islamic republic would fulfil its obligations were the United States to agree to the proposal, according to excerpts released by state news agency IRNA.
The strait is crucial for the world's oil supply and central to the conflict between the US and Iran, which remains deadlocked after nearly seven months.
"Coordination with the leader of the revolution (the supreme leader)... has been carried out," Pezeshkian said.
"If the US accepts it and fulfils its obligations, we will do the same, and there will be no issue in this regard," he added.
Pezeshkian said that a six-member team in Iran has been meeting for discussions and has "the authority to make decisions".
This team includes representatives from "various organisations and bodies, including the military, the parliament and the government".
The Ireland team’s press conference the day before the first of its Nations League games against Israel has been delayed as pressure to boycott the matches grows.
Journalists in Debrecen, Hungary — where Israel’s "home" game is to be played Sunday — were left waiting Saturday after being told the press conference was being pushed back until after training. That was 15 minutes before it was supposed to begin.
Training was also delayed, however, with Irish broadcaster RTÉ reporting the players were still in their hotel when it was supposed to begin.
The team has been coming under increasing pressure in Ireland, where affinity with Palestinians is strong, to boycott the two games — the first on Sunday and the second, Ireland’s “home” game, in Backa Topola, Serbia on Oct. 4.
Ireland midfielder Jason Knight said after Thursday’s 1-0 loss in Kosovo that the players were in a difficult situation and that he didn’t think the matches should be going ahead.
The Iraqi government said Saturday it was holding talks with the United States to secure an exemption from the ban on Iranian airlines, which has disrupted travel for patients, students and pilgrims.
All Iraqi airports enforced the ban this week, resulting in major disruption at the airport of the holy city of Najaf, the main destination for Iranian flights to Iraq.
"The Iraqi government is holding direct talks with the American side to exempt certain Iraqi airports from these measures," the prime minister's media office said.
An exemption would allow flights to resume "for humanitarian reasons, including medical treatment, education, religious visits, and for the interest of civilians," it added.
Israeli forces use artillery shelling to target the outskirts of Yater in southern Lebanon, according to local media.
Israeli forces and military vehicles are stationed by Birzeit University north of Ramallah in the occupied West Bank, according to Palestinian media.
The university, meanwhile, has condemned the Israeli military raid, claiming "intimidation" of students during final exams is "flagrant and explicit violation" of conventions and laws that protect education.
Saudi Arabia's military spokesperson, Maj. Gen. Turki al-Malki, claimed early Saturday that a ballistic missile launched by the Iran-backed Houthi rebels in neighboring Yemen was intercepted and destroyed.
Al-Maliki said the missile was fired toward the southwestern city of Khamis Mushait.
There was no immediate statement of responsibility, though it can take days for the Houthis to issue one.
A regional body representing Arab Gulf states, the Gulf Cooperation Council, condemned the latest Houthi attacks as a "grave escalation and threat to regional security" and urged the international community to respond.
A passenger bus overturned in Iran, killing 11 people and injuring 24 others, state television reported Saturday.
The crash occurred on the Saveh-Hamedan freeway in central Markazi province. Provincial traffic police said driver fatigue and drowsiness caused the crash.
Authorities did not immediately say where the bus was headed.
Iran has one of the world’s worst traffic safety records. Crashes kill more than 17,000 people a year. Experts blame the high toll on unsafe vehicles, widespread disregard for traffic regulations and inadequate emergency services.
Earlier this month, a fuel tanker crashed into other vehicles and exploded near the western city of Sanandaj, killing 11 people and injuring seven others.
Libya's National Oil Corporation said on Saturday it has shut down one of the refining units at the Zawiya refinery due to the continued forced closure of the Sharara crude pipeline valve by armed groups belonging to the Petroleum Facilities Guard.
The corporation warned that ongoing disruptions to the flow of crude could directly impact state oil revenue, increase fuel import costs and harm the national economy.
The closure has reduced cumulative production at the Sharara field by 942,376 barrels over five days through Friday, causing direct financial losses of about $95 million, the NOC said.
Lost output on Friday alone totalled 222,014 barrels, according to NOC.

articles.title: Trump rejects Iran's Hormuz plan; Yemen forces advance in Taiz
articles.body:

The natural springs and ancient pools of the occupied West Bank have long provided a respite from the oppressive summer heat. They also have been a lifeline for Palestinian communities, which rely on them for tourism and irrigation for their farmland.
But for the 2.8 million Palestinians who live in the territory, those springs and the stone reservoirs they fill are increasingly out of reach as Israeli settlers — encouraged by a hard-line government facing reelection — have stepped up efforts both to seize the springs and other heritage sites.
In one case this summer, water from a natural spring to the Palestinian village of Fasayil was illegally diverted to an ancient pool nearby. Whoever siphoned the water used it to fill up that pool, declaring it a new tourist attraction named after Herod, the Roman-appointed king of Judea.
Read the full story here.
Oscar-nominated actor Florence Pugh has said she was never "scared" to speak up for Palestine, while promoting her new movie East of Eden.
In an exclusive interview with Variety, the actor said no one ever advised her to keep quiet on the issue, and she was confused about why so many weren't voicing their support.
"I don't know why it took so long for people to start talking and for people to actually feel sympathy," Pugh told Vanity Fair.
ussian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said at the UN Saturday that Moscow is ready to help stabilize the situation in the Strait of Hormuz and the wider Gulf region, as the US-Iran conflict drags on.
"We need trust in the relationships between the Gulf states, the Arab states, and Iran. We need stable regional architecture," Lavrov told leaders at the UN General Assembly.
"Russia, together with other responsible states, stands ready to constructively contribute to stabilizing this strategically important region."
Attacks targeting Libya's energy infrastructure, or any actions that could undermine it, may constitute grounds for sanctions under relevant UN Security Council resolutions, the UN Support Mission in Libya said on Saturday.
The warning comes as the Sharara-Zawiya oil pipeline remains closed, causing losses in crude production and public revenues and raising risks to fuel supplies and electricity generation, the mission said in a statement.
US intelligence agencies have assessed that Saudi Arabia has not ruled out developing a nuclear weapons programme, according to classified documents provided to Congress and described to The Washington Post by US officials.
The assessment is raising fresh questions about US President Donald Trump’s agreement to help Riyadh establish a civilian nuclear industry. Some US lawmakers fear the deal could give Saudi Arabia the means to produce nuclear material that might eventually be used as a weapon, although the intelligence finding does not say the kingdom has decided to build one.
The agreement, announced in July, would allow US companies to pursue nuclear energy projects in Saudi Arabia. The Trump administration says the partnership will strengthen ties with Riyadh, uphold non-proliferation standards, and reduce the prospect of the kingdom turning to Russia or China for nuclear technology.
The University of Southern California (USC) ended the sale of human cadavers for Israeli military training on Thursday, closing a programme that ran for over five years.
A report by Annenberg Media in 2024 revealed that the University of California San Diego (UCSD) supplied bodies to the University of California (USC), which were then sold to the US Navy and used for training Israeli army medics.
The revelation sparked public outcry, with protests demanding an end to the programme.
USC's medical school said it would not renew its cadaver contracts because it would no longer supply bodies for the US Navy programme.
Israeli drone strike inside the so-called "ceasefire" zone in west Nuseirat, Gaza, kills at least one Palestinian and injured multiple others, according to local media.
US President Donald Trump said Saturday that he had rejected a plan proposed by Iran on the strategic Strait of Hormuz, which Tehran says would have opened the waterway within seven days.
"I reject their proposal," Trump told reporters outside the White House.
"They want to make a deal where they open the Strait immediately because they're losing so badly," he said. "They want to make a deal and I think that's fine. I like making a deal too."
Players from Ireland's football team voted on Saturday to fulfil a Nations League tie with Israel despite player unease over the war in Gaza.
"We carried out a vote amongst the squad to establish their sentiment on fulfilling the (Israel) fixtures," Football Association of Ireland head David Courell told reporters in Debrecen, Hungary, where the game will take place on Sunday.
"It was a significant majority that was returned with the intention to continue," he said.
Egypt’s then-intelligence chief travelled to Israel 11 days before Hamas’s 7 October 2023 attack and warned that the group appeared to be preparing a major assault, according to an investigation by The Atlantic.
The report comes amid intensifying pressure on Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to allow an independent inquiry into Israel’s failures ahead of the attack, as the country approaches an election next month.
Abbas Kamel arrived in Israel on 26 September 2023 aboard a plane linked to Egyptian intelligence, The Atlantic reported on Friday, citing an Israeli airport flight log and officials from Israel, Egypt and other countries who were briefed on the visit after the attack. The plane spent 67 minutes on the ground before returning to Cairo.
Saudi Arabia's Grand Mufti Saleh bin Fawzan al-Fawzan has exhorted the coalition forces fighting against Yemen's Houthis to be ready to sacrifice their lives in the conflict, the Saudi Press Agency reported on Friday.
Addressing soldiers on the frontlines of the conflict and in stationed along the country's borders, the mufti's statement comes as Yemen slides further back into civil war, with the Houthis advancing on government-held territory.
Ireland cancelled their pre-match press conference ahead of Sunday's Nations League game against Israel in Hungary, and their training session has also been delayed, the Israeli FA press officer said on Saturday.
The game has been under the spotlight since the sides were drawn together in February, with Ireland one of Europe's most outspoken critics of Israel's genocidal war in Gaza. There have been numerous protests in Ireland asking for the team not to fulfil the fixtures with Israel.
Ireland were due to hold the press conference on Saturday but shortly before the scheduled start at 10:15 a.m. local time (0815 GMT), reporters were informed that this would now take place following the team's training session at the stadium in Debrecen.
Iran's top security body denies that Iran is planning for military moves over bans on Iranian flights, according to state media.
Thousands of people rallied in Madrid on Saturday to protest the Spanish government's handling of a recent migrant influx into Ceuta, accusing it of failing to protect the country's borders and calling for an early general election.
Demonstrators, many waving red and yellow Spanish flags, chanted "Ceuta is not for sale, Ceuta must be defended" as they marched through the centre of the Spanish capital.
Ceuta, a Spanish territory located in North Africa, has been embroiled in a humanitarian crisis since more than 70,000 migrants arrived from neighbouring Morocco on July 30 and 31.
Most returned in the following hours, but thousands have remained for weeks, many sleeping on the streets, straining the small city's resources and creating a political crisis for Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez.
The protest was organised by right-leaning civil society platform Sociedad Civil Espanola and backed by the conservative People's Party (PP) and far-right Vox.
US actor Adam Brody said he wants a "free Palestine" on Friday while promoting his show Nobody Wants This, after several Hollywood actors were arrested during a protest against the arrival of Israel's ICC fugitive Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
In an interview with GQ, Brody, known for his breakout role in the series The O.C., said he wants to noted as being among those who believe a genocide is occurring in Gaza.
“Put me down as thinking it’s a genocide. Put me down as wanting a free Palestine,” Brody said when asked if he would like to speak about the topic.
One person injured following reported Israeli fire in the Beit Lahia area of northern Gaza, according to Palestinian media.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said Tehran's new plan to reopen the strategic Strait of Hormuz was coordinated with supreme leader Mojtaba Khamenei, state media reported Saturday, quoting an interview with US media.
Pezeshkian also told broadcaster CBS that the Islamic republic would fulfil its obligations were the United States to agree to the proposal, according to excerpts released by state news agency IRNA.
The strait is crucial for the world's oil supply and central to the conflict between the US and Iran, which remains deadlocked after nearly seven months.
"Coordination with the leader of the revolution (the supreme leader)... has been carried out," Pezeshkian said.
"If the US accepts it and fulfils its obligations, we will do the same, and there will be no issue in this regard," he added.
Pezeshkian said that a six-member team in Iran has been meeting for discussions and has "the authority to make decisions".
This team includes representatives from "various organisations and bodies, including the military, the parliament and the government".
The Ireland team’s press conference the day before the first of its Nations League games against Israel has been delayed as pressure to boycott the matches grows.
Journalists in Debrecen, Hungary — where Israel’s "home" game is to be played Sunday — were left waiting Saturday after being told the press conference was being pushed back until after training. That was 15 minutes before it was supposed to begin.
Training was also delayed, however, with Irish broadcaster RTÉ reporting the players were still in their hotel when it was supposed to begin.
The team has been coming under increasing pressure in Ireland, where affinity with Palestinians is strong, to boycott the two games — the first on Sunday and the second, Ireland’s “home” game, in Backa Topola, Serbia on Oct. 4.
Ireland midfielder Jason Knight said after Thursday’s 1-0 loss in Kosovo that the players were in a difficult situation and that he didn’t think the matches should be going ahead.
The Iraqi government said Saturday it was holding talks with the United States to secure an exemption from the ban on Iranian airlines, which has disrupted travel for patients, students and pilgrims.
All Iraqi airports enforced the ban this week, resulting in major disruption at the airport of the holy city of Najaf, the main destination for Iranian flights to Iraq.
"The Iraqi government is holding direct talks with the American side to exempt certain Iraqi airports from these measures," the prime minister's media office said.
An exemption would allow flights to resume "for humanitarian reasons, including medical treatment, education, religious visits, and for the interest of civilians," it added.
Israeli forces use artillery shelling to target the outskirts of Yater in southern Lebanon, according to local media.
Israeli forces and military vehicles are stationed by Birzeit University north of Ramallah in the occupied West Bank, according to Palestinian media.
The university, meanwhile, has condemned the Israeli military raid, claiming "intimidation" of students during final exams is "flagrant and explicit violation" of conventions and laws that protect education.
Saudi Arabia's military spokesperson, Maj. Gen. Turki al-Malki, claimed early Saturday that a ballistic missile launched by the Iran-backed Houthi rebels in neighboring Yemen was intercepted and destroyed.
Al-Maliki said the missile was fired toward the southwestern city of Khamis Mushait.
There was no immediate statement of responsibility, though it can take days for the Houthis to issue one.
A regional body representing Arab Gulf states, the Gulf Cooperation Council, condemned the latest Houthi attacks as a "grave escalation and threat to regional security" and urged the international community to respond.
A passenger bus overturned in Iran, killing 11 people and injuring 24 others, state television reported Saturday.
The crash occurred on the Saveh-Hamedan freeway in central Markazi province. Provincial traffic police said driver fatigue and drowsiness caused the crash.
Authorities did not immediately say where the bus was headed.
Iran has one of the world’s worst traffic safety records. Crashes kill more than 17,000 people a year. Experts blame the high toll on unsafe vehicles, widespread disregard for traffic regulations and inadequate emergency services.
Earlier this month, a fuel tanker crashed into other vehicles and exploded near the western city of Sanandaj, killing 11 people and injuring seven others.
Libya's National Oil Corporation said on Saturday it has shut down one of the refining units at the Zawiya refinery due to the continued forced closure of the Sharara crude pipeline valve by armed groups belonging to the Petroleum Facilities Guard.
The corporation warned that ongoing disruptions to the flow of crude could directly impact state oil revenue, increase fuel import costs and harm the national economy.
The closure has reduced cumulative production at the Sharara field by 942,376 barrels over five days through Friday, causing direct financial losses of about $95 million, the NOC said.
Lost output on Friday alone totalled 222,014 barrels, according to NOC.

articles.title: Russian nuclear strike threat against Lithuania sparks alarm, then disappears
articles.body:
Russian President Vladimir Putin on Friday addressed for the first time European concerns that Russia could escalate its confrontation with Western European countries, categorically rejecting the possibility. At the same time, Putin offered a pessimistic assessment of prospects for progress toward a ceasefire in Ukraine, blaming a massive Ukrainian attack on Moscow during Russia's parliamentary "elections."
Responding to warnings voiced in Europe over the past week about the possibility of a direct military confrontation with Russia, Putin said: "Many in Europe say they expect an attack by the Russian Federation and therefore must prepare for military action, for war with Russia. I want to emphasize once again that we are not preparing for any military action against Europe. We have no such plans. Most importantly, there is no reason for it."
Putin nevertheless heightened tensions with the Baltic states by mocking a statement by Estonian Defense Minister Martin Herem, who said his country must be prepared to repel any attack and "destroy anyone who crosses the border."
"This is a provocation," Putin said. "The circus has already left, but the clowns remain."
Putin's remarks came hours after Russia's state-run RIA Novosti news agency removed an opinion column in which the author threatened another Baltic state, Lithuania, with a blitzkrieg and nuclear strike. The column was removed after several hours, with the agency saying it did not conform to its editorial position or the official policy of the Russian Federation.
One scenario raised in the West this week is that Russia and its ally Belarus could attempt to seize the Suwalki Gap, the strip of territory between Poland and Lithuania that separates Belarus from the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad and provides the Baltic states' only land connection to the rest of NATO.
The deleted column was written by commentator Alexander Nosovich after Lithuania's parliament moved this week to advance a proposal that would lift the country's ban on stationing nuclear weapons on its territory.
The column, headlined "Russia is in for another special military operation. It will be very short," said in part: "European countries continue to push the issue of moving unconventional weapons to Russia's borders and have chosen a country willing to become a nuclear depot."
Nosovich went on to threaten Lithuania with an invasion and even a nuclear strike.
"Russia can even afford to forgo deploying ground troops. Just missiles with the appropriate warheads," he wrote. "The solution is not merely quick, it is lightning-fast. Don't think too much about seconds."
Elsewhere in the column, Nosovich described Lithuania as "a suicidal country with no brains whatsoever," a "useful idiot" and "a small but proud kamikaze in Russia's near abroad."
Shortly after publication, however, the column was deleted. Anyone visiting the original link on RIA Novosti's website encountered an editor's note saying: "The article by freelance author Alexander Nosovich was removed from the website because it did not correspond to the editorial board's views, editorial policy or the official policy of the Russian Federation."
Before it was removed, the threatening column circulated on social media and caused alarm among parts of the Lithuanian public. An official Lithuanian military spokesperson issued a statement seeking to reassure the public: "In light of Russia's propaganda statement, we remind you that Russia routinely tries to intimidate its neighbors using hostile rhetoric. This is a common Russian practice, and no additional action should be taken as a result of these remarks."
Over the past roughly 35 years, Russia has lost much of its strategic position around the Baltic Sea. The former Soviet republics of Estonia, Lithuania and Latvia joined NATO in the early 2000s. About two decades later, Finland and Sweden abandoned decades of military nonalignment and joined the alliance. Russia's Baltic Sea coastline now includes the Kaliningrad exclave, whose land connections to the rest of Russia require transit through neighboring countries.
'Ukraine as cannon fodder'
Turning to the war in Ukraine, Putin said Friday that before there could be progress toward a settlement, Kyiv must "feel the power of Russia's retaliatory strikes" following Ukraine's massive drone attack on Moscow this week.
The Ukrainian attack came on the final day of Russia's parliamentary "elections," in which Putin's United Russia party won as expected.
"Polling stations were attacked," Putin said. "One of the attacks targeted a school where there was a polling station. They began attacking the homes of regional election commission chairs. In one case, a regional commission chair was wounded, her husband was wounded and her child was wounded. In another case, unfortunately, it ended in tragedy and an election commission chair was killed. We must make Kyiv understand that strikes deep inside Russian territory will only make the situation worse."
Addressing the role of Western European countries in the war in Ukraine, Putin said: "They want Ukraine to continue serving as cannon fodder, as a tool in the struggle against Russia."
Putin also showed no willingness to accept a proposal to halt reciprocal attacks on energy facilities in Russia and Ukraine.
"They have no means to counter our advanced weapons or to end the blockade we have imposed on their Black Sea coast," he said. "They need to remember that they are the ones who started all of this."

articles.title: Foreign Affairs: World learning from Iran’s ‘precise mass’ warfare as costly Western systems falter
articles.body:
Foreign Affairs: World learning from Iran’s ‘precise mass’ warfare as costly Western systems falter
TEHRAN — In a stunning admission that challenges the foundations of modern Western military doctrine, the influential American journal Foreign Affairs has published a comprehensive analysis revealing how Iran has successfully dismantled the aggressive war plans of the United States and Israel.
The detailed report serves as a post-mortem on the hubris of the Pentagon, explicitly stating that the future of global warfare is being dictated by the very strategies pioneered by Tehran, and that the world is now actively learning from the Iranian model of endurance and precision.
Foreign Affairs recounts the initial phase of the conflict, noting that when the United States and Israel launched their aggression against Iran, they expected a swift and decisive victory. According to the article, American planners anticipated that they would quickly overwhelm the government. The publication details the sheer scale of the assault, stating that in the war’s first 24 hours, American and Israeli forces hit roughly 1,000 targets. Over the following 39 days, they struck 12,000 more, with the stated intent of laying waste to Iran’s military infrastructure and eliminating top leadership. Yet, Foreign Affairs acknowledges that more than six months later, Iran not only remains intact but is arguably stronger than before. The journal concedes that Tehran immediately replaced its lost officials, struck back at Washington, and successfully shuttered the Strait of Hormuz, thereby driving up global energy prices and securing newfound political leverage that has left US officials deeply frustrated.
At the core of the Foreign Affairs analysis is the concept of “precise mass,” which the journal defines as high-volume, low-cost, precision-guided weapons. The publication notes that the age of this doctrine is well underway, stating that it is no longer possible for the US military to win a full-blown war simply by using small numbers of expensive, exquisite weapons to dazzle opponents. Crucially, the journal admits that offense is currently cheaper than defense, observing that the price of effective interceptors has yet to fall to the level of attack drones and missiles. It points out that militaries cannot endlessly block salvos of 35,000 dollar Shahed-136 attack drones with 4-million-dollar Patriot missiles.
Foreign Affairs further notes that the world is learning from Iran, building on lessons that were already emerging in other conflicts. The journal provides an extensive list of nations that are now pivoting to adopt this Iranian-style strategy. The publication says six European states, including France, Germany, and the United Kingdom, have signed a letter of intent to jointly develop a one-way attack drone, and Saudi Arabia has unveiled its own attack drone modeled on the Shahed. Even Japan has requested a record 55.6 billion-dollar defense budget, largely to purchase vast quantities of attack drones.
The report by Foreign Affairs also addresses the failure of the American air campaign to neutralize Iran’s capabilities. It reveals that in the years before the war, Iran built a vast underground network of missile infrastructure spread across its territory that has proved impossible for US and Israeli forces to eliminate. The United States struggled significantly to destroy these dispersed production facilities, which Foreign Affairs notes inverted the assumptions that have guided American airpower campaigns since Operation Desert Storm in 1991.
Foreign Affairs provides a scathing critique of the organizational inertia within the US military. The article explains that the most powerful militaries are organized around small numbers of exquisite, expensive, and hard-to-produce platforms like Tomahawk missiles and F-35s. These units are trained to avoid wasting systems, whereas “precise mass” requires units to move quickly and prioritize volume over perfection. Because the US is locked into these legacy structures, it has struggled to adapt. Washington is now finding itself burning through its stockpiles of Tomahawks, SM-6 missiles, and other expensive systems to deal with the damage inflicted by Iran, leaving the US scrambling to resupply its own stocks and those of partners in places like Taiwan and Ukraine.
Regarding the role of technology, Foreign Affairs admits that while the US has utilized artificial intelligence systems to identify and recommend targets—even citing the use of the Maven Smart System—these advantages are not the deciding factor. The journal acknowledges that the current race to artificial general intelligence is not the primary driver of how AI is shaping warfare.
In its concluding remarks, Foreign Affairs issues a stark warning to the American defense establishment. It insists that the country’s reliance on exquisite, expensive, and hard-to-produce weapons is no longer sufficient to win wars or protect allies. The journal stresses that the United States must stop carrying on as if the Cold War just ended. It argues that if the US wants to maintain its military edge, it has no choice but to embrace the reality of “precise mass”—a strategy that Iran has already mastered and demonstrated to the world. Ultimately, Foreign Affairs admits that through indigenous resilience and the successful deployment of cost-effective strike capabilities, Iran has proven that a determined nation can stymie even the most conventionally powerful military in the world.

articles.title: Iran, Russia, China must set up a balanced structure in BRICS
articles.body:
To learn more about the details, Mehr news agency's correspondent has conducted an interview with Dr. Leonid Savin Editor-in-Chief and Managing Director of Katehon, an influential Russian Think Tank.
Let’s review the interview in questions and answers.
Q: Given Russia’s conduct since the outbreak of the US-Israeli war against Iran, how would you assess Moscow’s approach and actions in the political, diplomatic, military, and intelligence spheres? To what extent have these actions been consistent with Tehran’s expectations of a strategic partner?
A: First of all, Russia and Iran signed new special agreement some time ago that bring our partnership into new level of cooperation. On diplomatic international level Russia supports Iran for different spheres of activity – from rejection of foreign interference and imposed sanctions to justification of nuclear program of Iran (and Russia is involved into construction process of Busher plant). Military and intelligence coordination is not open for public. We know about some supplies of Russian technics and equipment like aircrafts and helicopters. And before Iran provided to Russia drone technologies (“Sheheed” model that in Russia got name “Geran” and then developed for reactive strike drone). Western media also blame Russia for providing to Iran data intelligence, cause of space surveillance available for Russian military. But real scale of military/intelligence cooperation is unknown cause of sensitive information and secret issues. Counter-terrorism interaction also was always on high level and this activity
Personally, I think that both countries can and need to do more to enlarge bilateral partnership. To organize defense pact, at least for Caspian region
Q: Some argue that Russia has acted cautiously in response to the war against Iran. Is this caution primarily driven by Russia’s involvement in the war in Ukraine and its concerns about a direct confrontation with the United States, or does Moscow fundamentally seek to avoid becoming involved in a war that could put its own interests at risk?
A: We understand very well, that the collective West interested to destroy Russia by any means. The same strategy used against Iran. China also seems for the West like potential adversary and before there were many attempts to bring domestic problems for the China through different tools of manipulations. Also, Ukrainian conflict by fact is proxy war against Russia led by the West. The most significant role in support of Kiev’s regime and against Russia played by leaders of the UK, USA, France and Germany. BBC team organized fake report about Bucha in 2022 when Russian troops was withdrawal. In general, political elites of the West always tried to deceive Russian leadership and there no any trust anymore.
Also, we understand risk of escalation till nuclear war. And would like to avoid it. But if the West and his proxies will do more provocations against Russia (and they do it in regular way) Moscow will need to do response. From this point of view Russian interests mostly focused on keeping unity and secure periphery as well as technological development and achievement of the full independence (autarky). Of course, another important strategic line is army reorganization to be more effective and use of advanced weapon systems. Defense ministry and corporations linked with military industrial production now care about it. Ukrainian conflict was and still experience for Russian military and security services.
Q: With Trump’s return to office, there was widespread speculation in the media that Russia and Ukraine were moving closer to a ceasefire agreement, but such an agreement ultimately failed to materialize. In your view, what were the main obstacles to a ceasefire between the two sides? Was the dispute over territory and security guarantees the primary issue, or does the disagreement run deeper, involving fundamentally different views about the future of European security and Russia’s relationship with the West?
A: It never was closer. Russia ready to sign peace agreement but only on conditions proposed before – denazification and demilitarization of Ukraine, respect of Russian geopolitical interests and organization of clear security frame. Ukraine cannot be member of NATO. Russian people in Ukraine must be respected and their right respected. As well as about Russian Orthodox Church in Ukraine. Crimea and regions of ex-Ukraine where people voted to be with Russia as its part will stay in Russia and will never return to Ukraine. Actually, from European point of view, it is not violation cause after 1999 when part of Serbia (Kosovo) proclaimed self-independence, it was supported by NATO and the West. So, what we see in Ukraine now is just continuation of the policy once used by the West.
Concerning Russian view on future we are more interested to develop active relationship with Global South. There was term like “Turn to the East”, but really to the South too. And Iran is also part of it.
Q: In light of the war in Ukraine, the US-Israeli war against Iran, and increasing US pressure on China, does Moscow view these developments as separate crises, or does it see them as part of a broader strategic competition between the United States and non-Western powers, as well as an effort to reshape the existing international order?
A: Of course, it is strategic competition effected by emergence of the multipolar world order. West led by the US just would like to keep own hegemony (military, political, economic and also moral). We are wanting more justice international system. This is the reason. If you see on historical perspectives there were the same disturbance during transition from one type of order to another. But now multipolar moment is unique cause the West losing his dominance like never before.
Q: How would you assess Iran’s response and resistance to the US and Israeli attacks? In your view, to what extent has Iran been able to maintain the initiative, withstand military pressure, and influence the calculations of its adversaries during this confrontation?
A: It is very appreciated and Russian public applause to Iran, especially to decision makers for this response. It was very strong and at the same time very smart. To block Hormuz strait was geopolitical nightmare for the US and its allies in region. Both the US and Israel understood own misfortune over Iran. Despite own victims resulted by illegal and criminal strikes of the US and Israel Iran and its people stands firm.
Q: Could the war against Iran become a turning point in the security order of the Middle East? If so, what role does Russia envision for itself in the emerging regional order, and how might Moscow’s relations with Iran, China, and the United States change in the aftermath of the war?
A: For my opinion it is already changed security environment of the region. And neighbor countries already reacted on this change, I mean Mecca pact between Turkey, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia. Iran also projected new lines of control and interests near own borders. We can add allies of Iran in Yemen, but also in Iraq, Lebanon and other countries. Zionists would like to eliminate them all and it is the reason of genocide in Palestine and bombing Lebanon, but in practice it is not possible. Like decades before resistance will be revived because of the mentality and strategic culture.
If speak about relations of great powers there is clear that Russia and China will continue to strengthen cooperation. But the US will have more problems in future. Geopolitical influence of the US in the Middle East will decline. Many partners inside NATO not trust to the Washington anymore. There also tensions because Israeli lobby and part of politicians inside the US not welcome this trend. Let’s see what happens after November elections in the Congress. There are many signs that against Trump growing antipathy in camp of Republicans and Democrats also not happy with his policy.
Realistically there still will be tensions and conflict. To achieve multipolarity we need to create effective structure. Why it is important? Because unipolar world still has it – World bank and IMF in economy, NATO in military, G7 politically. So, Russia, China, Iran, other members of BRICS need to create counter balance, effective and complete.
MNA

articles.title: Russia’s air defenses can’t protect all its strategic sites once Ukraine’s ballistic missiles are ready, expert says
articles.body:
Russia's best defenses against ballistic missiles ring Moscow, leaving much of the rest of the country exposed to Ukraine's growing missile arsenal. That concentration is why Ukraine's homegrown ballistic missiles could cause Russia real trouble beyond the capital, even as Russia's air defenses show gaps elsewhere, expert Vadym Kushnikov says, Ukrainian Radio reports.
Russia has the systems to stop ballistic missiles, Kushnikov continues, but it has massed the best of them around Moscow: the S-500 "Prometey", with interceptors adapted from the A-135, the Soviet-era shield built to defend the capital from missiles.
Other regions, by his assessment, are left more open to Ukraine's massed and combined strikes. That matters now that Ukraine's own ballistic missile, such as the Sapsan, is entering combat.
The best defenses ring Moscow
"If you analyze the characteristics, Russia today has concentrated its most modern S-500 complexes, with 77N6-N and 77N6-N1 interceptors, in Moscow Oblast," Kushnikov says.
Elsewhere, he said, Russia is short of air-defense complexes, the S-400 among them, a shortfall he said is visible in satellite imagery.
Ukraine's ballistic program grows
Ukraine's deep-strike arsenal has been shifting from foreign-supplied systems to homegrown ones. Alongside its Neptune and Flamingo cruise missiles, it now fields the Sapsan, an Iskander-class ballistic missile with a range of about 500 kilometers, which President Volodymyr Zelenskyy confirmed was in combat late last year.
A domestic ballistic missile will let Ukraine strike deep inside Russia without waiting for a Western green light.
Production faces hard hurdles
Building them is the hard part. Ukraine's rocket-engineering tradition runs deep, Kushnikov suggests, but its production sites, mostly in the east, are direct targets of Russian strikes.
The missiles also depend on components that are difficult to make, chiefly solid-fuel rocket engines and the guidance that steers a warhead flying at five times the speed of sound along a ballistic arc.
"The combination of all these factors is exactly what our engineers have worked on for years, building the Ukrainian ballistic shield," he adds.
