articles.title: The global system is entering an age of technological entropy
articles.body:
The global system is entering an age of technological entropy
The “profound changes unseen in a century” often mentioned by Xi Jinping are no longer merely abstract concepts found in books; they represent the systemic collapse and restructuring currently experienced by the global system.
For centuries, the world operated under a singular order – dominated by the West, characterized by linear development and a hegemonic steady state – which established fixed power structures, rules of engagement, and development paradigms. As we enter the second quarter of the 21st century, this long-standing old order has reached a critical juncture marked by runaway entropy, the collapse of paradigms, and a civilizational transition.
This entropic shift of order is essentially a global transitional state where the rules of the old system fail, its structures loosen, and its momentum wanes, while a new system undergoes pluralistic growth and iterative restructuring without yet having fully crystallized. Unlike the traditional restructuring of global patterns seen in historical dynastic changes or great-power rivalries, the core transformation of this ‘once-in-a-century’ shift is driven by the convergence of three forces: the fundamental reshaping of technology, the shifting of geopolitical centers of gravity, and the escalation of strategic competition to higher dimensions. Together, these forces are driving a comprehensive, systemic iteration of global politics, military affairs, economics, public opinion, and governance.
Adopting a holistic perspective, this article systematically deconstructs the core characteristics, underlying operational logic, and certain future evolutionary trends of this global entropic shift. Moving beyond the interpretation of fragmented events, it identifies the fundamental laws and ultimate trajectory of the transformation of the global landscape in this new era.
I. Six core characteristics of the entropic shift of order: The disintegration of the old steady state and the normalization of global pluralistic disorder
Current global geopolitical conflicts, economic fluctuations, technological rivalries, and public opinion polarization are, in essence, concrete manifestations of this entropic shift in order. The steady-state equilibrium established by the traditional Western-centric order has completely disintegrated. The global landscape now exhibits four core characteristics: intensifying headwinds, accelerating fragmentation, the resonance of risks, and the generalization of strategic competition. Uncertainty, asymmetry, and cross-domain transmission have become the new normal of the global landscape.
First, geopolitical power has undergone complete decentralization, and the absolute advantages once held by traditional major powers have fully eroded.
The geopolitical logic that prevailed for a century – where victory was determined by sheer national scale, military force, or resource endowment – has become completely obsolete; technological democratization has emerged as the core variable reshaping regional landscapes.
In the core geopolitical regions of Eurasia and the Middle East, the large-scale deployment of artificial intelligence, autonomous weapons, and intelligent reconnaissance systems has drastically lowered the threshold for war and deterrence, effectively erasing the military ‘generation gap’ that once separated traditional major powers. Europe’s security landscape has moved beyond the US monopoly; France and Germany are pursuing strategic autonomy, while Russia is leveraging intelligent hardware to challenge Western military hegemony, leading to a stratification and fragmentation of regional power. The Middle East has completely shed the old order defined by resource dominance and control by major powers; small and medium-sized states – and even non-state actors like the Houthis – can now exert asymmetric influence and disrupt regional shipping and geopolitics using low-cost intelligent equipment, causing the absolute control once held by major powers to steadily crumble.
Geopolitical power is no longer tethered to territory, troop numbers, or resource volume; instead, it is anchored in technological computing power, intelligent warfare capabilities, and the pace of technological iteration. Global geopolitical rivalry has entered a new phase where small nations can act as counterweights and non-state actors can disrupt the status quo.
Second, strategic deterrence systems have become stratified and diffuse, shifting global security risks from great-power confrontation to a state of uncontrolled volatility across all domains.
The ‘balance of terror’ established by the rigid US-Soviet bipolar nuclear standoff during the Cold War has collapsed, marking a paradigm shift in the global nuclear landscape; nuclear weapons have evolved from an ultimate deterrent for total mutual restraint into leverage for controlling regional dynamics.
Nuclear deterrence is now clearly stratified: Top-tier nuclear powers maintain a strategic last-resort capability while avoiding direct hot wars; mid-tier nuclear states rely on limited arsenals for regional self-preservation; and non-nuclear states seek security under the umbrella of major powers. Nuclear rivalry has become instrumentalized and normalized, serving as a standard tool for major powers to draw red lines and signal strategic intent.
Meanwhile, nuclear risks have become widespread; while the likelihood of direct nuclear confrontation between major powers has declined, risks associated with proliferation, technology leaks, algorithmic miscalculation, and covert regional nuclear maneuvering are rising. Compounded by the deep integration of intelligent weaponry and nuclear technology, global security governance has shifted from a model of great-power checks and balances to a complex challenge of managing risks that are multidimensional, covert, and pervasive across all domains.
Third, the global development landscape is shifting from West to East, and the Western-centric system that has prevailed for five centuries is unraveling.
The most historic transformation in this round of upheaval is the holistic shift of the global geopolitical, economic, and civilizational center of gravity from the Atlantic to the Eurasian landmass and Asia as a whole, fundamentally overturning the underlying structure of Western global dominance that has persisted for five centuries.
Economically, the interconnected development of Asian blocs – including China, ASEAN, India, and the Middle East – is accelerating the formation of a pan-Eurasian economic cycle; the era of Western dominance over global supply chains, trade rules, and economic orders is drawing to a close, while the Global South is gaining a powerful voice in development discourse. Regarding security, the security landscapes of Europe, the Middle East, and the Asia-Pacific are becoming deeply intertwined; the geopolitical value of the continental landmass is making a full comeback, while the reach and control of traditional maritime hegemony continue to wane.
In terms of civilization and governance, Asian concepts of diverse coexistence and mutually beneficial cooperation are countering the Western logic of zero-sum hegemony; the resurgence of diverse civilizations is breaking the Western monopoly on civilization, emerging multilateral mechanisms are gradually replacing traditional Western-led institutions, and the pluralistic nature of global governance is becoming increasingly distinct.
Fourth, the credibility of the hegemonic system has collapsed, and the Western-led global rules-based system has comprehensively failed.
Trump’s transactional ‘America First’ diplomacy served as the critical turning point that broke the back of American-style hegemony, definitively ending the era of absolute US unilateral global control. The foundations of US hegemony – built after World War II upon alliance systems, rule-setting dominance, and the provision of public goods – have been thoroughly dismantled; alliance credibility has been squandered, multilateral systems have eroded, and the globalized order has fractured, transforming the US from an order builder into an order destroyer.
Although the Biden administration briefly attempted remedial measures, these failed to restore US credibility. Global deficits in trust and institutional confidence regarding the US have become entrenched; unilateralism and protectionism run rampant, double standards in traditional international rules have become glaring, and global governance has fallen into a vacuum of entropic change – where old rules have failed but new ones have yet to be established.
Fifth, the dimension of state-level rivalry has undergone a comprehensive escalation, with the battle for perception and public opinion emerging as a core, invisible battlefield.
The proliferation of digital technology has fundamentally restructured the model of great-power competition, shifting the focus of rivalry from traditional physical confrontation to precision-targeted cognitive warfare. Technologies such as 5G, algorithmic recommendation, and big-data profiling have constructed an information ecosystem characterized by pervasive reach, the solidification of echo chambers, and emotional dominance.
Leveraging their long-standing monopoly on discourse, the US and the West continuously export polarizing narratives, manufacture bloc-based confrontations, and fracture social consensus in other nations. The digital era has dismantled the official barriers of traditional diplomacy; ordinary citizens and non-governmental entities have become pivotal nodes in the global strategic game, with public sentiment and perception directly influencing geopolitical dynamics and diplomatic decisions. Public opinion manipulation and the shaping of perceptions achieve the strategic goal of subduing the enemy without fighting, while cognitive polarization and public opinion divides have become major drivers of disorder in the global order.
Sixth, the key actors in the global economy and governance are undergoing a comprehensive transformation, completely shattering traditional monopolistic patterns.
In the economic sphere, the traditional globalization model – which prioritized efficiency above all – has become obsolete. Geopolitical conflicts, technological blockades, and investment barriers are forcing the global economy to shift toward a development logic that prioritizes resilience and regional self-containment; regional integration is replacing global integration as a core mechanism for hedging against risk, while emerging markets and the Global South have become key stabilizers of the global economy.
In the realm of governance, the effectiveness of traditional Western-dominated institutions – such as the UN, IMF, and World Bank – is steadily declining, whereas emerging multilateral platforms like the SCO, BRICS, and G20 are rising rapidly. Global conflict resolution models are shifting from Western-led coercive intervention to diverse, consultative, and cooperative governance. Simultaneously, the global influence of non-governmental forces and industry elites continues to grow, shifting the landscape of global governance actors from one dominated solely by sovereign states to a new pattern of coexistence among governments, international institutions, and non-governmental entities.
II. Four new operational logics of order reconstruction: A new-era strategic paradigm breaking free from Western conventions
The entropic shift in the global order signifies far more than mere turbulence; it represents a fundamental and disruptive transformation of the underlying logic governing global operations. Current global competition, cooperation, and conflict can no longer be explained by the outdated Western realist paradigms of hegemony through strength, zero-sum games, and victory through force.
A new operational logic – tailored to a multipolar, digital, and regionalized world – has taken shape, fundamentally rewriting the underlying rules governing the rise of major powers, regional development, and global governance.
First, the logic of core national power: A shift from dominance through sheer scale to victory through technology and resilience.
Traditional international competition was a contest of sheer scale – territorial size, military tonnage, and aggregate economic output – whereby major powers could leverage their massive size to establish hegemonic monopolies and exert unilateral dominance. In the current era of shifting order and entropy, however, the primary benchmarks for a nation’s core competitiveness have become technological computing power, the capacity for intelligent iteration, supply chain resilience, and the ability to withstand risks.
Intelligent weaponry is reshaping the military balance of power; digital technology governs the discourse on public opinion and perception; autonomous industrial chains hedge against the risks of geopolitical sanctions; and regional closed-loop economic systems buffer against global volatility. Small and medium-sized nations can achieve asymmetric checks and balances through breakthroughs in specific technologies. Conversely, without technological innovation and systemic resilience, a major power’s sheer size risks becoming an inefficient burden – a reality that fundamentally shatters the Western historical logic equating size with hegemony.
Secondly, the logic of great power rise: shifting from hegemonic succession to rule reshaping.
Centuries of Western historical narrative have entrenched a realist paradigm – that rising implies conflict, growing strength implies a bid for dominance, and hegemony inevitably changes hands. Indeed, all Western international relations theories are essentially distillations of the history of European colonial rivalry. Yet, the current restructuring of the global landscape has completely transcended the old trap of hegemonic cycles.
The rise of emerging powers – exemplified by China – eschews military expansion, the pursuit of hegemonic status, and bloc-based confrontation; instead, it achieves developmental breakthroughs through civilizational mutual learning, regional synergy, and mutually beneficial cooperation. At its peak, the Tang Dynasty accounted for 80% of Asia’s GDP, and Zheng He’s fleet was ten times the size of Columbus’; despite possessing such overwhelming strength, China never followed the Western path of colonial conquest or regional monopoly. This proves that strength does not equate to hegemony, nor does rising equate to conflict; an Eastern logic of symbiosis is replacing the Western logic of dominance-seeking, establishing a brand-new paradigm for the rise of great powers.
Thirdly, the logic of security and stability: shifting from external balancing to autonomous resilience.
Since the Cold War, global security has maintained a precarious equilibrium based on great-power standoffs, alliance entanglements, and the balancing of forces. Control over the security agenda rested in the hands of a few Western powers, leaving most nations with no choice but to attach themselves to the strong and passively seek to avoid risk. In this era of entropic shifts in the global order, security risks have become diffuse and unpredictable, and the stability provided by external checks and balances has completely collapsed; consequently, autonomy and controllability, diversified hedging strategies, and systemic resilience have become the core pillars of security.
Militarily, nations are building autonomous defense systems powered by intelligent technologies; economically, they are establishing regional closed-loop industrial chains to mitigate the risks of decoupling; financially, they are promoting local currency settlements to hedge against the weaponization of the US dollar; and in the realm of public opinion, they are constructing independent discourse systems to break cognitive monopolies. Nations are moving away from reliance on the protection of major powers, instead seizing the initiative in their own security and development by leveraging systemic resilience and regional cooperation.
Fourth, the logic of global governance is shifting from Western monopoly to pluralistic, shared governance.
Traditional global governance was a game dominated by a handful of Western developed nations – where rules were set, standards defined, and benefits monopolized by the West, leaving developing countries to merely accept and adapt passively. The entropic shift in the global order has shattered this monopoly; the collective rise of the Global South and the growing influence of emerging multilateral mechanisms have led to a comprehensive diversification of governance actors, rules, and philosophies.
The core of governance has shifted from the strong controlling the weak to equal consultation among diverse actors; rules have evolved from self-serving Western unilateral standards into win-win principles that prioritize fairness and broad-based benefits; and the logic of development has moved beyond zero-sum plunder toward inclusive coexistence and mutual learning, marking the true entry of global governance into a new era of multilateralism.
III. Future trajectory of global order entropy change: Multipolar consolidation, resilient symbiosis, and the restoration of civilizational roles
While the current entropy change in the global order appears chaotic and fraught with risk, it is by no means random turbulence or internal attrition; rather, it represents the inevitable growing pains accompanying the demise of the old order and the birth of the new. By grounding our analysis in the fundamental logic of this transformation, we can clearly foresee the major trends of global evolution over the coming decades. Three certain trends will dominate the global landscape during the second quarter of the 21st century, effectively ending the old era of Western-centric hegemony.
First, the global landscape will shift decisively from unipolar volatility to a multipolar steady state, with hegemonic influence undergoing a continuous and irreversible decline.
The era of absolute US hegemony has definitively ended. While American hegemony will not collapse overnight, it will continue to contract and decline in relative terms, shifting from a position of global dominance to that of a regional player. The global balance of power will continue to equalize; Asia’s status as a geopolitical center will be further consolidated, and the integration of the Eurasian landmass will steadily advance.
Deep interconnectedness among Asian blocs – including China, ASEAN, India, and the Middle East – will forge a cluster of emerging powers capable of acting as a counterweight to the Western system. Old models of bloc confrontation and zero-sum games will gradually fade, giving way to a mainstream global political landscape defined by great-power competition and cooperation, diversified checks and balances, and regional autonomy. Multipolarity will evolve from a mere trend into a solidified, stable global order.
Second, global development will shift decisively from efficiency-first to resilience-first, leading to the full formation of regional symbiotic systems.
Globalization will not disappear, but it will undergo a fundamental transformation and upgrade. The old model of globalization – characterized by extensive growth, homogenization, and Western dominance – is ending, while a new model defined by precision, regionalization, and diversification is rising. Nations will continue to diversify, localize, and autonomize their industrial and supply chains, prioritizing security and stability.
Regional economic synergy and closed-loop systems will serve as the core pillars for hedging against geopolitical conflicts, trade protectionism, and technological blockades. Emerging regional mechanisms – such as RCEP, SCO economic cooperation, and BRICS cooperation – will continue to enhance quality and efficiency, building regional development systems that are mutually beneficial and independent of the West. The global economy will break free from the constraints of singular Western rules, establishing a new development landscape characterized by diverse, parallel paths and resilient symbiosis.
Third, global competition is shifting profoundly from physical confrontation to a contest of rules and civilizations, marking a comprehensive resurgence of Eastern civilizational values.
The core of future great-power competition will no longer lie in military might, territorial disputes, or resource plundering, but in the ultimate contest over technological standards, governance norms, civilizational paradigms, and cognitive narratives. The flaws of the Western civilizational logic – characterized by zero-sum games, hegemony, and confrontation – have become glaringly apparent, rendering it ill-suited to the development needs of a diverse world.
In contrast, the Asia-Pacific region’s enduring civilizational ethos – rooted in mutual learning, symbiosis, harmony amid diversity, and win-win cooperation – will serve as the core foundation for reshaping the global civilizational order. From the millennia-old legacies of Xuanzang’s translation work, Yang Liangyao’s diplomatic voyages, and Zheng He’s friendly expeditions, to the vibrant contemporary practices of mutual learning and people-to-people connectivity across the Asia-Pacific, this Eastern civilization of symbiosis will continue to counter Western narratives of conflict and rewrite the fundamental rules of global civilizational competition.
Fourth, global governance is transitioning from elite monopoly to broad-based participation, with fairness and inclusivity becoming the prevailing trends of the era.
Future global governance will thoroughly dismantle the monopoly held by a handful of Western nations and elites; the Global South will see a sustained rise in its voice and influence, emerging multilateral mechanisms will become the primary vehicles for governance, and the participation of non-governmental actors and civil society will deepen.
Global public issues – such as nuclear arms control, artificial intelligence, climate governance, and public health – will break free from the constraints of geopolitical maneuvering and bloc-based confrontation, returning to the essence of multilateral consultation and win-win cooperation. Global governance will cease to be a tool for the powerful and instead become a platform for the shared development of all humanity, with fairness, inclusivity, and mutual benefit defining the new era of global governance.
Embracing the right path of Eastern symbiosis amid order reconstruction
Viewed from a macro perspective, the essence of this once-in-a-century transformation is a process – spanning centuries – of correcting the order, restoring the civilizational balance, and reshaping the global landscape. The entropic shift in the global order represents both the entropic decay and demise of the old Western hegemonic order and the entropic reduction and rebirth of a new, diverse global order.
All geopolitical conflicts, technological rivalries, economic fluctuations, and public opinion rifts are the inevitable growing pains accompanying the transition from the old order to the new. Centuries of Western history have taught the world only about hegemonic rivalry among the strong, whereas the Asia-Pacific region – with its millennia-old cultural heritage and the practical experience of emerging powers in the new era – is teaching the world how the strong can build bridges.
Future global competition is by no means a zero-sum game of hegemonic succession; rather, it is a contest of values regarding paths, civilizations, and rules. The old era defined by unilateralism, bloc confrontation, and zero-sum games has come to an end, while a new era characterized by multilateralism, openness, inclusiveness, and mutually beneficial symbiosis is rapidly unfolding.
Standing at the historical juncture of the second quarter of the 21st century, humanity will ultimately break free from the confines of the Western-dominated order and the traps of realist power struggles. By solidifying the foundations of development through technological innovation, fostering symbiotic strength through regional synergy, and resolving differences through mutual learning among civilizations, we will build a new global order that is fairer, more stable, more resilient, and more prosperous – thereby ushering in a new stage of civilization defined by diverse coexistence and sustainable development.

articles.title: Ukraine strikes Russian defense plant producing missile components, General Staff says
articles.body:
Russian Defence Ministry officials show off the Russia's 9M729 cruise missile at the military Patriot Park outside Moscow on January 23, 2019. (Vasily Maximov/AFP via Getty Images)
Ukrainian forces struck the Azov Optical-Mechanical Plant in Russia’s Rostov Oblast overnight on Sept. 26, Ukraine’s General Staff said.
A fire broke out at the plant’s foundry, while equipment in five production buildings was damaged, according to the military. The extent of the damage could not be immediately verified.
The plant, located in the city of Azov, is part of Russia’s Tactical Missiles Corporation and produces opto-mechanical and optoelectronic equipment, electronics for artillery, missile and anti-tank weapons, as well as radar homing systems for guided missiles. Ukraine’s military intelligence also lists the facility as part of Russia’s defense-industrial complex.
The General Staff said the plant produces equipment used by the Russian military and described the strike as an effort to reduce Russia’s military-industrial capabilities.
The strike on the Azov plant followed a separate Ukrainian attack on Russia’s Ilsky oil refinery in Krasnodar Krai overnight. Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces said the refinery, located about 400 kilometers (250 miles) from the drone launch area, was targeted by the 1st Separate Center of the Unmanned Systems Forces, the 414th Unmanned Systems Brigade, known as "Madyar’s Birds," and other Ukrainian units.
Ukrainian defense company Fire Point said the refinery was hit by FP-1 drones and subsequently halted operations. According to the company, three primary oil-processing units and a tank farm were damaged in the strike.
Olena Goncharova is the Special Correspondent for the Kyiv Independent, where she has previously worked as a development manager and Canadian correspondent. She first joined the Kyiv Post, Ukraine's oldest English-language newspaper, as a staff writer in January 2012 and became the newspaper’s Canadian correspondent in June 2018. She is based in Edmonton, Alberta. Olena has a master’s degree in publishing and editing from the Institute of Journalism in Taras Shevchenko National University in Kyiv. Olena was a 2016 Alfred Friendly Press Partners fellow who worked for the Pittsburgh Post-Gazette for six months. The program is administered by the University of Missouri School of Journalism in Columbia.

The arson attack took place in Munich on Sept. 3, when several incendiary devices were thrown from a passing car onto a construction site near the headquarters of Rohde & Schwarz and Helsing.

articles.title: Araghchi outlines Iran’s diplomatic conditions, and regional priorities at NY
articles.body:
Araghchi outlines Iran’s diplomatic conditions, and regional priorities at NY
TEHRAN— Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has used a series of meetings, diplomatic engagements and media appearances on the sidelines of the 81st United Nations General Assembly to lay out Tehran’s positions on negotiations with Washington, the Strait of Hormuz, Iran’s nuclear program, regional security, sanctions and the future of multilateral cooperation.
Across his remarks, Araghchi presented diplomacy as Iran’s preferred avenue for resolving disputes, while insisting that negotiations must be conducted on the basis of sovereign equality, international law and reciprocal commitments rather than military pressure or coercion.
His comments also linked the security of the Strait of Hormuz to the wider regional situation, while outlining a specific seven-day mechanism for restoring normal maritime traffic if the United States accepts Tehran's conditions previously conveyed to Washington.
Diplomacy remains open, but Iran rejects coercion
Speaking to reporters outside the UN Security Council, Araghchi said Iran remained committed to international law, the UN Charter and diplomacy, pointing to the negotiations that led to the 2015 nuclear agreement and Iran’s subsequent diplomatic efforts.
He said Tehran had repeatedly kept the door to negotiations open over the past two years, but argued that Washington had responded in bad faith and repeatedly chosen military action and pressure over diplomacy.
According to Araghchi, this history has created deep distrust in Tehran over the prospect of simply returning to negotiations without credible guarantees against a repetition of military action.
He said Iran would not accept threats, intimidation or pressure as a substitute for diplomacy.
“The UN Charter is not optional. Sovereignty is not conditional. Diplomacy does not mean surrender. And peace cannot be built through threats of destruction,” Araghchi said.
Iran sets out seven-day framework for reopening Hormuz
The Strait of Hormuz emerged as one of the central issues in Araghchi’s discussions in New York.
The foreign minister said Iran had conveyed, through Qatar, a specific seven-day plan to the United States. Under the proposal, he said, the process of restoring normal maritime traffic could be completed within seven days if Washington accepted the necessary conditions.
Araghchi subsequently provided additional details, saying the seven-day period would begin immediately once the United States accepted the plan.
He said the technical implementation could be completed within four or five days, allowing the strait to reopen on the sixth day, followed by US entry into a final agreement on the seventh day.
The measures required from Washington, he said, had already been communicated to the United States and were incorporated into the Islamabad memorandum of understanding.
“If there is sufficient seriousness on the American side, this will happen, and the Strait of Hormuz will reopen,” Araghchi said.
He stressed that Iran’s proposal should be understood within the framework of reciprocal commitments rather than as a unilateral concession.
Islamabad memorandum and the Oman track
Araghchi said that following mediation efforts by Pakistan and Qatar, Iran and the United States signed the Islamabad memorandum on June 17.
Under Article 5 of the memorandum, Iran committed to making the necessary arrangements to facilitate the safe passage of ships.
Iran, he said, immediately began technical discussions with Oman to implement that commitment and restore maritime traffic to pre-war levels.
According to Araghchi, maritime traffic reached approximately 60 percent of its pre-war level within two weeks of implementation.
He said subsequent unilateral US measures and military action halted the implementation of the memorandum, arguing that Washington had chosen military action instead of using the dispute-resolution mechanism contained in the agreement.
Iran, he emphasized, had nevertheless continued to keep diplomatic channels open.
Tehran links Hormuz security to regional stability
Araghchi reaffirmed Iran’s commitment to safe and secure shipping, but rejected the idea that maritime security could be restored through additional military deployments, threats, blockades or economic pressure.
He said the Strait of Hormuz had remained open until February 28, 2026, and argued that the subsequent disruption of maritime traffic was, from Tehran’s perspective, a consequence of the conflict and military actions against Iran.
“A country cannot be bombed, threatened with destruction, subjected to a naval blockade and coercive measures, and at the same time be expected to automatically restore security and shipping to normal,” he said.
Araghchi also criticized the role of certain regional states, arguing that some had allowed their territory, military bases, airspace, logistical infrastructure or intelligence facilities to be used in connection with military operations against Iran.
In his meetings with regional counterparts, however, he emphasized Iran’s preference for regional security mechanisms based on cooperation among neighboring states.
Iran and Saudi Arabia: Focus on regional security cooperation
In a meeting with Saudi Foreign Minister Faisal bin Farhan, Araghchi emphasized Tehran’s determination to strengthen mutual trust and promote regional security through cooperation among countries in the region.
He briefed his Saudi counterpart on the understanding reached between Iran and Oman regarding safe maritime routes through the Strait of Hormuz.
The two ministers also discussed bilateral relations and ways of expanding cooperation in areas of mutual interest.
Araghchi called for greater participation by influential regional states in security arrangements, while referring to the experience of the past seven months and the use of the territory and facilities of some regional countries in military operations against Iran.
The meeting underscored Tehran’s emphasis on the principle that regional security should be addressed collectively by regional states.
Iran briefs India on Hormuz and diplomatic efforts
Araghchi also held talks with Indian Foreign Minister Subrahmanyam Jaishankar in New York, discussing bilateral relations, regional developments and international issues.
The Iranian foreign minister briefed his Indian counterpart on Iran’s talks with Oman over establishing safe maritime routes through the Strait of Hormuz.
He also outlined Tehran’s position regarding US violations of previous commitments and military actions against Iran, including a maritime blockade and attacks on Iranian commercial shipping.
Araghchi said the international community had a responsibility to hold those responsible for aggression accountable.
The two ministers also discussed efforts by mediators to convey the conditions and essential elements required for a return to the diplomatic process.
They agreed on the importance of using available diplomatic capacities to prevent further escalation and discussed implementation of existing bilateral economic and trade understandings.
Tehran calls for greater Iran-Arab dialogue
In a separate meeting with Arab League Secretary General Nabil Fahmy, Araghchi called for increased dialogue and interaction between Iran and Arab countries.
He described regional security as an integrated and indivisible issue requiring shared responsibility and constructive engagement.
The two sides discussed regional developments, particularly the situation in Palestine and the escalation of Israeli military actions in Palestine and Lebanon.
Araghchi said stronger interaction among regional countries could help address misunderstandings and concerns that Tehran attributes, in part, to hostile propaganda.
He emphasized Iran’s determination to strengthen mutual trust with neighboring states and called for greater regional cooperation.
Iran defends its nuclear program and NPT commitments
Iran’s nuclear program was another major element of Araghchi’s diplomatic message in New York.
He rejected recent allegations concerning Iran’s nuclear activities as political rather than technical or legal in nature.
Araghchi described claims that Iran was on the verge of acquiring nuclear weapons as false, saying such allegations had been repeatedly raised by Israel and subsequently echoed by the United States and European countries.
He stressed that Iran has been a party to the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty since 1970 and has been subject to extensive International Atomic Energy Agency monitoring for decades.
From Tehran’s perspective, Araghchi argued, it is contradictory for Washington to claim to support the international nonproliferation regime while targeting peaceful nuclear facilities operating under IAEA safeguards.
He characterized attacks on such facilities as inconsistent with international obligations and argued that technical and legal mechanisms, rather than military action, should determine the future of nuclear verification.
Iran accuses US of economic pressure and “economic terrorism”
Araghchi also devoted significant attention to the impact of unilateral sanctions on Iran.
He accused Washington of using economic deprivation as an instrument of political pressure and said sanctions had affected access to trade, financial resources, medicines, technology, education and scientific cooperation.
In his address to the Global Development Initiative, he argued that the consequences of such measures extend beyond governments and directly affect ordinary people.
He described the humanitarian consequences of sanctions as “economic terrorism” and called on the United Nations to oppose unilateral coercive measures and demand their complete and unconditional removal.
He also linked the sanctions issue to the broader question of sustainable development, arguing that developing countries require greater access to finance, technology, knowledge and international cooperation rather than additional economic restrictions.
Development, South-South cooperation and multilateralism
At the fifth anniversary meeting of the Global Development Initiative, Araghchi placed development at the center of Iran’s broader foreign-policy agenda.
He said developing countries continue to confront poverty, hunger, inequality, debt burdens, financing shortages, technology gaps and environmental challenges. These pressures have been exacerbated by conflicts, protectionism, unilateral coercive measures and the use of force.
Araghchi welcomed the initiative launched by Chinese President Xi Jinping in 2021 and highlighted its work in poverty reduction, food security, development financing, green development, industrialization and the digital economy.
Iran, he said, attaches particular importance to the initiative’s potential to strengthen South-South cooperation by mobilizing the knowledge, technology and capabilities of developing countries.
He called for international solidarity to be translated into concrete development outcomes and said the voices of developing countries should have a greater role in global development governance.
ECO as a platform for regional integration
Araghchi also addressed the 27th Informal Meeting of the Economic Cooperation Organization Council of Ministers in New York, calling for stronger regional cooperation and solidarity among ECO member states.
He said ECO could play a greater role in promoting peace, stability, connectivity and sustainable development.
The foreign minister highlighted recent progress within the organization, including the resumption of ministerial meetings, the five-year roadmap for mining cooperation, the ten-year strategy for sustainable and resilient transport, and efforts to amend the ECOTA trade agreement.
He also pointed to expanding transport corridors and links with major cargo and logistics hubs, including routes connected to China, as an important factor in strengthening the region’s role in international trade and transit.
Tourism, intra-regional trade, energy, agriculture, industry, human resources and environmental cooperation, he said, should remain among ECO’s key priorities.
Iran is scheduled to host the 18th ECO Summit in Tehran on December 3–4, 2026.
Iran’s account of the conflict and civilian impact
Across his statements in New York, Araghchi repeatedly referred to US and Israeli aggression against the country.
He said thousands of Iranians had been killed, including women and children, and accused the United States and Israel of targeting civilian and critical infrastructure.
Among the examples cited by the foreign minister were the killing of 168 students and teachers at a school in Minab, an attack on the Lamerd sports complex, damage to the Pasteur Institute of Iran and attacks on residential areas and other civilian facilities.
Araghchi argued that these incidents should be investigated within the framework of international law and that accountability should apply regardless of political alliances.
He also criticized efforts to portray the conflict in a manner that reverses the positions of victim and aggressor.
 
  
A consistent message from NY
Taken together, Araghchi’s meetings and public statements in New York presented several interconnected themes in Iran’s foreign-policy position.
At the diplomatic level, Tehran says it remains open to negotiations but wants guarantees against a recurrence of military action and insists that diplomacy cannot take place under coercion.
On the nuclear issue, Iran continues to emphasize its NPT membership, cooperation with international monitoring mechanisms and opposition to military action against nuclear facilities.
On the Strait of Hormuz, Tehran has presented a concrete seven-day framework for restoring maritime traffic, linking implementation to conditions already communicated to Washington and incorporated into the Islamabad memorandum.
At the regional level, Iran is calling for security arrangements based on dialogue and cooperation among neighboring countries, while seeking closer engagement with Saudi Arabia, India, Arab states and other regional partners.
And at the global level, Araghchi has called for stronger multilateralism, sovereign equality, South-South cooperation and an international development agenda free from unilateral coercive measures.
The common thread running through his remarks was that Iran considers diplomacy and international law essential to resolving disputes, but rejects attempts to use military, economic or political pressure to dictate the terms of that diplomacy.

articles.title: Russia, Ukraine trade deadly strikes as 7 people are killed
articles.body:
Seven people were killed in Russian and Ukrainian strikes Saturday, including four in Ukraine and three in Russia's southern Krasnodar region, local officials said, as Moscow and Kyiv continued a surge in long-range drone and missile attacks.
Russia has intensified its aerial campaign against Ukraine, deploying cruise and ballistic missiles, glide bombs and jet-powered drones as fighting along the front line has slowed more than four years after Moscow launched its full-scale invasion.
Two women were killed after a Russian strike destroyed a home in Zaporizhzhia, trapping them beneath the rubble, according to the regional military administration. A separate Russian attack on the city of Sumy killed two people, local officials said.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Saturday that Russia was escalating its attacks and urged Kyiv's international partners to respond with stronger measures.
"It is essential that our partners not forget: Russia is escalating every single day," Zelenskyy wrote Saturday. "If the Russians have chosen to make their strikes even more brutal, the world must choose stronger responses to keep the war from spreading further."
Zelenskyy said residential areas in Kyiv and Zaporizhzhia, as well as parts of the Odesa, Sumy and Kharkiv regions, had come under attack.
Ukraine's Air Force said its air defenses shot down 134 of 173 Russian drones launched overnight. The claim could not be independently verified.
In Kyiv, officials reported damage across several districts after Russian drones struck overnight. A drone hit an area between a five-story residential building and a commercial property in the Solomianskyi district, damaging an office building, according to the Kyiv City Military Administration.
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said five people were injured and that emergency crews were carrying out search and rescue operations. Fires were also reported near warehouses in the Darnytskyi district and at a store after a drone fell inside a shopping center in the Sviatoshynskyi district.
Two people were injured in the wider Kyiv region after a Russian drone attack caused a fire at a warehouse in the Boryspil district, Ukraine's State Emergency Service said.
In Odesa region, Gov. Oleh Kiper described the overnight assault as a "massive" attack on civilian infrastructure. More than 10 private and apartment buildings were damaged, along with a hotel and restaurant complex and administrative buildings at a business facility, he said.
Russia's Defense Ministry said its strikes in Kyiv damaged a data center that it claimed supported mobile internet services and Starlink satellite communications used by Ukraine's armed forces. The claim could not be independently verified.
Moscow also said its forces struck a port facility, road bridge and logistics center in the Odesa region and a dry-cargo vessel in the Black Sea that it alleged was carrying military supplies.
Ukraine, meanwhile, has continued using long-range drones to target Russian oil and industrial infrastructure, seeking to disrupt revenue streams and supplies that support Moscow's war effort.
A Ukrainian drone attack in Russia's southern Krasnodar region killed three people and injured two others, regional officials said.
Gov. Veniamin Kondratyev said the attack damaged a residential building and sparked fires at two industrial facilities in the Seversky district.
The regional emergency headquarters later said the fires had been extinguished and that about 26,000 residents were without electricity.
Ukraine's General Staff said its forces had targeted the Ilsky oil refinery in the Seversky district. Russian officials did not confirm the facility had been hit, and the claim could not be independently verified.
In neighboring Rostov region, Gov. Yury Slyusar said five people were injured in overnight Ukrainian drone attacks, including a child. He said drones struck residential buildings in Taganrog and Azov and that air defenses had downed more than 30 drones over several parts of the region.
Falling drone debris damaged apartment buildings, private homes, industrial facilities, a school, a cultural center and vehicles in Azov, according to Slyusar.
Russia's Defense Ministry separately claimed that its air defenses had destroyed 645 Ukrainian drones over 13 regions, as well as over the Black Sea, the Sea of Azov and Crimea. The figure could not be independently verified.
The latest attacks underscore the continuing expansion of the war's aerial dimension, with both sides increasingly relying on long-range drones to strike targets far from the front lines.
Ukraine has sought tougher sanctions against Moscow and restrictions on trade that it says could reduce Russia's ability to finance the war. Zelenskyy renewed that appeal after the latest strikes, calling on U.S. President Donald Trump to implement additional measures against Russia and urging European leaders to impose further sanctions.
Despite repeated diplomatic efforts, there has been no confirmed breakthrough toward ending the war. Both Moscow and Kyiv deny deliberately targeting civilians and say their attacks are directed at military targets or infrastructure connected to military operations.
Independent verification of battlefield and casualty claims remains difficult because of the ongoing fighting.

articles.title: Iran will make no nuclear concessions, Iranian official says
articles.body:
Iran will show no flexibility over its nuclear program even if the United States accepts its proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, which calls for steps including the lifting of a US naval blockade on Iranian ports, a senior Iranian official told Reuters on Friday.
The official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said the waterway would remain closed until the United States meets “all of Iran’s conditions.”
According to a US official later on Friday, the United States is having positive, constructive discussions with Iran through mediators and continues to discuss nuclear issues.
Under Iran’s proposal, Tehran has offered to reopen the strategically vital Strait of Hormuz. Within seven days, hostilities would end on all fronts, including Lebanon; the United States would lift its blockade on Iranian ports, release Iran’s frozen funds, and waive its oil sanctions, Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Thursday.
Araghchi reiterated to reporters at the UN on Friday that the “choice rests with the US” to accept and implement Iran’s proposed seven-day plan. The conditions outlined in the plan are not new, he said, as they were already included in the June MoU. He added that the Strait of Hormuz would not reopen until the plan’s conditions were fulfilled. “Iran will not surrender its sovereign rights under pressure,” Araghchi said.
The proposal follows a sharp escalation in Middle East tensions after seven months of war between Iran and the United States, with Iran-backed Houthi militias in Yemen launching missiles and drones at Saudi Arabia.
The strait has become the central bargaining chip in efforts to end the US-Iran conflict, with Iran seeking relief from the US blockade that is choking its economy and Washington seeking free passage for ships on the global oil supply route now blocked by Tehran.
Pezeshkian hopes a deal with Washington can be reached before US midterms
In a meeting with journalists on Thursday on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said he hoped a deal with Washington to end the hostilities could be reached before the US midterm elections on November 3.
Tehran said it would be prepared to engage in detailed negotiations over its nuclear program only after its conditions are met by the US.
But the official said Iran would give no concessions over its rights, including enriching uranium or shipping its highly enriched uranium out of the country, one of the main US demands.
Israel, the United States and other Western states have long accused Iran of seeking nuclear weapons, including pointing to its move to enrich uranium to 60%, far higher than needed for civilian uses and closer to the 90% needed for a weapon. Iran denies seeking nuclear weapons.
The International Atomic Energy Agency estimates that Iran had 440.9 kg of uranium enriched to 60% when Israel and the US attacked Iranian nuclear facilities in June 2025. How much of that has survived is unclear.
Iranian authorities have said that Iran could agree to dilute its most highly enriched uranium.
In May, Reuters reported that Iran's Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei has issued a directive that the country's HEU should not be sent abroad, according to two senior Iranian sources.

articles.title: U.S. Navy’s new sub-launched warhead enters development
articles.body:
- The U.S. Navy's W93 warhead and Mk7 reentry body entered engineering and manufacturing development after passing Milestone B this year.
- It is the first new U.S. nuclear warhead and reentry system program started in nearly four decades.
The U.S. Navy’s new submarine-launched nuclear warhead, the W93, has moved into full-scale development, the first U.S. nuclear warhead and reentry body program started in nearly 40 years.
The Navy’s Strategic Systems Programs office said the W93 and its Mk7 reentry body, the cone-shaped shell that carries the warhead back through the atmosphere to its target, passed Milestone B this year and have entered engineering and manufacturing development. In this phase, engineers finish the production design and prove the weapon can be built in the numbers the Navy needs. The office did not say when the milestone was reached or give a date for first production.
“W93/Mk7 will provide flexibility and adaptability to meet future Warfighter needs and ensure an uninterrupted at sea deterrent for the sea-based leg of the nuclear triad,” said Vice Adm. Douglas Williams, director of Strategic Systems Programs. “We were able to accelerate our entry into this next phase because of the dedicated partnership between PAE SSP, National Nuclear Security Administration, and our industry base. This is what working at hyper-speed looks like.”
The Navy runs the program with the National Nuclear Security Administration, the Department of Energy agency that designs and builds U.S. nuclear warheads, and its national laboratories. Los Alamos National Laboratory in New Mexico is designing the warhead.
“Credible deterrence demands that we move with urgency, and the progress we’re making on W93/Mk7 demonstrates exactly that,” said Brandon Williams, administrator of the National Nuclear Security Administration.
The W93 will arm the Trident II D5 ballistic missiles carried by U.S. Navy ballistic missile submarines, the part of the U.S. nuclear force that stays hidden at sea. Those missiles now carry two warheads: the W76, in service since 1978, and the W88, which entered the stockpile in 1988. The W76 rides in the Mk4 reentry body and the W88 in the Mk5.
Los Alamos said the W93 design uses nuclear components that were tested before the United States stopped explosive nuclear testing, updated with modern materials. The lab said the warhead is expected to go aboard Ohio-class submarines, likely starting in the mid-2030s, and later move to the new Columbia-class submarines as they replace the Ohio class.
The program completed its feasibility and design options phase in March 2025, according to Los Alamos, producing draft military requirements and a description of the conditions the weapon must survive from storage to detonation.
Britain is tied to the program through the Mk7. The United Kingdom will use the same reentry body for its own new warhead, the A21, known as Astraea. The British Ministry of Defence says Astraea is a sovereign design developed in parallel with the W93 and will arm the Royal Navy’s future Dreadnought-class submarines.
Strategic Systems Programs also maintains the Trident missile system on the Ohio-class boats and is integrating a life-extended version of the D5 on the Columbia class. The office is developing a follow-on missile, the D5LE2, as well as a nuclear-armed sea-launched cruise missile known as SLCM-N and the non-nuclear Conventional Prompt Strike hypersonic weapon.

articles.title: Russia accuses Europe of 'thwarting' Ukraine peace talks
articles.body:
Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov has accused European countries of doing “everything they can to thwart” prospects for peace talks between Russia and Ukraine during an address to the UN General Assembly in New York.
Lavrov accused the West of “pumping” Ukraine with weapons and helping Kiev target civilians and civilian infrastructure with drones and missiles.
“The West aspires to inflict a strategic defeat on Russia, but these aspirations will result in the warmongers being led into a strategic dead end,” he said on Saturday.
Lavrov said that Moscow would achieve its military aims in Ukraine "no matter" the circumstances.
"The aims of the special military operation will be achieved, the threat to Russian security will be eliminated, and peaceful life will come back. This will happen no matter the circumstances," he said.
Middle East
Turning to the Middle East, Lavrov said Russia was convinced it was time to resolve the “main issue” in the region by ensuring Palestinian statehood based on “countless” UN decisions.
He said that Moscow is ready to help stabilise the situation in the Strait of Hormuz and the wider Gulf region, as the US-Iran conflict drags on.
"We need trust in the relationships between the Gulf states, the Arab states, and Iran. We need stable regional architecture," Lavrov told leaders at the UN General Assembly.
"Russia, together with other responsible states, stands ready to constructively contribute to stabilising this strategically important region."
He called the killing of Iran’s late Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei in US-Israeli attacks "unacceptable".
Latin America
He also urged the US to immediately release former Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro and his wife.
Lavrov called on the United States to lift the 'siege' of Cuba and restrictions on trade with the largest island in the Caribbean.
Speaking at the United Nations General Assembly, Lavrov also said the US should strike Cuba off the list of state sponsors of terrorism.
On artificial intelligence, Lavrov said Moscow supports China’s initiative to establish a global organisation for cooperation on AI.
Lavrov-Wadephul meeting
Earlier, Lavrov met with his German counterpart Johann Wadephul, the first such meeting since the Russia-Ukraine war began in February 2022.
According to the Russian foreign ministry, the top diplomats discussed bilateral relations and “the situation surrounding Ukraine” during talks on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly.
The ministry stressed that Wadephul “reaffirmed the position of the German government that has been publicly stated on numerous occasions.”
Russia said that the meeting was requested by German officials.

articles.title: China rejects 'Cold War' mentality; Germany's FM Wadephul meets Russian counterpart Lavrov. Follow DW's UN General Assembly updates.
articles.body:
Germany's FM Wadephul meets Lavrov on UNGA sidelines
Published September 22, 2026last updated September 26, 2026
What you need to know
- German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul meets Russian counterpart Sergey Lavrov on sidelines of the UN General Assembly debate
- Wadephul addressed the UN later on Saturday and urged regulation on AI
- India urges deescalation in regards to Strait of Hormuz and Red Sea crises
- Chinese VP Han Zheng slams 'unilateral military actions,' says big countries should follow rules
We are continuing our coverage of the 81 UN General Assembly from September 22-28, 2026:
Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.
Germany calls for AI regulation, urges 'profound' UN reform
Germany's Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul opened his UN General Assembly speech by warning about the extraordinary power of artificial intelligence and its implications for the world. He also addressed the erosion of international institutions in a world of rising nationalism.
"When a technology has the power to fundamentally change the world, we need to ask who controls it, who sets the rules, who is accountable," Wadephul said, adding that AI has the potential to upend the economy and "endanger the infrastructure that keeps our societies running."
"AI holds extraordinary promise," Wadephul said. But he warned that a "critical tension" exists when the technology is concentrated in two countries and a few companies. Such power holds great responsibility to humanity, Wadephul said, saying that as power becomes global, so must the responsibilites.
"AI is not waiting for our institutions to catch up, our institutions have to catch up with AI" Wadephul said.
"We need to make sure that tech progress is guided by a framework that we all have a say in shaping," he added, calling effectively for global regulation of AI.
"Germany calls on UN member states to work towards common safety requirements for the most capable models," he said.
On the weakening of UN institutions, Wadephul warned of a UN "under pressure."
"There are great powers that believe that they fare better if they ignore the rules enshrined in the UN charter,"
Wadephul said that "the overwhelming majority of the 193 states represented in this assembly" are harmed when international institutions are under attack.
"If this erosion contitnues, we all stand to lose," he added.
Germany's foreign minister urged for the the new UN Secretary General to lead "a profound process of reform," as the world needs "a functioning UN that plays an active role in conflicts, rather than managing."
"Germany stands up for peace and security," Wadephul said, citing his country's commitment to support Ukraine.
A new nationalism is not the path for nations, Wadephul said, adding that "it would makes our lives narrower, poorer and less secure"
India urges deescalation amid Strait of Hormuz and Red Sea crises
India's Minister for External Affairs, Subrahmanyam Jaishankar, addressed the UN General Assembly, urging for deescalation and restraint from those involved in conflicts that have caused disruption to world navigation, in reference to the current crises in the Strait of Hormuz and Red Sea.
"In a globalized world the effects of war are felt worldwide," Jaishankar said.
"Countries far from conflicts are being penalized for no fault in this. Those most impacted, often have the least say," he added.
Jaishankar also denounced the security of seafarers caught in conflicts on the water.
"We must ensure that the safety and security of shipping and seafarers is never compromised," he said.
Saudi Arabia says international community 'absent' in Gulf crisis
At UN, the Foreign Minister of Saudi Arabia, Prince Faisal bin Farhan al Saud, called for the defense of freedom of navigation in all international waterways.
"The international community has been absent from assuming its responsibilities in confronting all that threatens international peace and security," bin Farhan told the United Nations General Assembly.
The Saudi foreign minister called for the restoration of the Strait of Hormuz to its "pre-28th February status." The US and Israel began their military operations against Iran on that date.
He condemned the fact that Saudi Arabia and other Gulf nations "have been subjected to flagrant Iranian attacks" targeting their security, resources, and civilians.
Saudi FM also denounced Israel's war in Gaza, saying it opposed the "continuing suffering of the Palestinian people."
"We stress that a just and lasting peace can only be achieved through the implementation of a two-state solution and the establishment of an independent Palestinian state and the 1967 borders, with East Jerusalem as its capital."
Russia offers to help with Strait of Hormuz crisis
Russia's Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said that Moscow can help stabilize the situation in the Strait of Hormuz and the wider Gulf region.
"We need trust in the relationships between the Gulf states, the Arab states, and Iran. We need stable regional architecture," Lavrov said in his speech to the UNGA.
"Russia, together with other responsible states, stands ready to constructively contribute to stabilizing this strategically important region," he added.
Lavrov claims Europe 'thwarts' Ukraine talks
Russia's Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov addressed the UNGA, shortly after meeting with his German counterpart Johann Wadephul.
In his speech to the general assembly, Lavrov accused European countries of "doing everything" to thwart talks to help end the conflict between Russia and Ukraine.
Russia's unprovoked invasion of its neighbor will soon mark its fifth anniversary next February.
"Europe is doing everything it can to thwart peace talks in which the (Donald) Trump administration is interested," he said, referring to the US government and the various rounds of talks it has held with the Russian and Ukrainian government, led by Trump's son in law Jared Kushner and adviser Steve Witkoff.
German FM Wadephul meets Russia's Lavrov during UN assembly
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul met his Russian counterpart Sergey Lavrov at the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York.
A correspondent for the Russian Interfax news agency reported Wadephul and Lavrov, followed by aides, shaking hands before the press was asked to leave.
Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said the meeting took place at the German initiative.
Moscow has been sanctioned by the EU over its full-scale invasion of Ukraine which the Kremlin launched in February 2022.
The last meeting between on this level was held in January of that year, between veteran diplomat Lavrov and Germany's then-top diplomat, Annalena Baerbock, who was on a visit to Moscow.
Lavrov and Wadephul's meeting was held as tensions between Berlin and Moscow have been high in recent weeks.
Germany has accused Russia of orchestrating an attempted drone attack on Leipzig airport, with each country ordering the closure of the other's consulate.
Moldova PM offers his country as testing ground for AI rules
Moldovan Prime Minister Vasile Tofan used part of his time before the General Assembly to present a vision of small nations serving as "regulatory sandboxes" for new technologies.
"Technology is moving faster than regulation almost everywhere, and artificial intelligence is widening that gap," said Tofan, who worked as an investor and businessman before becoming the head of Moldovan government two months ago.
"We want Moldova to become a place where emergent technologies can be tested responsibly through regulatory sandboxes, where regulators learn alongside companies, rules adjust with evidence, and good ideas do not wait years to reach the real economy."
"When an entrepreneur arrives with a technology for which the law has not caught up yet, the answer should not simply be 'There is no rule for this.' It should be 'Let us find a safe way to test it'," he said.
China cast itself as source of stability in changing world
Addressing the UN General Assembly, Chinese Vice President Han Zheng called for safeguarding the post-WWII order, saying the world wanted "peace, not war."
"We should turn into action the vision of common, comprehensive, cooperative and sustainable security, and reject the Cold War mindset and bloc confrontation," Han said.
"Major countries shoulder special responsibilities for safeguarding international peace and security and they should take the lead in complying with the rules, upholding the rule of law, and doing what's right."
"No matter how international dynamics evolve, China remains unchanged in its pursuit of peace and development, in its dedication to safeguarding fairness and justice and in its commitment to multilateralism," said the Chinese vice president.
"China will join hands with all other countries to build a community with a shared future for humanity, and make the world a better place for all of us."
China takes indirect swipes at US over Iran
Speaking at the UN on Saturday, Chinese Vice President Han Zheng said the world should reject "unilateral military actions that violate the UN charter and circumvent the Security Council authorization," in an apparent reference to the US attack on Iran.
"China holds that the sovereignty and security of the countries in the Middle east, including the Gulf, should be respected, international industrial and supply chains should be kept stable and unimpeded, and global trade should be safeguarded," he said.
In his speech, Han also spoke out against the US blockade of Cuba, albeit without explicitly mentioning the US.
He said China called on "the relevant country" to lift its blockade against Cuba and stop using the threat of force against the island nation.
In regards to Israel and the Palestinians, the Chinese official urged bringing the two-state solution back "on the right track" and "at an early date."
Welcome back
Welcome back to DW's coverage of the UN General Assembly Debate in New York City.
On day 5, China and Germany are some of the major countries addressing the event.
Stay tuned for more.
We are pausing our coverage
As the fourth day of the 81st UN General Assembly comes to a halt, we are pausing this blog for the night.
Today was another address-packed day, with several small island nations stressing the urgent need to address climate change, as they are most vulnerable to its consequences.
Norway and Sweden stressed the importance of continuing to support the UN, including with funds, as well as making it more representative by giving Africa a permanent seat on the Security Council.
Meanwhile, Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif took aim at India, rehashing in his address a short-lived conflict between the two countries last year. Sharif said his country faced "external aggression from India under a false pretext," adding that his country's response was "its inherent right of self-defense."
Before the session wrapped, India used its right of reply to address Pakistan's "bizarre remarks," and accuse its neighbor of terrorism. Pakistan was quick to respond, accusing New Delhi of "export[ing] terrorism and violence."
We will be back again tomorrow, when addresses from India, Germany, Russia, China, Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Canada, and others are scheduled.
Day 4 at UNGA: Egypt, Norway, Sweden, Mexico outline priorities during afternoon session
Small island states take aim at world leaders for inaction on climate change
The speakers for the small island nations of St. Kitts and Nevis, Samoa and Tonga called to attention the inaction of world leaders on climate change.
The island nations are disproportionately vulnerable to the climate crisis, with the deputy prime minister of Samoa, Mulipola Anarosa Ale Molioo, calling climate change "the single greatest threat" facing the country and the world.
Molioo stressed the need to scale up climate financing so small island nations weren't the ones bearing the burden of climate change.
Fatafehi Fakafanua, Prime Minister of Tonga, said Pacific leaders have been warning about the climate crisis, with little support for years.
Fakafanua said the question was not whether the world has heard the message of climate change but rather, he asked, "why has it still not acted?"
The deputy prime minister of St. Kitts and Nevis, Geoffrey Hanley, outlined some of the solutions his country has undertaken, such as investing in desalination and improving food security.
Hanley said that small states, who stand most at risk from the consequences of climate change, were still delivering big solutions.
But he said, because no small island state can perpetually adapt to the climate crisis, "adaptation cannot excuse inaction elsewhere."
Iran says it gave US 7-day plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz
Iran has given the US a seven-day plan that would involve reopening the critical Strait of Hormuz to maritime navigation, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Friday.
Speaking to reporters at the United Nations General Assembly on Friday, Araghchi said the plan was delivered via Qatar and the choice now rests with Washington to meet the conditions Tehran has laid out.
"Iran does not accept coercion, threats or intimidation, and Iran will not surrender its sovereign rights under pressure," he said.
Sharif blames India for 2025 clashes, calls for 'just and fair' Kashmir resolution
Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif also took aim at India in his speech as he discussed the limited military clashes between the uneasy neighbors last year.
"A year ago, Pakistan faced external aggression from India under a false pretext," the prime minister alleged. "Pakistan exercised its inherent right of self-defense under Article 51 of the United Nations charter."
He praised the country's military saying, "They silenced the enemy, repulsed its attack, and taught it a lesson it shall never ever forget," as the UN's TV feed cut to an Indian observer in the assembly shaking his head as he listened.
Pakistan considers Indian missile strikes on May 7 to be the start of the low-level conflict, that ran for less than a week, while India contends that the strikes were retalliation for an attack in Indian-administered Jammu and Kashmir in late April. New Delhi had accused Pakistan of supporting cross-border terrorism, which Islambad denied.
Sharif praised US President Donald Trump's "resolute and visionary leadership," crediting it with saving "hundreds of millions of lives in South Asia" by intervening and helping to broker a truce "when two nuclear neighbors stood at the brink of all-out war."
Sharif asked "who knows the extent of devastation that could have taken place" without Trump's "clarity of thought and action" at a critical moment.
He said it was necessary to ensure that South Asia "never reaches this precipice again," and said that doing so would require "a just and fair resolution of the Kashmir dispute."
He said Kashmiri people had been waiting eight decades for the UN to "fulfill its solemn commitment of a free and impartial plebiscite under its auspices." He also criticized recent "attempts to alter the legal status of Jammu and Kashmir through demographic reengineering and other illegal measures."
He also criticized India for its decision to hold a treat on the Indus River System in abeyance, saying this move had "no legal basis whatsoever."

Before the session wrapped, India used its right of reply to address Pakistan's "bizarre remarks," and accuse its neighbor of terrorism. Pakistan was quick to respond, accusing New Delhi of "export[ing] terrorism and violence."

The speakers for the small island nations of St. Kitts and Nevis, Samoa and Tonga called to attention the inaction of world leaders on climate change.

Molioo stressed the need to scale up climate financing so small island nations weren't the ones bearing the burden of climate change.

Fakafanua said the question was not whether the world has heard the message of climate change but rather, he asked, "why has it still not acted?"

Sharif praised US President Donald Trump's "resolute and visionary leadership," crediting it with saving "hundreds of millions of lives in South Asia" by intervening and helping to broker a truce "when two nuclear neighbors stood at the brink of all-out war."

He said it was necessary to ensure that South Asia "never reaches this precipice again," and said that doing so would require "a just and fair resolution of the Kashmir dispute."
He said Kashmiri people had been waiting eight decades for the UN to "fulfill its solemn commitment of a free and impartial plebiscite under its auspices." He also criticized recent "attempts to alter the legal status of Jammu and Kashmir through demographic reengineering and other illegal measures."
