articles.title: Defense Ministry: Iran’s underground defense infrastructure disrupts enemy calculations
articles.body:
Defense Ministry: Iran’s underground defense infrastructure disrupts enemy calculations
TEHRAN – Iran’s Defense Ministry spokesman says the country’s systematic move toward deep-underground defense infrastructure has significantly altered the strategic balance of power in West Asia, forcing hostile actors to recalibrate their failed military assumptions.
“Part of the strategic capabilities of the Armed Forces have in recent years been deployed in secure environments and underground infrastructure, a move that has frustrated the enemy’s calculations regarding Iran’s defense capabilities and weapons production capacity,” Brigadier General Reza Talaei-Nik said on Saturday.
He added, “The recent wars imposed costs and inflicted damage on Iran, yet the enemy failed to achieve its main strategic objectives, while Iran also imposed costs on them.”
General Talaei-Nik contextualized these developments within the broader evolution of contemporary warfare. He noted that the nature of recent conflicts has transcended traditional kinetic engagements, evolving into a sophisticated struggle where military prowess is merely one component of a larger, multidimensional battlefield.
He described the wars launched by the US and Israel against Iran in June 2025 and February 2026 as wars of technology, specialists, and hybrid warfare, saying that, alongside the military arena, social, economic, media, and cognitive domains had become major fields of confrontation.
He underscored that the current era of warfare bears no resemblance to the Iraqi-imposed war in the 1980s. The velocity of operations, the ubiquity of advanced digital weaponry, and the sheer geographical breadth of the recent conflicts represent a fundamental paradigm shift from the war imposed on Iran by Saddam Hussein’s regime, the spokesman noted.
The resilience displayed by the Iranian defense apparatus has been tested significantly over the past sixteen months. Since June 2025, Iran has been the target of two distinct campaigns of foreign aggression. The first was a 12-day criminal offensive in June 2025, followed by a more prolonged, 40-day campaign that commenced in late February.
Despite the intensity of these offensives, the strategic depth afforded by Iran’s underground infrastructure ensured the continuity of command, control, and retaliatory capacity.
Following the cessation of the second war, a fragile period of diplomatic engagement led to the Islamabad memorandum of understanding (MoU) on June 17, aimed at establishing a durable ceasefire. However, the US has repeatedly violated the tenets of this agreement, escalating tensions in July through waves of airstrikes and an illegal naval blockade. In an exercise of decisive sovereignty, the Iranian Armed Forces responded by conducting precision strikes against strategic American assets across West Asia and enforcing the closure of the Strait of Hormuz.
The failure of the enemy’s campaigns confirms that Iran’s strategic posture has moved beyond mere defensive capability; it has evolved into a comprehensive system of active deterrence. The ongoing integration of subterranean infrastructure with advanced early-warning systems and indigenous missile technology ensures that Iran’s defense remains resilient, regardless of the technological edge claimed by aggressors.
Moving forward, the Iranian defense doctrine continues to emphasize the necessity of simultaneous growth across military, cognitive, and economic sectors. As General Talaei-Nik emphasized, maintaining this deterrence is a prerequisite for national sovereignty. By proving that the most advanced weapons systems and air raids cannot decapitate the Islamic Republic’s retaliatory capabilities, Iran has established a new reality: the cost of aggression against the nation has become prohibitively high, effectively neutralizing the strategic objectives of the United States and its regional allies. The path ahead remains one of fortified resilience, where the interplay of technology and resolve ensures that Iran remains the primary architect of its own security.

articles.title: US strikes on Ecuadorian fishing boats raise humanitarian concerns but Trump admin not wavering
articles.body:
While the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, was being decorated in Quito by Ecuador’s president for “helping to promote peace in the region”, 10 Ecuadorian fishers whose boat had been blown up by US forces were adrift in the eastern Pacific.
On 8 September, a day before Rubio arrived, a US patrol vessel intercepted the fishing boat Don Rufo in international waters near Ecuador.
“The gringos were all armed as if they were going to war,” said the boat’s captain, Mero Calderón, 50. “I tried to show them our catch to prove that we were there working, but they wouldn’t listen,” he added.
“They brought two huge bombs aboard, took us to their ship, handcuffed and blindfolded us, and blew our boat to pieces,” said Calderón, who along with five other fishers, was handed over to local authorities.
But another 10 crew members were fishing farther out to sea in a smaller boat that was not equipped to make it back to shore. The Ecuadorian navy only rescued them on 10 September, when Rubio was already in Peru preparing to return to the US.
US Southern Command posted an edited 14-second video of the operation and said “intelligence confirmed” that the vessel was being used by a gang as a “floating refuelling station” for speedboats allegedly carrying drugs – which the fishers deny.
It was one of eight operations involving Ecuadorian boats in just more than two weeks – the latest on 16 September – to follow the same pattern. Unlike the nearly 70 US airstrikes in the Pacific and Caribbean that have killed 234 people since last year, crews were removed before the vessels were sunk.
Also, rather than unilateral US attacks, the new wave of operations has the open support of Ecuador’s far-right president, Daniel Noboa, who is calling them “joint operations”.
Donald Trump has compared the drug trafficking operations to the campaign against the Islamic state. “Like ISIS, they should be killed, exiled or detained as enemy combatants without the possibility of release, which is what we’re doing,” Trump said on Tuesday.
Some analysts see the shift as an indication that the US’s military strategy against drug trafficking in Latin America has entered a new phase.
“Noboa has offered Ecuador as a ‘laboratory’ for the implementation of this new phase,” said Will Freeman, a fellow for Latin America studies at the Council on Foreign Relations.
Although Ecuador does not produce cocaine like neighbouring Colombia and Peru, over the past decade it has become a major trafficking hub because of its access to the Pacific, including the area where the attacks on boats have been taking place.
Noboa has responded with a controversial “iron-fist” approach to the gangs, issuing repeated states of emergency and expanding the role of the armed forces.
This crackdown however has done little to reduce violence, and instead has eroded human rights. The most notable example of human rights abuse came last year in the case of the “Guayaquil Four”, the forced disappearance of four Afro-Ecuadorian boys between the age of 11 and 15. All four boys were found dead, there bodies charred and dismembered.
Despite pushback from voters, Noboa signed an agreement with the White House authorising joint operations and granting US military personnel involved in counter-narcotics operations immunity from criminal prosecution. The operations have also extended to land, with US troops taking part in raids last Thursday.
“Noboa is interested in the optics of a very lethal crackdown and in making Ecuador a place where the Trump administration can refine those methods and show them off,” said Freeman, who has also reported on the boat attacks in Ecuador for the New Yorker magazine.
Trump has pressured Latin American presidents to join an anti-drug cartel coalition he created called Shield of the Americas. With Peru and Colombia recently joining, the group now includes all but the few countries still governed by the left, such as Mexico and Brazil – where a far-right senator is a serious contender in October’s election.
So far, the coalition’s primary goal appears to have been increasing joint operations against alleged drug traffickers.
Adam Isacson, director for defence oversight at the Washington Office on Latin America, expects joint operations to expand across the region.
Isacson stressed that though more people are being turned over to local authorities instead of killed, the US is “still doing the bad old stuff”. On 19 September, four people were killed in the Caribbean. As with the other airstrikes, the US has not disclosed their identities or any of the alleged evidence linking them to criminal activity.
During his trip to Ecuador, Rubio said the decision on what approach to take was “a strike-by-strike or operation-by-operation determination” that depended on the threat and location of the boat, but that the US would “still blow up ships if need be”.
Human rights organisations have described the airstrikes as extrajudicial killings, and a special rapporteur for the UN human rights council has concluded that there are “reasonable grounds to believe” that they constitute “crimes against humanity”.
Despite Trump’s claims, available data show they have had no impact on the volume of cocaine entering the country.
Journalists and human rights groups have managed to identify some of the victims, who in many cases were innocent or, when suspected of involvement in criminal activity, poor people at the bottom of trafficking networks.
In Ecuador, the local NGO Permanent Committee for the Defence of Human Rights estimates that more than 220 fishers have been subjected to “violent boardings, arbitrary detentions, enforced disappearances, torture and the destruction of vessels” in this year’s US operations.
None of the fishers remains in custody and, while some are still facing prosecution, many have already been acquitted for lack of evidence.
“Fishers are losing their livelihoods when the US destroys the boats. Besides, if the US says the vessels were being used to refuel drug boats, why destroy the evidence?” said the committee’s lawyer, Fernando Bastías.
A US Southern Command spokesperson said it conducts operations “in compliance with US and international law” and that leaving boats “intact could permit their reuse by criminal networks”.
Although the US and Ecuador have celebrated the recent operations on social media, three cases from earlier this year remain unclaimed.
The first was on 20 January, when the fishing vessel Fiorella disappeared with eight crew members on board; days earlier, some of them had told relatives they were being monitored by drones and by a vessel on which they said they had seen a US flag.
Human rights organisations and journalists identified two more cases with similar patterns in late March, although the fishers survived. The Washington Post reported that the three cases were part of a covert CIA programme, and the agency declined to comment.
A US Southern Command spokesperson said it had no knowledge of, nor were its forces “involved in the incidents described in reports involving the Fiorella”.
Both the husband and brother of María Mero, 43, were aboard the Fiorella: Gabriel Aladino Mero Delgado, 44, and Jefferson Ariel Mero Cueva, 25. “Where did they take them? Do they have them in the US, in a prison somewhere? We don’t want any trouble; we just want them to send them back to us,” she told the Guardian.
The families say they have spent months trying to get answers from the Ecuadorian government, so far without success.
“They were fishers, not criminals. Let the great president come here to my house and see whether I have luxuries, anything that would show I’m a drug trafficker. No, because all of us here are poor, and we just want our loved ones back,” added Mero.

articles.title: Saudi Arabia has not ruled out developing nuclear weapons, US intelligence warns - report
articles.body:
US intelligence assessments said Saudi Arabia has not ruled out developing a nuclear weapons program, according to classified documents provided to Congress and reviewed by officials who spoke to The Washington Post.
The assessment was included in classified documents as part of a review of a US-Saudi agreement to expand civilian nuclear cooperation.
The intelligence assessment raised concerns among some US lawmakers over the agreement reached by US President Donald Trump’s administration, which would allow American companies to pursue tens of billions of dollars in nuclear energy projects in Saudi Arabia.
The deal has also drawn scrutiny because it could eventually allow Saudi Arabia to enrich uranium to 20%, according to The Washington Post.
The agreement initially limits enrichment to below 5% but permits the limit to rise to 20% after an additional study and written agreement.
The paper did note that uranium enriched to 20% is still below weapons-grade levels.
US Senators warn the agreement could give Saudi Arabia the ability to develop a bomb
The agreement is currently subject to a 90-day congressional review period, during which lawmakers can seek to block it.
A group of Democratic senators, led by Ed Markey of Massachusetts and Jeff Merkley of Oregon, said in a letter to Secretary of State Marco Rubio that the agreement could give Saudi Arabia the ability to enrich uranium and potentially develop nuclear weapons.
“The Trump administration is departing from precedent, adopting looser restrictions, and caving to Saudi demands,” the senators wrote.
Merkley said that the US should not rely on assurances from the Saudi government regarding its nuclear intentions.
He also questioned why Riyadh would seek the ability to enrich uranium domestically if its nuclear program were intended solely for civilian purposes.
The Saudi government did not respond directly to questions from The Washington Post but referred the newspaper to an earlier statement by Saudi Energy Minister Abdulaziz bin Salman, who said the program would be “peaceful” and developed with “the highest levels of responsibility and transparency.”
The State Department also defended the agreement, saying that the US “does not and will not support a Saudi nuclear weapons program.”
The department said the agreement would expand nuclear energy cooperation while maintaining what it described as the strongest nonproliferation standards that could be achieved diplomatically.
The intelligence community’s assessment was included alongside input from the State Department, according to US officials who spoke to the newspaper on condition of anonymity because they were discussing classified information.
The State Department’s assessment was described as more confident in the agreement’s safeguards and Saudi assurances.
The CIA declined to comment.
Another concern was that the agreement did not require Saudi Arabia to adopt the International Atomic Energy Agency’s Additional Protocol, which gives the agency broader access to nuclear facilities and research sites.
Twenty nuclear nonproliferation experts, including former IAEA director general Hans Blix, warned in a letter to Congress this past week that the inspection arrangements could make it difficult to determine whether Saudi Arabia was secretly developing nuclear weapons at undeclared facilities.
Saudi Arabia will develop a nuclear weapon if Iran does
Concerns over Saudi Arabia’s nuclear ambitions have also been linked to comments by Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman in 2018 that Riyadh would develop a nuclear weapon if Iran did so.
The Trump administration conducted joint Israeli strikes on Iranian nuclear facilities in 2025 and in 2026, but Iran’s enriched uranium is believed to have survived the attacks under the rubble of the damaged facilities.
The possibility of Saudi Arabia developing nuclear weapons has raised concerns among some US lawmakers that nuclear activity in the kingdom could contribute to a broader regional arms race.
The Trump administration has said the nuclear agreement is intended to strengthen US-Saudi ties and prevent Riyadh from deepening cooperation with countries such as Russia and China.
The agreement could also have implications for US efforts to secure Saudi normalization of relations with Israel.
Trump has said normalization remains a requirement for the nuclear deal, although Saudi Arabia has not agreed to establish diplomatic relations with Israel while the Israeli government continues to oppose the establishment of a Palestinian state.

articles.title: Russia accuses Europe of doing 'everything it can to thwart' prospect of Ukraine peace talks
articles.body:
Kanyshai Butun and Burc Eruygur
26 September 2026•Update: 26 September 2026
Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov on Saturday accused European countries of doing “everything they can to thwart” prospects for peace talks between Russia and Ukraine during an address to the UN General Assembly in New York.
Lavrov accused the West of “pumping” Ukraine with weapons and helping Kyiv target civilians and civilian infrastructure with drones and missiles.
“The West aspires to inflict a strategic defeat on Russia, but these aspirations will result in the warmongers being led into a strategic dead end,” he said.
Turning to the Middle East, Lavrov said Russia was convinced it was time to resolve the “main issue” in the region by ensuring Palestinian statehood based on “countless” UN decisions.
He also urged the US to immediately release former Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro and his wife, and called the use of force to kill Iran’s late Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei “unacceptable.”
On artificial intelligence, Lavrov said Moscow supports China’s initiative to establish a global organization for cooperation on AI.

articles.title: Air Force Injects $87M into IVEWS F-16 Electronic Warfare Upgrades
articles.body:
The Air Force has invested $87.4 million to upgrade the F-16 Fighting Falcon‘s electronic warfare capabilities, bolstering the fighter’s self-protection against increasingly advanced threats.
Bringing the total program value to $1.92 billion, the move is expected to jump-start fielding by funding low-rate initial production of the AN/ALQ-257 Integrated Viper Electronic Warfare Suite, or IVEWS, which is integrated into the fighter’s airframe.
This money is intended to produce an upgraded Viper for use in the Middle East, as part of an effort pushed by the U.S. military’s Central Command.
Work on the low-rate initial production batch at the company’s Illinois facility is expected to conclude by the end of 2029. The Air Force Lifecycle Management Center, Wright-Patterson, Ohio, oversees the contract.
The Need
The company says the new EW system is sorely needed for the F-16’s future fights.
“You cannot defeat what you cannot see,” said Shalini Gupta, vice president of electronic warfare and targeting at Northrop Grumman, in a statement to Air & Space Forces Magazine. “A modern EW suite is essential for operations in contested airspace. We are producing fully functional, flight-proven systems now. From day one, our customers gain the ability to geolocate threats with a single aircraft, and the confidence that comes with having a U.S. program of record system on board.”
The F-16 has seen a lot of action in Operation Epic Fury, and while its existing capabilities have handled Iranian air defenses and electronic warfare capabilities, peer adversaries such as the Chinese military have more sophisticated means to foil the jet fighter’s aims.
The Air Force issued an urgent operational need statement in 2025 that triggered a congressionally supplied $187 million in its fiscal 2026 reconciliation bill, which sped up system qualification and flight testing.
After CENTCOM’s operational need statement, Northrop and the Air Force made the effort a priority.
“This is one of many efforts to keep our fourth-gen platforms competitive as the adversary advances,” Lt. Gen. Derek France, then-commander of Air Forces Central, said in September 2025 about IVEWS. “That’s the bumper sticker, if you will.”
The recently announced additional $87.4 million LRIP modification fuels the initial production of the Viper suites. Full-rate production of the suites for the full 450-aircraft fleet is scheduled to follow this initial batch.
The initial production tranche for the Air Force was to outfit 72 Block 50 F-16s with IVEWS, with more likely to arrive as production ramps up, the company’s vice president of targeting and survivability Jim Conroy told Air & Space Forces Magazine in a 2025 interview.
Iran operates radar-guided and electro-optical/infrared (EO/IR) air defense systems. Non-traditional Houthi air defense systems proved a particular challenge for U.S. aircraft, including F-16s, during last year’s Operation Rough Rider against the group in Yemen.
During Operation Epic Fury, the Air Force used its Block 50 F-16s in a suppression of enemy air defenses role and deployed most of its Wild Weasel SEAD F-16 units to support operations against Iran. Those units’ F-16s can carry AGM-88 anti-radiation missiles and are equipped with HARM Targeting System, or HTS, pods—a capability the Air Force’s other fourth-generation fighter, the F-15E Strike Eagle, lacks.
The System
IVEWS is an ultra-wideband, sophisticated EW system capable of radar warning, active jamming, and detecting, identifying, and locating threats, suited for fifth- and sixth-generation aircraft.
It can also conduct single-aircraft autonomous geolocation, meaning one aircraft can find an enemy radar and map a threat while actively using the aircraft’s jammer. Older systems required multiple aircraft to triangulate a radar location and required pilots to shut off jammers when mapping threats.
Under the USAF “Big Iron” software compliance standard, teams will be able to quickly update IVEWS system software files without hardware modifications or grounding the aircraft for days, weeks, or months.
IVEWS began flight tests in 2024 and has undergone more than 550 hours of effective testing across 300 sorties during operational assessments, Northrop Vice President for Mission Systems Mike Minahan said in a July call with reporters.
The system works in conjunction with the AN/AG-83 Scalable Agile Beam Radar. The radar uses an Active Electronically Scanned Array (AESA) to enable faster target tracking.
As of mid-May, Northrop had delivered 1,000 SABR radars to its F-16 customers. The new radar uses digital tracking as opposed to the legacy AN/APG-66 and AN-APG-68 radars that it is replacing.
IVEWS, the SABR, and the upgraded LITENING LA pod, which gives the aircraft a 50 percent increase in the range of its targeting system, are crucial to keeping the aging F-16 combat-worthy. The pod is also used on the F-15E Strike Eagle, A-10 Thunderbolt II, B-52 Stratofortress, and the Navy F/A-18 Super Hornet.
IVEWS would likely be equipped on possible future Air Force new-build “F-16G” purchases the service will consider, Air & Space Forces Magazine reported.
The LITENING LA, an upgrade from the current LITENING pod, entered flight testing in December, according to Northrop officials.

articles.title: Iran will defend itself against any threat or military attack: Pezeshkian
articles.body:
Iran will defend itself against any threat or military attack: Pezeshkian
TEHRAN— Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian has reaffirmed Tehran’s readiness to pursue diplomacy with Washington over the nuclear issue and other outstanding disputes, while stressing that negotiations can succeed only if they are based on mutual commitments, respect for international law and tangible steps to rebuild trust.
In an interview with CBS News during his visit to New York for the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly, Pezeshkian said Iran does not seek war or confrontation, but would defend itself against any threat or military attack.
The president’s remarks came amid renewed diplomatic activity surrounding the Iranian nuclear program and the Strait of Hormuz, with Tehran maintaining that any return to negotiations must be accompanied by practical guarantees that previous agreements will not again be disregarded.
Trust at the center of Iran-US diplomacy
Pezeshkian said Iran had previously reached understandings with the United States, but that the diplomatic process had been undermined by Washington’s failure to honor its commitments.
He pointed in particular to the US withdrawal from the 2015 nuclear agreement and subsequent military actions against Iran, arguing that these developments had created a profound atmosphere of mistrust between the two countries.
For Tehran, he said, the issue is therefore not simply whether negotiations can resume, but whether agreements reached through diplomacy will be implemented in practice.
Pezeshkian said Iran was prepared to negotiate within the framework of international law and the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons (NPT), including arrangements concerning nuclear monitoring and inspections.
His comments followed an Iranian proposal for the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and the resumption of negotiations, with Tehran presenting the two issues as part of a broader diplomatic framework for reducing tensions. CBS reported that Iran had offered to reopen the strategic
waterway within seven days and restart talks as an initial step toward a longer-term nuclear agreement.
Iran reiterates peaceful nature of nuclear program
Pezeshkian again rejected any suggestion that Iran seeks to develop nuclear weapons, saying the country has never pursued such a goal.
He also said disagreements over inspections could be resolved through negotiations and mutually agreed arrangements. Asked directly whether Iran would allow UN nuclear inspectors to return, he answered affirmatively, adding that the details of inspections could be addressed within a negotiated framework.
The Iranian president also criticized attacks on Iranian nuclear facilities, arguing that such sites had been subject to international monitoring and questioning the legal justification for targeting facilities associated with a program Tehran maintains is peaceful.
From Tehran’s perspective, the central issue is that verification and monitoring should take place through established international mechanisms rather than military action.
Iran has repeatedly maintained that it is prepared to provide assurances concerning the peaceful nature of its nuclear activities while insisting on its rights under the NPT. Iranian officials have also argued that military attacks on nuclear facilities undermine the very diplomatic mechanisms designed to resolve disputes over nuclear activities.
Direct Trump meeting requires more than a gesture
Asked about the possibility of a direct meeting with US President Donald Trump, Pezeshkian said the accumulated mistrust between Tehran and Washington could not be overcome merely through a face-to-face encounter.
He referred to the US withdrawal from the 2015 nuclear agreement and military attacks that 'took place even as diplomatic channels were being pursued.'
Pezeshkian said Iran needs practical evidence that Washington is prepared to honor agreements and is not seeking to overthrow the Iranian government.
His position effectively places implementation and guarantees at the center of any future diplomatic process: Tehran, he indicated, is not opposed to negotiations, but does not consider negotiations meaningful if pressure, threats and military action continue alongside them.
CBS reported that US and Iranian officials had already held indirect discussions through mediators on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly, although no direct meeting between Trump and Pezeshkian took place.
Hormuz: Iran links reopening to implementation of arrangements
The Strait of Hormuz was another major focus of the interview.
Pezeshkian said Iran could return to an earlier framework concerning the strategic waterway if Washington accepted the arrangements previously discussed. He stressed that implementation should be based on reciprocal commitments and dialogue.
The issue has become one of the most sensitive dimensions of the broader Iran-US confrontation because the strait is a critical international energy corridor and lies at the heart of the security architecture of the Persian Gulf.
Iran has maintained that the security and navigation arrangements in the waterway cannot be separated from the wider military confrontation and the commitments contained in previously negotiated understandings.
The latest Iranian proposal, according to international reporting, calls for the reopening of the strait within seven days if the United States takes corresponding steps to reduce military pressure and lift its blockade of Iranian ports.
Pezeshkian’s comments indicate that Tehran views the issue not as a unilateral concession, but as part of a reciprocal diplomatic arrangement in which commitments by both sides would be implemented simultaneously.
Iran calls for regional dialogue
Turning to wider regional developments, Pezeshkian said Iran does not seek conflict with its neighbors and favors resolving regional disputes through dialogue, mutual respect and adherence to international rules.
He said neighboring countries could work together to develop the region and establish mechanisms that would strengthen collective security rather than relying on external military intervention.
The position reflects Tehran’s longstanding emphasis on regional arrangements involving neighboring states, particularly in the Persian Gulf, rather than security frameworks dominated by extra-regional military powers.
Pezeshkian also criticized economic sanctions, arguing that their consequences extend beyond governments and affect ordinary people, particularly patients, elderly citizens and low-income groups.
He called for an approach grounded in justice and respect for human rights, linking the humanitarian consequences of sanctions to the broader question of international responsibility.
Coordination with the Leader
Pezeshkian also provided an account of his recent contacts with Leader of the Islamic Revolution Ayatollah Seyyed Mojtaba Hosseini Khamenei, saying he had met with him twice, including a meeting lasting approximately seven hours.
The president described the Leader as being in good physical condition and said Iran’s diplomatic approach is coordinated with the Leader.
He further explained that a six-member team comprising representatives of the military, Parliament and government has been authorized to conduct consultations and discuss decisions related to the diplomatic process.
Rejecting claims about wartime shelters
Pezeshkian also rejected reports that he had been confined to a shelter during the war imposed on Iran by the United States and the Israeli regime.
He said government affairs had continued during the conflict, with the president holding meetings with ministers and other officials while taking precautions against possible attacks.
Asked about reports that Iranian officials had operated from shelters, he stressed that the government could not have continued functioning had its leadership simply remained confined underground. CBS quoted him as saying that “if we were in a shelter, nothing would have gotten done.”
US detainees and the question of trust
On the detention of two US citizens in Iran, Pezeshkian questioned whether releasing them alone would be sufficient to restore confidence between Tehran and Washington.
He referred to previous cases in which Iran fulfilled commitments without receiving reciprocal action from the United States.
His response again reflected the central theme of the interview: Tehran’s concern is not simply the making of commitments but their implementation by both sides.
Iran rejects threats against Trump
Pezeshkian was also asked about threats against Trump and members of his family.
The Iranian president rejected the suggestion that the Iranian government was pursuing such actions, arguing that if Tehran intended to act against the US president or his family, it would not be engaged in negotiations.
The statement was also framed as part of Iran’s broader position that disputes with Washington should be addressed through diplomatic channels rather than assassination threats or military confrontation.
Taken together, Pezeshkian’s remarks presented a consistent message: Iran remains open to diplomacy, including negotiations with the United States over its nuclear program, but does not view dialogue as compatible with continued military pressure, coercive demands or the unilateral abandonment of agreements.
For Tehran, the restoration of trust would require more than diplomatic declarations. It would require concrete action, reciprocal commitments and mechanisms capable of ensuring that agreements reached at the negotiating table are implemented in practice.
The president’s comments also placed the nuclear issue within a wider framework that includes regional security, the Strait of Hormuz, sanctions and Iran’s right to defend itself.

articles.title: Iran ready for talks but never accept bullying, coercion
articles.body:
The president made the remarks in an exclusive interview with CBS News’ “Face the Nation,” broadcast late on Friday. The Iranian president expounded on Iran’s stance on domestic issues as well as regional and international developments during the interview conducted in New York City, where he addressed the 81st session of the UN General Assembly earlier in the week.
On Iran’s nuclear program and inspection of its sites in return for sanctions relief, Pezeshkian said that Iran has never sought nuclear weapons. He said that the US and Israel assassinated the Leader of the Islamic Revolution, Ayatollah Seyyed Ali Khamenei, whose religious decree bans the development of nuclear weapons.
Pezeshkian also said that Iran was in the middle of negotiations and had reached an agreement with the US when it was attacked. “America’s intention is not to resolve the issue. America’s intention is to overthrow our administration. Israel says in their own speech, what they’re doing is neutralizing the government, not negotiating,” he said, according to a transcript shared on the CBS News website.
“We are doing everything humanly possible, but not through bullying and coercion intended to force us into submission. We’re already negotiating. Why are they concurrently attacking us?” Pezeshkian said, according to the same transcript.
On Iran’s seven-day plan to re-open the Strait of Hormuz – a proposal conveyed to the US by Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi through mediator Qatar on the sidelines of the UNGA – President Pezeshkian said that the implementation of the plan will begin as soon as the US accepts the plan.
Pezeshkian said that the seven-day plan pursues the same goals as the Memorandum of Understanding (MoU), which Iran and the US signed in mid-June.
According to the president, there is deep distrust between Tehran and Washington, which stems from the latter’s actions. He said that the US tore apart the 2015 nuclear deal and twice attacked Iran, in 2025 and 2026, when the two sides were in the midst of negotiations, and then breached the memorandum.
“Basically, we need to determine now what exactly we want to reach an understanding on. If we don't abide by what we have written down as necessary, can we really resolve it through dialogue?” said Pezeshkian, as quoted by CBS News.
“The first thing that needs to happen is that the distrust created by this war has to be overcome. We need to abide by what we have written down. The United States needs to show that it does not intend to overthrow our government or our administration,” he added.
Asked whether Leader of the Islamic Revolution Ayatollah Sayyid Mojtaba Khamenei had advised Pezeshkian to pursue diplomacy, the president said all discussions and decisions had been coordinated.
Pezeshkian said a six-member team had been formed in Iran, comprising representatives from the military, parliament, administration and other institutions. The team has the authority to make decisions and implement them in coordination, he added.
Asked why he came to New York despite the risks, Pezeshkian rejected claims that Iranian officials had been hiding in shelters during the war. He said he remained active, visiting several ministries each day and holding meetings with ministers.
MNA

articles.title: From Russia with “Russophobia”: Kremlin propaganda accounts are posing as “angry Latvians” to influence the country’s Telegram communities
articles.body:
After Latvia banned broadcasts by Russian federal television channels, Telegram became a key platform for Kremlin propaganda in the country. The Insider estimates that around one-third of socio-political channels in Latvia’s Telegram ecosystem are controlled by Russian propagandists posing as “angry Latvians” — and the figure rises to upwards of 65% when only Russian-language channels are included in the count. The channels portray life in Latvia as getting worse, blaming anti-Russian sanctions for harming the Baltic states while calling for an end to support for Ukraine.
Methodology
The Insider collected data from 72 Latvian socio-political channels (353,000 posts from January 1, 2025) and analyzed the network of reposts from these channels. Of the 93,000 shares, 30.3% were reposts between the channels themselves, while 43.7% came from Russian state media, official government channels, military bloggers, and pro-war “Z-channels.” Together, these account for three-quarters of all shared content. For content analysis, a sample of up to 200 posts — stratified by month — was taken from each channel, totaling more than 12,000 posts. Each post was examined for pro-Kremlin and anti-Ukrainian narratives. These narratives were identified in 65 Telegram channels.
All of the channels analyzed by The Insider publish in Russian, and some operate anonymously. The largest are linked to the state-run media group Rossiya Segodnya, which includes RT. They are run by RT editorial staff, in-house RT journalists, or frequent contributors to the channel. At least one channel was previously part of the disinformation network overseen by the late Wagner Group co-founder Yevgeny Prigozhin.
None of the people behind the five largest channels have actually lived in Latvia in recent years. Some have left for Russia and others for Belarus. From abroad, they criticize Latvian government policies while presenting themselves as voices of the country’s “outraged citizens.”
The channels regularly repost one another’s content and amplify material from other Russian propagandists, including RT head Margarita Simonyan. They also promote pro-government Belarusian social media accounts.
The channels repeat a common set of narratives that closely mirror Kremlin messaging: that Russian speakers in Latvia are being persecuted, that Nazism is on the rise in the Baltic states, and that ordinary people in the country are becoming poorer. The channels blame these problems on Riga’s support for Ukraine, arguing that public money is being diverted to the war.
Aleksejs Rosļikovs’ channel
The largest channel, with about 30,000 subscribers, is run by Aleksejs Rosļikovs, a former member of Latvia’s parliament, the Saeima.
Rosļikovs, 42, is a controversial figure in Latvian politics. Before entering public life, he spent years in business, running a confectionery company and later owning several private security firms, a taxi dispatch service, and a car rental company. He went on to serve in the Saeima and later on the Riga City Council.
Latvian authorities have opened a criminal case against him on suspicion of inciting ethnic hatred. The case stems from a June 5, 2025, speech in parliament in which Rosļikovs made an obscene gesture toward fellow lawmakers and ended his remarks in Russian by saying, “There are more of us; Russian is our language.”
In the spring of 2026, Rosļikovs left Latvia for Belarus. From there, he continues to run his Telegram channel and says he plans to run again for the Saeima with his Stability! party. He has told potential voters that if elected, parliamentary immunity would allow him to return to Latvia and that he would seek to lift sanctions on Russia.
Over the past month, Rosļikovs’ Telegram channel gained several thousand subscribers, and in early September,he unexpectedly made the platform private, limiting access to subscribers only. Rosļikovs also runs personal accounts on Facebook (where he has about 16,000 followers) and Instagram (where he has around 109,000). Alongside political commentary, he posts videos of himself working out and taking ice plunges, a Russian Orthodox tradition in which participants immerse themselves in near-freezing water in January to mark the baptism of Jesus.
Baltnews
The second most significant channel, Baltnews (@baltnews), is run by the editorial staff of the “Russia Today” International Information Agency — as is explicitly stated on the publication’s website. The channel has 24,000 subscribers.
Its editorial team publishes dozens of posts a day, quotes Russian and Belarusian propaganda outlets, and reposts content from other channels in the network. In the past year alone, Baltnews reposted content from the BelVPO channel 149 times and from the “Belvestnik” channel 107 times.
The publication also claims that due to ongoing financial aid to Ukraine, the standard of living for Latvians has declined, and that Russophobia is so rampant in the country that it has forced Russian speakers to emigrate. Particular emphasis is placed on the idea that neighboring countries do not respect Latvia and openly mock it.
Even positive news, such as falling prices in stores, are presented in a negative light: “According to estimates by Latvian retail chains, a basket of groceries that used to cost 50 euros now costs 46.28 euros. Savings of 3.72 euros are hardly going to save the local poor or those rapidly approaching poverty.”
Even positive news, such as falling prices in stores, are presented in a negative light
The channel’s editor-in-chief is 34-year-old Riga native Andrejs Starikovs. After Latvian authorities banned the publication in 2018 and opened criminal cases against its staff, Starikovs moved to Moscow.
In addition to running his propaganda page, Starikovs also produces films commissioned by the Russian authorities.
The “Baltic Antifascists” page
The third most significant page in the pro-Russian network is the channel of the organization “Baltic Antifascists,” which has nearly 20,000 subscribers. The organization and the channel were created in November 2022 and are led by 62-year-old Sergejs Vasiļjevs, a native of Latvia.
The “Baltic Antifascists” page actively accuses the Latvian authorities of Nazism and Russophobia. Vasilyev refers to Latvia itself exclusively as a territory “temporarily occupied by NATO troops.”
Vasiļjevs refers to Latvia exclusively as a territory “temporarily occupied by NATO troops”
Criminal cases have now been opened against him and several others for gathering intelligence on behalf of the FSB.
Vasiļjevs himself does not deny gathering data for Russian security agencies, speaking openly about it during live broadcasts. For example, one of the organization’s tasks was to gather information on the bulldozer operators who demolished Soviet monuments.
“We launched a poll [via a Telegram channel] and a flood of opinions came in. We collected all these files and forwarded them to the Investigative Committee of Russia. Now we have a number of suspects in the vandalism case [on Russian territory],” Vasilyev openly boasted in an interview.
The administrators also used the “Baltic Antifascists” group to gather information about Russian opposition events, Latvian volunteers fighting on the side of the Ukrainian Armed Forces, as well as NATO equipment and facilities in the Baltic states.
Vasilyev also has a co-defendant in his criminal case over the collection of information for Russia’s security services: 26-year-old Latvian citizen and St. Petersburg State University student Tatiana Andriets. In 2022, Andriets traveled to Riga for vacation and participated in a protest against the demolition of Soviet monuments. Latvian authorities charged her with “aiding a foreign state” and forming a criminal group. She spent nine months in pretrial detention and is currently under house arrest while her trial is ongoing.
Although Andriets is not a Russian citizen, Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova has repeatedly commented on her case, calling the trial “political” in nature.
Alexei Stefanov, Ruslan Pankratov, and Nikolai Mezhevich
Three other major public pages are run by journalists and political analysts associated with Russia Today who appear as regular guests on Russian television programs such as Solovyov Live, Zvezda, and REN TV. These include the personal channel of “Russia Today” special correspondent Alexei Stefanov, with 16,000 subscribers; the channel of political scientist Ruslan Pankratov from the Institute of CIS Countries (12,000 subscribers); and the channel of Nikolai Mezhevich, a researcher at the Institute of Europe of the Russian Academy of Sciences (12,000 subscribers).
They regularly repost each other’s content. For example, over the past year, Mezhevich’s channel has mentioned Stefanov’s channel 200 times. Stefanov himself constantly cites the channel “Latviyskaya Kochka” (lit. “Latvian Bump”) which reposts content from Margarita Simonyan’s public pages and those of other Russian propagandists.
In addition to narratives about the oppression of Russians in Latvia, the channels offer advice on how to move to Russia, promote content about the “horrible Nazis in Kyiv,” and scare their audience by claiming that war will soon break out on Latvian territory if the country does not change its attitude towards Moscow.
The network also includes smaller public channels with notable backgrounds. One is “Zloi Pribalt” (@wagner_baltika), whose name and logo match channels from Yevgeny Prigozhin’s former Wagner-linked media network. It has only about 1,200 subscribers but is the most prolific channel in the network, publishing about 66,000 posts since Jan. 1, 2025.

articles.title: US intelligence says Saudi Arabia has not abandoned its nuclear weapons ambitions
articles.body:
US intelligence says Saudi Arabia has not abandoned its nuclear weapons ambitions
TEHRAN — Classified U.S. intelligence submitted to Congress reveals that Saudi Arabia has not abandoned plans to develop nuclear weapons, according to a Washington Post report citing American officials.
The assessment, published in the paper on September 25, arrived alongside State Department briefing documents reviewing the Trump administration’s 30-year “civil nuclear cooperation agreement” with Riyadh, exposing blatant double standards in American foreign policy.
The deal is undergoing a 90-day congressional review period, where House Democrats have already introduced a joint resolution of disapproval to block it.
The agreement signed under Section 123 of the Atomic Energy Act initially limits Saudi uranium enrichment below five percent, but permits an increase to 20 percent after further joint review.
Crucially, the agreement fails to require Riyadh to sign the IAEA’s Additional Protocol, depriving international inspectors of snap access to undeclared facilities.
20 nonproliferation experts, including former IAEA director general Hans Blix, warned Congress in a joint letter that omitting the Additional Protocol makes covert weapons development nearly impossible to detect.
Democratic senators Ed Markey and Jeff Merkley pressed Secretary of State Marco Rubio, writing that Washington is “caving to Saudi demands by agreeing to a process that is all but certain to allow Riyadh to acquire the means to enrich uranium and possibly develop nuclear weapons.”
Senator Merkley called claims of a purely civilian program bogus, noting that Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman previously warned the kingdom would build a bomb “if Iran acquired one.”
The contrast with Iran highlights deep Western hypocrisy. The Islamic Republic has categorically ruled out non-conventional weapons, adhering to a binding religious decree issued by the martyred Leader of the Islamic Revolution, Ayatollah Seyyed Ali Khamenei.
Continuous IAEA inspections have consistently verified the peaceful character of Iran’s energy infrastructure. Nevertheless, Washington and Tel Aviv have bombed Iranian facilities under baseless pretexts.
Additionally, lucrative financial incentives appear to eclipse proliferation concerns.
The arrangement opens tens of billions of dollars in construction contracts for American nuclear vendors, notably Westinghouse Electric.
Lawmakers highlighted that Westinghouse’s majority owner shares close ties with Newmark, a real estate firm run by the sons of Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick.
The senators also pointed out that former White House envoy Jared Kushner secured a $2 billion investment from the Saudi sovereign wealth fund shortly after leaving office.
While Washington has subjected peaceful Iranian infrastructure to aggressive strikes and illegal sanctions, it has agreed to actively equip a dynastic rentier monarchy with the tools needed to construct a nuclear arsenal.

articles.title: Trump rejects Iran’s seven-day ceasefire plan, sees renewed bombing after midterms
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump has rejected Iran’s proposal for a seven-day ceasefire and told aides he expects U.S. bombing of Iran to resume after the November midterm elections, The Wall Street Journal reported, citing U.S. officials. The reported position comes as Washington and Tehran continue indirect negotiations over the Strait of Hormuz, sanctions and Iran’s nuclear program.
Tehran’s proposal would reopen the Strait of Hormuz and restart nuclear negotiations in exchange for Washington lifting its blockade of Iranian ports, releasing some frozen Iranian assets and easing sanctions on Iranian oil exports. Iran has separately outlined a seven-day roadmap centered on those demands.
Trump has publicly argued that Iran is under severe economic pressure and seeking an agreement that would come after the midterms and dismantle its nuclear program.
Privately, however, he remains skeptical that Tehran would ultimately meet U.S. demands and has told aides that he considers another bombing campaign likely, according to U.S. officials.
The position suggests the conflict, currently suspended between active warfare and a negotiated settlement, could move back toward military confrontation. Officials cautioned, however, that Trump’s approach has shifted repeatedly during the seven-month conflict and could change again in the coming weeks, including after the midterm elections.
Trump reluctant to return to major combat
The scale of any strikes Trump is considering remains unclear.
Officials said he is reluctant to restart major combat operations in part because the United States wants to preserve dwindling stocks of munitions for other possible conflicts.
At the same time, Trump has repeatedly used the threat of large-scale military action to try to break diplomatic deadlocks with Iran. On several occasions he has followed through with strikes, while stopping short of some of his most sweeping threats.
Trump insisted during his speech to the United Nations this week that electoral politics would not determine his policy toward Iran.
“The Republican Party is running, and I’ll be helping them, but I am not running. I gave absolutely no credence and will not give credence through the election when it comes to Iran,” he told world leaders during the annual General Assembly in New York. “The only thing that does is that Iran will never have a nuclear weapon.”
Trump has also urged Republican voters to behave as though he himself were on the ballot in November.
Seven-day plan puts Hormuz at center of talks
Despite Trump’s rejection of the proposal, negotiations between Washington and Tehran are continuing through regional mediators, a U.S. official said.
An American-led effort to keep oil tankers moving through the Strait of Hormuz despite Iranian threats has reduced Washington’s urgency to reach an agreement, according to the official.
Qatar and other regional governments have been trying to revive the negotiations on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly.
During a meeting in Qatar on Sunday, Iran raised the possibility of a seven-day pause in fighting that could lead to an end to Iranian attacks on commercial shipping in exchange for the United States lifting its blockade, according to people familiar with the discussions.
Under Tehran’s proposal, Washington would lift the naval blockade, release some frozen Iranian assets and ease sanctions on Iranian oil exports. Iran, in return, would reopen the Strait of Hormuz and begin negotiations over its nuclear program.
The United States has told Iran and regional mediators that Trump has no intention of lifting the maritime blockade, according to officials familiar with the negotiations.
Washington believes that continued economic pressure will eventually push Tehran toward an agreement on terms more favorable to the United States and Arab states in the Persian Gulf.
Tehran divided over how far to compromise
Arab mediators said Iranian diplomats have put forward several proposals aimed at ending the war and have acknowledged the worsening economic crisis inside Iran.
But the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, Iran’s powerful military and economic force, has resisted new formulas for an agreement and has signaled that it is prepared for a prolonged conflict.
The IRGC has effectively dominated decision-making in Iran since the war began in February and wants negotiations to return closer to the preliminary agreement Trump reached with Tehran in June.
That arrangement envisioned sanctions relief for Iranian oil sales, access to frozen Iranian funds and recognition of a role for Tehran in administering traffic through the Strait of Hormuz in exchange for reopening the strategic waterway.
For now, Washington is refusing to surrender what it sees as one of its strongest sources of leverage, while Tehran is seeking to revive the concessions contained in the earlier deal. That leaves the two sides still negotiating, but with Trump privately preparing his aides for the possibility that diplomacy could once again give way to airstrikes.

articles.title: Five killed, over 20 injured in overnight strikes as Russia, Ukraine trade blame
articles.body:
Russia and Ukraine have traded accusations concerning overnight airstrikes that killed five people and injured over 20 others.
“Five people were injured in a hostile overnight drone attack. Casualties include one person in Taganrog and four in Azov — among them a child — following the impact of drones on residential buildings,” said Yury Slyusar, governor of Russia’s southern Rostov region, on Telegram on Saturday.
Slyusar said all of those injured had been hospitalised. He claimed that more than 30 drones were downed by air defences over multiple cities in the region, including the city of Rostov-on-Don, as well as over the Azovsky, Myasnikovsky and Neklinovsky districts.
In the city of Azov, falling drones damaged apartment buildings, private homes, industrial facilities, a school, a cultural center and vehicles, Slyusar stated.
Veniamin Kondratyev, governor of the neighboring Krasnodar region, said a drone attack in Seversky district damaged a residential building and caused fires at two industrial facilities in the area.
The operational headquarters of the Krasnodar region later reported that three people were killed and two others injured in the region, adding that the fires at industrial facilities have been extinguished and that about 26,000 residents are currently without electricity.
Ukraine's General Staff claimed that it launched an overnight attack on the Ilsky oil refinery, situated in the Seversky district.
The Russian Defence Ministry claimed it downed 645 Ukrainian drones over 13 regions, as well as over the Black Sea, the Sea of Azov and Crimea, which Moscow annexed in 2014.
The ministry further claimed that overnight Russian strikes in Ukraine hit a data centre that “facilitated mobile internet operations and supported Starlink satellite communication systems for the Ukrainian Armed Forces” in the capital Kiev.
It also claimed hitting a port facility, a road bridge, and a logistics centre in Ukraine’s southern Odesa region, as well as a dry-cargo vessel “transporting military supplies” in the Black Sea.
Strikes in Ukraine
In the Ukrainian capital, the Kiev City Military Administration said a drone struck between a five-story residential building and a commercial establishment in the city’s Solomianskyi district, where an office building was also damaged.
Kiev Mayor Vitali Klitschko said five people had been injured, adding that search and rescue efforts in the area were ongoing.
He later said a fire broke out near warehouse buildings in the Darnytskyi district, while another fire occurred at a store after a drone fell on the territory of a shopping centre in the Sviatoshynskyi district.
In the broader Kiev region, two people were injured in the Boryspil district, where a fire broke out in a warehouse building, according to Ukraine's State Emergency Service.
Meanwhile, Odesa Governor Oleh Kiper said a “massive” attack took place on the region’s civilian infrastructure, damaging the facades and windows of more than 10 private homes and apartment buildings, a hotel and restaurant complex, and administrative buildings at a business facility in the southern part of the region.
Elsewhere, in the southeastern Zaporizhzhia region, two people were killed and seven others injured in the regional capital, according to local authorities.
"We ask (US) President (Donald) Trump to implement the Lindsey Graham Act against Russia and everyone who props up its war financially," Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on X, commenting on the overnight strikes. He further called on European leaders to impose additional sanctions on Moscow.
Ukraine’s Air Force claimed that the country’s air defences shot down 134 of 173 drones launched by Russia overnight.
Independent verification of the claims is difficult due to the ongoing war.
Moscow and Kiev have ramped up strikes in recent months, targeting each other’s logistics centres, ports and energy infrastructure.
Both sides deny deliberately targeting civilian infrastructure, maintaining the strikes are directed at military targets or facilities linked to military activities.

articles.title: SBU’s Alpha Special Forces Claim Hit on Rostov’s Azov Optical-Mechanical Plant
articles.body:
Ukrainian forces said they
struck the Azov Optical-Mechanical Plant in southern Russia’s Rostov region overnight into Saturday.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) said its Alpha Special Operations Center hit the plant in a joint operation with the Ukrainian Navy.
The SBU called the facility a key supplier of components used in precision weapons.
“This enterprise is one of the key optoelectronic sites of the Russian Tactical Missile Weapons Corporation. The plant produces radar and infrared homing heads for guided missiles, thermal imaging devices, and electronic systems for high-precision artillery,” the agency wrote in its press release.
The attack reportedly damaged the plant’s “optical and foundry production facilities, the assembly area, the galvanic shop and the printed circuit board manufacturing shop,” it added.
The plant was also reportedly struck in a Ukrainian attack on July 10.
The SBU also claimed it hit a Pantsir-S2 air defense system in the same region, likely as part of an operation to suppress local air defenses.
The agency also claimed involvement in hitting the Ilsky Oil Refinery in Russia’s Krasnodar Krai overnight.
Domestic missiles used
The operation used an array of domestically built weapons, including the Ruta, Palanytsia and Bars drone missiles, as well as Neptune anti-ship missiles, according to the SBU.
The Neptune missile was used to sink the flagship of Russia’s Black Sea Fleet, the Moskva, in April 2022. Ukraine unveiled an updated version in August 2025, with reports suggesting it has a range of up to 1,000 km (621 miles) – a jump from the 300 km (186 miles) range listed in a 2020 brochure for the original model.
Russia’s 7th-Largest Refinery in Perm Reportedly Offline After Friday Attack
The Palanytsia, which Kyiv described as a drone-missile hybrid, was first unveiled in 2024 and later upgraded in 2025, bringing the reported range to 650 km (400 miles).
The Ruta and Bars are classified similarly, with President Volodymyr Zelensky announcing successful tests of the former in late 2024.
Confirmed combat use of the Ruta was reported in 2025, followed by upgrades in 2026 that included a heavier warhead, a reported range of over 450 kilometers (280 miles), and a guidance system said to be immune to electronic warfare (EW) jamming.
The Bars, with a 700-800 kilometers (435-500 miles) range and a 50-100-kilogram (110-220-pound) warhead, was unveiled in April 2025.
