articles.title: The intelligence war is turning against the Houthis
articles.body:
The intelligence war is turning against the Houthis
Russian satellite intelligence and Iranian command integration helped the Houthis exploit weaknesses on Yemen’s western front. Now that system is itself under attack.
The collapse of Yemen’s western front was not primarily the result of sheer Houthi numbers. It resulted from a fused Russian-Iranian command system in which elements of Russia’s space-based geospatial intelligence (GEOINT) and signals intelligence (SIGINT) capabilities were integrated into an Iranian-led command-and-control (C2) system supporting Houthi operations. Human penetration of Tariq Saleh’s National Resistance Forces gave that system the access required to turn technical collection into a battlefield advantage.
Through Project AURORAH, the GEOINT and SIGINT fusion system I created, I identified and sequenced Russian military reconnaissance over Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Qatar, Bahrain, Iraq, Israel, the UAE and Jordan during the Iran-US war. A compartmented special-access programme (SAP) within the project reconstructed Russian orbital collection as a single multisensor system, including the sequences that preceded Iran’s precision strikes on countries across the region and on US military assets. That work later considerably assisted a major CNN investigation into Russian military geospatial satellite support for Iranian precision targeting across the Middle East.
The underlying principle had already emerged over Iran: orbital intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance (ISR) was no longer merely supporting operations, but helping construct the operational picture of the battlespace before strikes were carried out. That use of satellite intelligence was already visible during the Iran war. Russian GEOINT mapped how forces were deployed, their movement corridors, headquarters and logistical changes, while SIGINT mapped the sources of electronic signals, communications patterns and command relationships.
The advantage came from sequencing different forms of satellite collection over time, not from any single spacecraft. Different reconnaissance satellites provided complementary geographic and electromagnetic coverage, allowing changes in how forces moved and operated to be followed over time rather than captured as isolated snapshots. During the Iran war, this combination of different forms of satellite intelligence had already shown how Russian satellite intelligence could sharpen Iranian precision operations.
In Yemen, Iran provided the operational integration. Russian-derived intelligence was combined with Houthi tactical reporting and human access to build a detailed picture of how Tariq Saleh’s command actually functioned: which headquarters remained responsive, where reported positions diverged from reality, which formations were poorly coordinated, and where gaps existed in command, reporting and communications between the National Resistance Forces (NRF) and the Saudi-led Joint Forces Command (JFC). That picture made weaknesses along the western coastal front possible to exploit.
This is where the front broke. One command-and-control pathway connected JFC headquarters with elements of the NRF; another connected those forces with one another and with their own senior command. Once both became unreliable, inaccurate information flowed upwards while confused or manipulated instructions flowed downwards.
The consequences were specific. One NRF commander acknowledged an order to hold a blocking position and then withdrew. Another reported that a non-NRF Yemeni formation had vacated a military airfield when personnel were still there, giving commanders an inaccurate picture of where friendly forces were positioned and contributing to casualties after a strike. A Saudi special forces task force at Mokha was the first to recognise that reported force deployments no longer matched the reality on the ground.
Saudi strike missions had been prepared, but airpower could not be used freely when the locations of friendly forces could no longer be reliably confirmed. The problem was compounded when some NRF brigades discovered during activation that 50 to 60 percent of registered personnel had failed to report, despite months of JFC biometric registration, salary restoration and force consolidation. As coordination around the critical military hub of Jabal al-Nar deteriorated, NRF formations began leaving positions before the main Houthi forces had reached them.
That debacle has become the central learning event of the campaign. Combined Saudi-Yemeni and Saudi-Pakistani Joint Terminal Attack Controller (JTAC) teams are now being embedded with major northern formations, restoring an authenticated link between forces on the ground and the JFC’s strike system. Saudi Operational Mentoring and Liaison Teams (OMLT) are also providing direct links to the JFC and independently verifying the manpower, location and readiness of Yemeni formations. At the same time, positive authentication of commands, compartmented reporting and redundant encrypted communications are closing the vulnerabilities exposed at Mokha.
Saudi Arabia has used a similar approach before, against a different adversary. In January 2026, JFC military counterintelligence mapped and systematically degraded the Abu Dhabi command-and-control system supporting Southern Transitional Council (STC) operations in southern Yemen, while liaison and targeting mechanisms maintained a reliable picture of operations on the ground. Once that external layer was removed, UAE task forces and aligned formations rapidly lost their freedom of action and withdrew under pressure from the Saudi-led campaign.
The system now supporting the Houthis is far more sophisticated. Russia provides satellite-based intelligence and signals intelligence; Iran integrates that information into Houthi command and operations. But that sophistication also creates vulnerabilities: the system depends on secure communications, specialist personnel, intelligence-fusion nodes, technical advisers and continuous links between Sanaa and battlefield headquarters.
Those vulnerabilities are now being targeted. On the evening of September 19, the Iranian-led top-level command-and-control structure in Sanaa suffered a massive blow. Confirmed senior Houthi battlefield losses now include at least two major generals, seven brigadier generals and 32 colonels, many removed alongside their immediate aides, staff and communications elements. There are also strong indications that figures above the rank of major general have been neutralised within the highest levels of the Houthi command structure, together with associated foreign personnel, although those details remain deliberately withheld for now.
The effect is more important than the count. Front-line command is being systematically degraded while senior command nodes in Sanaa are simultaneously coming under precise JFC air strikes, disrupting the chain between intelligence collection, decision-making, targeting and execution. Headquarters forced to relocate, surviving commanders attempting to reconnect with subordinate units and remaining junior Iranian advisers establishing alternative pathways all generate fresh signatures that can be detected, correlated and geolocated.
This is why the Houthi advance is now struggling to reproduce the momentum of the West Coast breakthrough. The command links they exploited are being hardened, while their own externally supported command-and-control network is being progressively blinded and exposed. The failure on the West Coast has therefore become a lesson the Saudi-led forces are acting on, rather than a permanent weakness in their military structure.
The Saudi-led JFC’s broader transformation in C6ISR – the systems connecting command, communications, intelligence and combat capabilities – target development and faster sensor-to-shooter integration has changed the military equation since 2015. At the same time, sustained Houthi escalation has exhausted the restraint that governed Saudi policy for years. The major Saudi-led campaign now taking shape will therefore begin against an adversary whose external command support is already under sustained attack.
That is the decisive difference. The Russian-Iranian system sustaining and amplifying Houthi military power is being degraded before major Saudi-led air, land and naval operations are fully under way, while the tactical failures exposed at Mokha are being corrected within the Saudi-led JFC. The Houthis exploited a compromised command system once; they are now being forced to fight while the external system that magnified their own effectiveness is systematically dismantled.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

articles.title: Saudi Arabia has not ruled out nuclear weapons: report
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Saudi Arabia has not ruled out nuclear weapons: report
US intelligence agencies have assessed that Saudi Arabia has not ruled out developing a nuclear weapons programme, according to classified documents provided to Congress and described to The Washington Post by US officials.
The assessment is raising fresh questions about US President Donald Trump’s agreement to help Riyadh establish a civilian nuclear industry. Some US lawmakers fear the deal could give Saudi Arabia the means to produce nuclear material that might eventually be used as a weapon, although the intelligence finding does not say the kingdom has decided to build one.
The agreement, announced in July, would allow US companies to pursue nuclear energy projects in Saudi Arabia. The Trump administration says the partnership will strengthen ties with Riyadh, uphold non-proliferation standards, and reduce the prospect of the kingdom turning to Russia or China for nuclear technology.
But Democratic lawmakers say the deal's restrictions do not go far enough. Under the agreement, Saudi uranium enrichment would initially be limited to less than five percent. That ceiling could rise to 20% following a further study and written agreement, according to The Washington Post.
The agreement also does not require Saudi Arabia to adopt the International Atomic Energy Agency’s Additional Protocol, which would give inspectors broader access to nuclear sites and information.
In a letter to Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Friday, senators led by Ed Markey and Jeff Merkley accused the administration of accepting weaker safeguards that could enable Riyadh to acquire uranium-enrichment capabilities.
Their concerns have been sharpened by the intelligence assessment, which officials said was among classified material sent to Congress last month. The State Department’s contribution to those documents appeared more confident in the deal’s safeguards and Saudi assurances, the officials told the newspaper.
Saudi Arabia did not answer the newspaper’s questions directly. Instead, it referred to an earlier statement by Energy Minister Abdulaziz bin Salman saying its nuclear programme would be peaceful and pursued with responsibility and transparency. The State Department said the US "does not and will not support a Saudi nuclear weapon program".
Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman said in 2018 that Saudi Arabia would seek a nuclear weapon if Iran developed one. That conditional statement has long fuelled concern that an Iranian bomb could trigger a regional arms race.
Congress is reviewing the agreement and could move to block it, though opponents would need sufficient votes to overcome a possible presidential veto.
Its future may also depend on diplomacy over Israel: a senior US administration official told The Washington Post that Saudi normalisation with Israel remains a condition of the deal, while analysts said Riyadh is unlikely to take that step as long as Israel rules out a Palestinian state.

articles.title: US and China move to ease tensions with tariff cuts and new AI dialogue
articles.body:
China and the United States have agreed on $30 billion in reciprocal tariff reductions and the opening of a dialogue on artificial intelligence as part of an eight-point agreement reached following Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit to Washington. The announcement was issued by China’s Foreign Ministry shortly after Xi landed in Beijing at the end of a three-day visit to the United States.
According to the Chinese Foreign Ministry, Xi Jinping and Donald Trump agreed to build “a constructive relationship of strategic stability” between China and the United States, based on mutual respect, fairness and reciprocity. The provision, the first of eight, is intended to establish a broad framework for relations between the world’s two largest economies following months of trade tensions and technological competition.
At the heart of the agreement is the $30 billion reciprocal tariff reduction arrangement, covering products defined as “non-sensitive” by both sides. U.S. tariff reductions will apply to agricultural products, seafood and medical equipment, while Chinese relief will apply to products including toys and small electrical appliances. The sides also approved the establishment and advancement of a joint trade council and an extension of the outcomes reached in previous trade talks in Kuala Lumpur.
The agreement follows directly from a decision made earlier this week to extend by another two months the trade “truce” between the two powers, which had been due to expire on Nov. 10, as U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Wednesday
Will the agreement ease tensions between the two powers?
The current agreement builds on understandings reached at the Busan summit in South Korea in October last year, where the sides announced a basic agreement on trade, which continued to take shape in further talks held in Beijing in May. As part of the new deal, according to the White House, China committed to purchasing at least 10 million tons of U.S. coal in each of 2027 and 2028, while the two sides established joint working groups to address agricultural market access and stabilization of the global oil supply.
One of the most notable provisions of the current agreement concerns the establishment of a dedicated dialogue channel — also dubbed the “super intelligence” channel — through which the two sides will exchange views on the risks and benefits of artificial intelligence technology. The first round of discussions under the dialogue is scheduled for November, while a separate communication channel will be established to handle AI-related incidents. The move marks one of the first mutual acknowledgments by Washington and Beijing of the need for international coordination surrounding the sensitive technology.
On broader foreign policy, the leaders agreed that Iran must uphold its commitment not to develop nuclear weapons — with the White House using stronger language, stating that Iran “can never” possess a nuclear weapon — and that transit fees should not be imposed on international waterways. Another provision addresses cooperation between Chinese and U.S. law enforcement authorities in combating drug trafficking, which the sides said has already produced tangible results, including dozens of arrests.
The three-day visit produced no major public breakthroughs, but the agreements announced at its conclusion — chiefly the tariff arrangement and AI dialogue — represent another attempt by the world’s two largest economies to contain tensions and keep trade channels open amid a dispute that has expanded in recent months to include export controls, rare-earth minerals, technology and the shipping industry.

articles.title: Russia expected to intensify hybrid war on Europe
articles.body:
Russia expected to intensify hybrid war on Europe
September 26, 2026
Just a few months ago, Russia's war was an distant reality for many people in Europe outside of Ukraine. If Russian drones occasionally entered the airspace of countries like Poland or Romania, even official statements seemed strangely dismissive and abstract. Even after a Russian drone struck a high-rise apartment building in the eastern Romanian city of Galati in late May this year, many EU and NATO representatives hesitated to accuse Russia of intentional action. At most, there was discussion of hybrid warfare.
The situation has changed radically since the summer. Drone overflights have become almost daily in certain parts of central and southeastern Europe, and there have even been crashes and explosions, particularly in countries bordering Ukraine. Alerts are becoming more frequent, with authorities increasingly having to close airspace or suspend operations at airports, as unauthorized flights are detected. Russia has been bombing border crossings, infrastructure and trains in Ukraine, but very close to other borders. Acts of sabotage are also increasingly common.
For the Baltic states, Poland, Moldova and Romania in particular, the war has long ceased to be "hybrid." More and more, politicians in these countries are saying that Russia is acting deliberately.
Drones violate Moldovan and Romanian airspace
This became evident this week in an unprecedented manner. Moldova recorded four drones entering Moldovan airspace, two of which exploded in Moldovan territory. Wreckage of another was also found. The country's northern airspace was closed temporarily.
Two drones also violated Romanian airspace; with one crashing near the northern town of Solca. A nearby border crossing with Ukraine a few dozen kilometers away was closed as a result. NATO aircraft were scrambled near the Danube Delta.
The scrambling of NATO aircraft has become more common in response to Russian air attacks in Ukraine.
In Poland, NATO fighter jets were scrambled twice in response to Russian attacks near the border with Ukraine. Two Polish border crossings were evacuated after a fire broke out at a Starlink ground station near the village of Wola Krobowska, 40 kilomters (ca. 25 miles) south of the Polish capital Warsaw, on Wednesday night. The station is used to route internet traffic through Poland to Ukraine.
On the same day, a Russian Mi-8 helicopter violated Polish airspace and remained there for 42 seconds according to the Polish military.
Polish Prime Minister Tusk says Europe needs to prepare
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk spoke very bluntly in Krakow on Thursday and said that Russia was refining its "disgusting forms of pressure" and Poland must be prepared for them.
Russian President Vladimir Putin "wants to exhaust Ukraine by destroying its industrial and energy infrastructure, but he also wants to exhaust Europe," Tusk said. He added that there was a suspicion that the fire at the Starlink ground station had been deliberate.
Earlier this month, Tusk had already warned the Polish parliament that there might be Russian drone and even missile attacks against those who supported Ukraine.
Moldovan President Maia Sandu also reacted very strongly on Thursday, saying that Russia's war was a danger to all of Europe and reasserting Moldova's support for Ukraine.
In Romania, reactions were less clear. Defense Minister Radu Miruta said that not more than a "diplomatic protest" was needed, though he acknowledged that the drone that had crashed in Solca had new technical features, which suggested it could be a newer type of Russian jet-powered drone. 
In New York on Wednesday, in his address to the United Nations General Assembly, Romanian President Nicusor Dan had said: "We are in the fifth year of the illegal, unprovoked and unjustified war of aggression waged on a large scale against Ukraine by a permanent member of the Security Council." He had added that as the "EU member state with the longest border with Ukraine, Romania has directly felt the effects of this war through repeated violations of our airspace."
And he too reasserted support for Ukraine: "We have said it before, and we say it again: Romania will stand with Ukraine and its people, who are acting in legitimate self-defense, for as long as it takes."
Attacks on western Europe from the Mediterranean?
Meanwhile, there is growing speculation that Russia could expand its war to Western Europe. On Thursday, the Spanish newspaper El Mundo published information about a CIA report warning that Russia could be preparing drone attacks on Italy, France and Spain. The attacks could be launched from international waters in the Mediterranean and from vessels that were part of Russia's shadow fleet.
There has been no official confirmation so far. French President Emmanuel Macron said that that the CIA had not informed France of this information, but he did say that the possibility Russia could launch an attack against Europe was "plausible."
At a press conference in Denmark on Thursday, politicians and military officials warned that Russia was expected to intensify its hybrid war against the West and NATO in the coming months. The situation is currently the most serious since the end of the Cold War," said Defense Minister Jeppe Bruus.
This article was originally published in German.

articles.title: Belgium Contracts Specialized Drones and Boats for Ukrainian De-Mining Efforts
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Belgium Contracts Specialized Drones and Boats for Ukrainian De-Mining Efforts
Belgium has ordered three specialized TRIDENT vessels designated for launching K-STER C underwater mine-countermeasure drones for Ukraine, according to Militarnyi on September 25.
The Belgian Ministry of Defense allocated €9.9 million ($11.3 million) for the procurement, with the contract officially awarded to Exail Robotics Belgium through a negotiated procedure without prior publication.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The TRIDENT (Tactical RHIB for Identification and Disposal of Explosive Naval Threats) serves as a tactical craft designed to locate and eliminate explosive naval hazards.
Manufactured by Belgian company Exail, the K-STER C is a lightweight underwater drone designed to destroy mines using a shaped charge integrated into its forward section.
Its swiveling warhead allows precise targeting of various submerged explosive devices, while its construction incorporates stealth technologies to minimize acoustic and magnetic signatures.
The device measures 1,500 mm in length, 445 mm in height, and weighs 55 kg in air. The head can tilt and rotate from +90° to −90°, enabling operators to neutralize targets from optimal angles.
Powered by a lithium-ion battery, the propulsion system relies on two horizontal and two vertical thrusters. It features a dual-frequency sonar for long-range detection and close-range targeting, along with a day/night camera and searchlight.
The drone operates autonomously for up to one hour, reaches top speeds of 5 knots (with operational speeds ranging from 0 to 3 knots), functions at depths down to 300 meters, and maintains an operational radius of up to 1,500 meters.
On June 18, 2026, Belgian Defense Minister Theo Francken outlined new plans for the delivery of F-16 fighter jets to Ukraine, announcing an increase in both the number and operational status of aircraft to be transferred. Speaking to journalists ahead of the NATO Defense Ministers Meeting, Francken said Belgium had revised its earlier commitments and would provide more F-16s than previously pledged.

articles.title: Ukraine's ex-defence minister Fedorov unveils new Army of Robots project
articles.body:
Ukraine's ex-defence minister Fedorov unveils new Army of Robots project
Former Ukrainian Defence Minister Mykhailo Fedorov has announced a new defence project called Army of Robots. The concept involves developing humanoid robots capable of carrying out simple frontline tasks instead of soldiers. Fedorov presented the project on 26 September at the IT Arena 2026 conference in Lviv.
Source: Oboronka, a defence industry project created within Ukrainska Pravda's holding company
Details: The new project is a continuation of the Air. Land. Economy concept that Fedorov's team has been working on since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion.
Quote: "There will be humanoid robots that will perform simple tasks: reloading a machine gun, replacing a battery or installing a sensor. These are things a robot can be taught quickly and carry out after a rapid deployment to the battlefield."
More details: Fedorov said the first goal of the Army of Robots project was for a humanoid robot to kill a Russian soldier within six months of the programme's launch. The project also aims to conduct its first operation involving robots and drones within the first 12 months, with the systems "communicating" through algorithms. Fedorov's team believes the project could change perceptions of what warfare will look like.
The project envisages creating a technological ecosystem to be developed by a "large private technology company", whose name will be announced later. The idea is for humanoid robots to operate autonomously alongside UAVs, unmanned ground vehicles and other classes of unmanned weapons.
Fedorov said the Army of Robots project is currently seeking engineers, teams and specialists in Ukraine and the West, as well as investment to develop robots capable of replacing Ukrainian infantry soldiers on the battlefield.
Project announcement. Video: Fedorov
In addition to this line of work, the Army of Robots project also envisages developing low-cost interceptor missiles and AI-based strike systems. Ukrainian and foreign defence companies specialising in software, weapons manufacturing and other technologies are being invited to take part in the project.
Background:
- In early September 2026, Fedorov announced plans to establish his own defence-tech company, with Alex Karp, CEO of US technology company Palantir, set to become its key investor.
- A venture fund is also being established in Kyiv to invest in defence companies and finance both startups and established manufacturers.

articles.title: Zelenskyy Calls On Trump To Enact Russia Sanctions After Deadly Attacks Across Ukraine
articles.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has called on US President Donald Trump to enact sanctions against Russia amid its deadly attacks across Ukraine, which have become increasingly frequent as cold weather starts to set in.
"Russia is escalating every single day," Zelenskyy wrote on social media on September 26. "We ask President Trump to implement the Lindsey Graham Act against Russia and everyone who props up its war financially."
The law, signed by Trump a week ago, gives the president sweeping new authority to impose sanctions and tariffs on Russia, its energy sector, and foreign governments and entities that help Moscow evade existing restrictions.
Zelenskyy said that Russia's latest strikes on Ukraine killed at least four people in the Zaporizhzhya and Sumy regions, partly occupied by Russian forces, and left more than a dozen more injured across the country.
Civilian and energy infrastructure was damaged in at least eight Ukrainian regions, including a kindergarden in the capital, Kyiv, and a university in the country's second-largest city, Kharkiv, he added.
In Zaporizhzhya, fire swept through the city's central market following the attack, local resident Olena told RFE/RL's Ukrainian Service -- the place where she had worked for more than 25 years is now covered in charred debris.
"The people won't come here anymore, that's for sure.... All the goods reeked of smoke," Olena said at the scene, adding that she would now have to relocate and search for a new place to work.
With a fifth wartime winter approaching, Russian strikes on Ukraine have become a daily occurrence.
Over the past four years, Moscow has sought to pressure Kyiv into accepting its hard-line demands by pounding the country's energy infrastructure and leaving thousands without heat or electricity amid freezing temperatures.
Since this summer, however, Kyiv has increasingly responded to Russian attacks with a campaign of long-range strikes targeting military and energy sites inside Russia.
The campaign has left Russia with nationwide fuel shortages and has stoked discontent among its citizens, who were largely disconnected from the war in Ukraine.
In the latest such strike on September 26, Ukrainian forces said they had hit the Ilsky oil refinery in Russia's southern Krasnodar region, describing the facility as helping fuel Moscow's war effort.
US Seeking Diplomatic Settlement
The developments came amid what appears to be renewed US interest in negotiating a diplomatic settlement to the long-running war, with the White House reportedly seeking to find a solution before winter.
At their latest meeting in New York this week, Zelenskyy told Trump he "hoped" that Washington would help to end the war "as soon as possible."
The Ukrainian president had told journalists that Washington had proposed holding what would be the first Ukraine-Russia-US meeting in many months at a relatively low "technical level," with the United Arab Emirates serving as host.
While there was no immediate confirmation from the United States, Russian President Vladimir Putin said that all peace proposals were "on the table" but added that Moscow had to weigh its interests.
Control of Ukraine’s eastern Donetsk region has been a central sticking point since US-led peace efforts began under the Trump administration in 2025.
Russia has vowed to seize the territory by force if Ukraine refuses to cede the areas it still holds, making Donetsk a major military priority.

articles.title: Fighting escalates as Yemeni forces hit Houthis, Saudi Arabia intercepts drones
articles.body:
Yemeni government forces have said they struck Houthi positions and supply lines in the southwestern province of Taiz.
Military spokesman Majid Abdullah al-Nazili published footage on the US social media platform X that he said showed strikes on Houthi fighters and supply routes in Dhubab and other parts of Taiz.
Dhubab is a coastal town in the Bab al Mandeb district overlooking the Red Sea near the northern entrance to the strategic strait.
Al-Nazili did not provide details on casualties or damage.
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree separately claimed Saudi warplanes carried out 14 airstrikes and a missile attack in the previous 24 hours in the Taiz, Amran, Marib and Saada provinces.
Meanwhile, Saudi air defences intercepted two drones launched early on Saturday by Houthis toward the Riyadh region.
Turki al-Maliki, spokesman of the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen, said Saudi forces were monitoring missile and drone threats directed toward the kingdom.
He said air defences intercepted and destroyed the drones launched toward the Riyadh region.
Maritime blockade
The Houthis have been engaged in renewed fighting with Yemen government forces since Yemen’s civil war reignited in July, when the group declared a maritime blockade on Riyadh.
Yemen has been engulfed in conflict since Houthis seized the national capital Sanaa and several provinces in 2014.
That prompted a Saudi-led Arab coalition to intervene in 2015 in support of the internationally recognised government.
Renewed fighting began in July, when the group declared a maritime blockade on Riyadh.
Houthis recently claimed advances along the Red Sea Coast and Bab el-Mandab Strait, and have also targeted the oil infrastructure of Saudi Arabia.

articles.title: Iran makes diplomatic push at UN with 24 meetings and Trump envoy talks
articles.body:
While Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s visit and speech at the UN General Assembly this week will be remembered mainly for the walkout by members of numerous delegations as he began speaking and for the relatively few diplomatic meetings he held during his stay in New York, the Iranian delegation sent to the gathering appears to have had a far busier diplomatic agenda.
Representing Iran at the gathering were President Masoud Pezeshkian and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, who is still in New York and, according to sources, is expected to remain there for the next several days.
According to a CNN review of Araghchi’s visit to New York, he met with representatives of at least 24 countries, including the foreign ministers of leading European powers. Netanyahu, by comparison, met with nine leaders during the General Assembly, including Argentine President Javier Milei, Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis and Slovenia’s new prime minister, Janez Janša.
Among others, Araghchi met with EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas and his counterparts from Britain, France, Germany, Spain, Portugal, the Netherlands, Poland, Russia and Ukraine. Araghchi also met with his Jordanian counterpart, Ayman Safadi, shortly after Iran attacked U.S. targets on the territory of the Hashemite Kingdom. Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian met with UN Secretary-General António Guterres and spoke with representatives of Western media outlets.
But the highlight of Iran’s diplomatic activity during the General Assembly was Araghchi’s meeting with Steve Witkoff, U.S. President Donald Trump’s envoy. After the meeting, Araghchi told Western journalists that he had put a new proposal on the negotiating table between Tehran and Washington. Although reports overnight said Trump had rejected the proposal and was preparing for further military strikes, from the Iranian perspective, the significance lay in the fact that the meeting took place at all.
Araghchi also heard tough messages directed at his country in other meetings. According to a BBC report, British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband told his Iranian counterpart: “The Foreign Secretary reiterated the UK’s unwavering resolve to combat threats from Iranian-linked groups on UK soil, including attacks on the British Jewish community.”
CNN, which has been engaged in an ongoing dispute with the Trump administration, wrote of the Iranian delegation’s arrival at the General Assembly: “Seven months after escaping with his life from a U.S.-coordinated Israeli airstrike that killed Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, Iran’s top diplomat walked the streets of Manhattan this week under the protection of the U.S. Secret Service.”
US economic pressure intensifies
Alongside Iran’s efforts to renew ties with Western countries, Washington appears to be seeking to use additional pressure to deepen Tehran’s isolation. According to a Wall Street Journal report, a senior U.S. Treasury official recently traveled to several countries in Europe and the Middle East that trade with Iran and delivered a message: “You either trade with Tehran or Washington.”
The newspaper noted that in recent days, Iranian airlines have been cut off from vital regional routes while the Islamic Republic’s leading commercial bank has been prevented from conducting transactions in the United Arab Emirates and Turkey. The measures come on top of sanctions imposed on Iran in recent years and the continuing U.S. naval blockade of Iranian seaports.
British lawyer Nigel Kushner, who has advised companies on Iran sanctions for two decades, told The Wall Street Journal that he had never seen such intense pressure brought to bear on Iran’s banking and aviation sectors.
“The U.S. has achieved greater impact in a matter of weeks than during the lengthier campaigns commenced from 2010” he said.
During his address to the General Assembly, Iranian President Pezeshkian acknowledged that U.S. sanctions posed a problem for his country but said they would ultimately have the opposite effect.
“The resistance of the Iranian people will only increase in the face of sanctions, increased pressure, increased bullying," Pezeshkian said. “We will never bow our head or bend at the knee.”

articles.title: War’s next tech leap: Person who built Ukraine’s “Army of Drones” is now building “Army of Robots”
articles.body:
The person who built Ukraine's "Army of Drones" is now building an "Army of Robots". Myhailo Fedorov, the former defense minister, has launched a private-sector push to robotize the war, wanting machines to take the deadliest jobs, evacuating the wounded, laying and clearing mines, and fighting, so soldiers come home, he wrote, announcing the effort at the IT Arena conference in Lviv.
The pitch rests on a track record. Fedorov's Army of Drones, launched in 2022, helped make drones the weapon behind more than 95 percent of Ukraine's battlefield hits. Over 700 makers now building them, and he is betting robotization is the next such leap.
Army of Robots is meant to be an ecosystem, not a company: investing in defense-tech firms, standing up R&D, testing with troops, and scaling fast, whatever works. Fedorov is running it from outside government, having left the defense ministry in July and started building a defense-tech company backed by Palantir chief Alex Karp.
Robots take the deadliest jobs
Fedorov's vision is a battlefield where machines go first. A sensor spots a threat, then a robot enters the danger zone, he says. Humanoid robots would carry ammunition and pull out the wounded, lay and clear minefields, scout, hold positions, and strike, taking the roles that today cost soldiers their lives. For now, it is a vision more than a fielded capability: Fedorov is describing where he wants the battlefield to go, not a robot force already in the fight.
The Army of Drones sets the model
The aim, Fedorov says, is to gather the best engineers, combat experience, and capital and point them at one goal: making robots fight instead of people. The obstacle is Russia, which he said has learned to quickly copy and scale military technology, so Ukraine must keep inventing the next cycle before the enemy does.
"Russia will stop only when we can break its backbone," he says, arguing that it will take Western capital, world-class engineers, and private initiative.

articles.title: Combat shows speed alone can’t catch Russia’s jet-powered drones, despite eight Ukrainian makers’ assurances. So why can’t they stop them?
articles.body:
Last winter, eight Ukrainian companies told the defense minister that their interceptors were ready to knock Russia's jet-powered drones out of the sky. They were not. A fast-flying drone is the easy part of the design, while combat testing exposed what the interceptors lacked in key features to chase an evading jet-powered Geran, presidential adviser Serhii Beskrestnov, known as Flash, said in an interview with NV.
Ukraine's answer to Russia's fast, hard-to-stop jet drones was supposed to be cheap interceptors, and last winter, their makers said they had them. But a jet Geran flies 450 to 500 kilometers an hour, up from the Geran-3's 320, varies its speed to slip past defenses, and will dodge harder once interceptors appear.
Catching one takes maneuverability, machine-vision target-lock, and fuel to loiter and search, not just speed, Flash said. Ukraine's cheap interceptors have already downed about half of Russia's slower drones, but the jet-powered systems have stayed a step ahead.
Eight makers said "ready"
At a meeting last winter called by Mykhailo Fedorov, then-defense minister, all eight interceptor makers reported the same thing: "everything's ready, the solution exists, it flies, we tested it, speed is sufficient," Flash recalled.
The mistake, he said, was that no one checked on them week to week. There were also too few jet Gerans in the skies then to test against.
"On the range, they showed: it flies. That was the problem," explained Flash.
Speed is the easy part
The engines are not the obstacle, Flash continues, since they can be bought abroad, and neither is a plane that flies fast in a straight line. The hard part is a machine agile enough to chase a jet-powered Geran, which is far more maneuverable than the propeller kind and will start changing altitude and throwing evasive maneuvers once interceptors appear.
Because an operator's aim frays at such speeds, he said, the decisive pieces are automatic target capture by machine vision and automatic terminal guidance.
"Building a construction that just flies fast is the easiest part," he added.
Mass orders must wait
That is why Ukraine cannot simply order thousands to blanket the country, Flash said: it first needs a proven design that works for any crew, from Security Service specialists to territorial defense soldiers, and is simple to launch, operate, and maintain.
Once such a sample exists, he said, scaling up is only a question of money. Meanwhile, the work is moving: a Ukrainian interceptor recently notched its first kills against jet Gerans and is heading toward mass production.

articles.title: Germany’s Wadephul meets Russia’s Lavrov amid tensions over ‘escalation’
articles.body:
NEW YORK — German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul held a surprise meeting with his Russian counterpart Sergey Lavrov at the U.N. on Saturday, just one day after he welcomed the U.S. invite for Russian President Vladimir Putin to the G20 summit.
"It was an intense conversation", Wadephul told German public television ZDF after the meeting, which lasted about 30 minutes. "Of course, we did not reach agreement on key points. It was important to me to make it clear that Germany does not accept incidents such as the drone attack in Leipzig, and that this is an escalation that is unacceptable. And I clearly warned Russia not to continue down this path. We can defend ourselves, we can fight back. And that's exactly what we'll do."
“Wadephul called on the Russian Federation to abandon its dangerous path of escalation toward Germany, Europe, and NATO,” a German official said after the meeting. The official was granted anonymity to discuss the meeting.
Advertisement
The minister also “condemned Russia’s ongoing and increasingly targeted aggression against the Ukrainian civilian population” and highlighted that, “every month, tens of thousands of Russian soldiers die in a hopeless war of attrition, while the Russian economy continues to collapse,” the official said.
The meeting of the German and the Russian ministers — the first of that kind since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 — comes amid high tensions between Berlin and Moscow.
Earlier this month, the German government accused Russian intelligence services of having orchestrated the attempted drone attack on a Ukrainian cargo plane at the Leipzig airport in Eastern Germany. In reaction, Germany imposed sanctions, including the closure of Russia's consulate in Bonn, to which Moscow responded with similar measures against Germany, notably the closure of Germany's consulate in St. Petersburg.
Germany and Russia also clashed during a U.N. Security Council meeting earlier this week, during which Wadephul slammed “Russia's reckless and dangerous escalation in Europe,” while Lavrov accused Europe of “criminal methods.”
The German official said that Wadephul “made clear” during Saturday's meeting “that incidents such as the recent attempted attack in Leipzig or other hybrid attacks would not shake Germany’s determination to support Ukraine, which is under attack. However, they would further damage bilateral relations with Germany, which have already been severely strained by Russia.”
The Russian side did not immediately provide a detailed readout of Saturday's meeting. Moscow's foreign ministry spokesperson, Maria Zakharova, instead referred to a polemic Russian report that calls into question the authenticity of the Bucha massacre, and that appears to have been put on the table during the ministers' meeting.
Advertisement
The meeting was also immediately overshadowed by different explanations over who had requested it.
Zakharova claimed that Wadephul had asked to meet Lavrov. Yet Wadephul told ZDF that he had agreed to meet Lavrov after the Russian foreign minister, through third-party intermediaries, signaled a willingness to engage in talks.
The reunion of Wadephul and Lavrov was held against the backdrop of renewed efforts by the U.S. and its Western allies to jumpstart peace talks between Russia and Ukraine. Earlier this week, the U.S. government issued an invitation to Putin for the G20 summit in Miami in December, raising the possibility of potential negotiations between the Russian president and his Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Florida.
While some other European leaders criticized that invitation, Wadephul said he welcomed the initiative, calling it "a litmus test for Putin."
“Opportunities like this must be seized,” Wadephul said on Friday.
Wadephul had added a caveat, however, saying that, “in my view, a ceasefire is also necessary in order to be able to negotiate in earnest.”
This article was updated with Wadephul's comments to ZDF.

articles.title: Pentagon brings in Ukrainian jamming maker to do to its candidate drones what Russia does to Ukraine’s, and see which survives
articles.body:
A Ukrainian jamming-systems maker went to a US Army base to do to candidate drones what Russia does to Ukraine's: flood them with electronic warfare (EW) and see which survives. Unwave company has tested four of its EW systems at Fort Carson in Colorado as part of the Pentagon's Drone Dominance program and has been asked to continue supporting it.
The Pentagon is using Drone Dominance to choose the drones it will buy at scale, more than 200,000 by 2027, and it needs to know they work under jamming, the condition that decides most drone fights in Ukraine.
So it brought in a Ukrainian electronic-warfare maker to supply that jamming, turning Ukraine's hard-won counter-drone experience into the test bench for American hardware. It follows a pattern in which US defense efforts adopt Ukrainian battlefield models.
Ukraine brings the jamming
From 24 August to 2 September, Unwave's team worked at the base, running scenarios that pitted its jammers against drones tasked with protecting fixed positions, moving vehicles, and infrastructure.
The crews operated from three separate positionsat short and long range to compare how drones from different manufacturers held up.
"Our mission was to create conditions as close to the real battlefield as possible," the company said, adding that it judged the tasks successfully completed but could not detail the scenarios for security reasons.
In all, 14 drone makers and three electronic-warfare firms took part.
Four systems on show
Unwave brought four:
- VIHA, which it calls Ukraine's first tactical-operational jammer for directed suppression of drones
- BOOMBOX, built to shield troops and positions from FPV and drop-drones
- SHATRO, for vehicles
- CHOVEN-2, a multi-frequency amplifier for cars.
Its participation was organized by Revenant Technologies, a US firm that specializes in bringing combat-proven defense tech to the American market, and helped design the scenarios using its ties to Ukraine and frontline experience.
A foothold in the US market
For Unwave, the value is a door into the alliance's security architecture. The event showed the importance of Ukrainian, American, and European specialists testing together, the company said, and "such interaction will help integrate Ukrainian technologies into the security architecture of our allies."
