Group of 14 Bipartisan US Senators Urge Trump to Block Putin From G20 Summit in Miami
A bipartisan group of 14 US senators sent a letter calling on President Donald Trump to rescind his invitation to Russian leader Vladimir Putin for the upcoming G20 summit scheduled for December in Miami, as reported by The Washington Post.
The initiative was spearheaded by Republican Senator Roger Wicker of Mississippi, chairman of the Senate Armed Services Committee, and Democratic Senator Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire, the lead Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, alongside six other Democrats and six other Republicans.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
"Putin alone bears responsibility for Russia’s full-scale aggressive war against Ukraine. Allowing his participation in the G20 summit in the United States raises serious concerns about legitimizing and normalizing a government that continues to launch daily strikes on civilian targets in Ukraine every day," the senators stated in the letter, according to The Washington Post.
The lawmakers also highlighted that Putin, Russian Finance Minister Anton Siluanov, and other members of the Russian delegation remain under US sanctions for actions Washington considers a threat to national security.
According to the signatories, failing to isolate Putin from the international community leaves him with far less motivation to end Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
The Washington Post noted that Siluanov’s previous attendance at a G20 finance ministers’ meeting in Asheville, North Carolina, last month drew sharp pushback from several nations.
European Union representatives specifically requested that the Russian minister be excluded from the official group photograph.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio previously announced that the United States had formally invited Vladimir Putin to attend the G20 summit scheduled for December in Miami.
Speaking after a meeting with Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov, Rubio expressed hope that Putin would attend, noting the summit could provide an opportunity for talks with US President Donald Trump and other global leaders.
Rubio also highlighted that Washington was open to playing a constructive role in facilitating a limited ceasefire involving energy and grain, stating that while such a step would not solve Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, it could help alleviate broader global pressures.

articles.title: Russian strikes on Kyiv data centers disrupt operations at several Ukrainian media outlets
articles.body:
Russian strikes on Kyiv data centers disrupt operations at several Ukrainian media outlets
Several Ukrainian media outlets reported disruptions to their operations on Sept. 26 following Russian strikes on data centers in Kyiv.
Russian forces intensified attacks on data centers in Kyiv in September, causing internet outages across the capital and disrupting access to some online services.
TV channel Novyny.Live said it had temporarily suspended broadcasting due to disruptions affecting some of its services following a Russian attack on infrastructure in Kyiv.
Military media outlet Armiia TV also suspended operations on Sept. 26 following Russian strikes.
Public broadcaster Suspilne said its website's video players were not working because they were operated by Cosmonova, whose data center was damaged on Sept. 25. On the following day, Cosmonova said its data center had been damaged by a Russian attack for the second time and was knocked out of operation.
A Russian attack on Sept. 23 damaged a Kyiv data center housing network equipment for internet provider UTELS, causing service disruptions. The attack also affected cloud service Fex.net and disrupted internet access for around 100,000 households in Kyiv and the surrounding region, the Digital Transformation Ministry said.
After another Russian attack on Kyiv on Sept. 24, providers Domonet, Kievnet, and Faust reported infrastructure damage and internet outages. Russia also destroyed a data center hosting MiroHost's infrastructure, with the company saying it could not yet estimate when services would be restored.
Another Russian attack damaged a Datagroup data center on Sept. 25.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said following a meeting with senior military officials on Sept. 25 that the Ukrainian government had decided to strengthen the protection of data centers and other critical communications infrastructure.
"This is the beginning of a phase where, since September, they have started taking it out systematically," Anatolii Frolenkov, a representative of the 1-IX internet exchange point, told the Kyiv Independent.
Despite the recent damage, Frolenkov said knocking out internet access across Ukraine would be extremely difficult.
Providers can limit the impact of individual strikes by duplicating network equipment, maintaining backup communications routes, and distributing infrastructure across different locations, including outside Ukraine, he said.
But that strategy is expensive, leaving many providers without sufficient backup infrastructure, more vulnerable when equipment is destroyed.
"The internet will not disappear completely," Frolenkov said. "There will be outages, there will be problems. It won't work as smoothly or as quickly, things may glitch, and operators may go down for a couple of hours because the infrastructure is being physically destroyed."

articles.title: Trump rejects Iranian proposal, expects war to continue after midterm elections
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump rejected Iran's seven-day proposal to open the Strait of Hormuz, he told reporters outside of the White House on Saturday.
Iran raised the initiative at the UN General Assembly in New York, saying it had been transmitted to the Americans via Qatari mediators and that it could reopen the strategic waterway and put an end to hostilities in the region within seven days.
But in comments to reporters at the White House, Trump said: "I reject their proposal. ... I rejected their deal.
"They want to make a deal to open the Hormuz Strait immediately because they're losing so badly," he said before leaving for Tennessee. "We're winning tremendously."
"They want to make a deal and I think that's fine, I like making a deal too. What they want to do is immediately open the Hormuz Strait ... because they have no money coming in, because they get their money from the Hormuz Strait," Trump said.
The US has imposed an economic blockade on Iran to put pressure on Tehran to lift its blockade of Hormuz, which has drastically reduced shipping through the strait, even though Trump again asserted that the US had control of the waterway.
Trump also expects the US military's bombing campaign to resume after the midterm elections, The Wall Street Journal reported on Friday. The WSJ first reported that Trump had rejected the proposal, citing unnamed US officials.
Araghchi calls for deal with the US before midterms
The Iranians also engaged their Saudi rivals regarding the Strait of Hormuz, underscoring the stakes of a seven-month-old conflict that has disrupted oil flows through a critical shipping lane and taken a toll on the global economy.
The report comes following comments by Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi that the deal in question, which calls for steps including the lifting of a US naval blockade on Iranian ports, "would be much better if it is done before the midterm election."
"If there is seriousness on the US side to come to a deal and reopen the Strait of Hormuz, everything is now prepared," Araghchi said. If the US were to agree, the warring parties could start wider talks "on mutually agreed subjects."
That could potentially include discussions of Iran's nuclear program. Trump has said Tehran must never acquire a nuclear bomb, while a senior Iranian official told Reuters that Iran would show no flexibility over its nuclear program even if the USaccepted its peace deal.
Araghchi added that the Strait of Hormuz would not reopen until the plan’s conditions were fulfilled. “Iran will not surrender its sovereign rights under pressure,” Araghchi said.
US having positive, constructive indirect discussions with Iran, US official says
A US official said on Friday that the United States is having positive, constructive discussions with Iran through mediators and continues to discuss nuclear issues.
Earlier on Friday, a senior Iranian official told Reuters that Iran will show no flexibility over its nuclear program even if the US accepts its proposal.
Tzvi Jasper and Reuters contributed to this report.

articles.title: ‘Safeguard the postwar order,’ China tells UN General Assembly
articles.body:
‘Safeguard the postwar order,’ China tells UN General Assembly
China's Vice President, Han Zheng, urged the world to defend the postwar international order on Saturday, telling the UN General Assembly that geopolitical conflicts, widening development gaps and mounting global challenges make multilateralism more urgent than ever.
“The world wants peace not war,” Mr. Han told the General Debate of the Assembly's 81st session.
He said the international system centered on the UN and the international order, underpinned by international law that emerged after World War Two “must be upheld,” calling for disputes to be settled through dialogue rather than “unilateral military actions that violate the UN Charter and circumvent Security Council authorization.”
With power comes responsibility
“Major countries shoulder special responsibilities for safeguarding international peace and security, and they should take the lead in complying with the rules, upholding the rule of law and doing what's right,” he said.
On the Middle East, Mr. Han said the sovereignty of regional States, including in the Gulf, should be respected, and called for reconstruction in Gaza to proceed “in accordance with the principle of the Palestinians governing Palestine,” alongside a return to the two-state solution.
On Ukraine, he pointed to “four points” put forward by President Xi Jinping as “the fundamental guidance for China in playing a continued constructive role in its own way for achieving a political settlement of the crisis.” He also called for an immediate end to the blockade and sanctions against Cuba.
Turning to development, Mr. Han called for a global partnership “based on unity and equality, and that is balanced and inclusive,” with priority given to poverty reduction, food security and energy transition. Developed countries, he said, should honour their financing and climate finance commitments.
‘People-centred’ AI
On artificial intelligence, he said the world “should take a people centered approach and develop AI for the positive and for good, narrow the digital divide and promote development that is universally beneficial.”
He added that “protectionism produces no winners,” calling for the World Trade Organization (WTO)-centred system to be defended.
On cultural exchange, Mr. Han said “diversity has created splendor in the world,” and that “condescension and the self-centered mindset have no place in the interactions among different cultures.”
Reaffirming support for the UN, he said: “Multilateralism is a choice made by humanity after going through scourges, and fairness and justice are the joint pursuit of the people of all countries.”
Amplify voice of the ‘Global South’
China backs UN reform, he said, but wants it to strengthen – not merely cut – the organization's bodies and mandates, while boosting the voice of the Global South.
He also praised outgoing Secretary-General António Guterres who leaves office at the end of 2026 and said China wants his successor to be someone who “honors the UN Charter, has exceptional capability, upholds integrity and fairness, and demonstrates courage and dedication.”
Mr. Han marked 55 years since General Assembly resolution 2758, adopted on 25 October 1971, which recognized the Government of the People's Republic of China as China's sole legitimate representative at the UN.
Since then, he said, China has been “a stabilizing force in times of volatility,” with the best record on peace and security among major powers and having made the largest contribution to peacekeeping operations of any permanent Security Council member.
He said China has driven around 30 per cent of global growth in recent years, mobilized more than $23 billion under the Global Development Initiative, and granted zero-tariff access to all African countries and least developed countries with which it has ties.
“China will join hands with all other countries to build a community with a shared future for humanity and make the world a better place for all of us,” Mr. Han said.

articles.title: Polish president “doesn’t like” Trump inviting Putin to G20 but will still attend summit
articles.body:

Polish President Karol Nawrocki “does not like” the fact that the Trump administration has invited Vladimir Putin to this year’s G20 summit in the United States, says his chief foreign policy aide.
However, Nawrocki, who is a close ally of Donald Trump, still plans to attend the event – which Poland has been invited to as a guest rather than a full G20 member – in order to represent Polish interests and push for full membership of the group.
🔴 "Nie podoba nam się to". Nawrocki ma problem po decyzji Trumpa
Prezydent Karol Nawrocki weźmie udział w grudniowym szczycie G20 w Miami, na który zaproszono również Władimira Putina. Szef Biura Polityki Międzynarodowej Kancelarii Prezydenta Marcin Przydacz przyznał na antenie…
— Wirtualna Polska (@wirtualnapolska) September 26, 2026
The G20, a major intergovernmental forum, holds an annual summit whose location rotates among members. This year’s event will take place in December at a golf resort in Miami owned by Trump.
On Wednesday this week, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced that Trump has invited Putin to attend the summit, saying that “we think it’s an opportunity for him to engage…with other world leaders” and “we hope that’s an invitation he’ll accept”.
“If you only meet with people that you agree with, then these are very nice meetings but nothing happens,” added Rubio. “In order to solve problems, you have to meet with people that you disagree with or the people that you might have some issues with.”
Marco Rubio on Russia:
We’ve invited President Putin to the G20. We think it’s an opportunity for him to engage not just with Trump, but with other world leaders.
We hope that’s an invitation he will accept. pic.twitter.com/e0GSz7Y8gm
— Clash Report (@clashreport) September 23, 2026
Last December, Rubio also announced Poland’s invitation to the summit as a guest, saying that it would be “assuming its rightful place in the G20”. In May this year, the US also “expressed its strong support for Poland’s accession to the G20 as a permanent member”.
Poland will be represented by Nawrocki, who is a vocal critic of Putin and Russia, and is himself on a Russian wanted list for his work leading efforts to demolish Soviet-era monuments in Poland.
In an interview on Sunday with news website Wirtualna Polska, the head of Nawrocki’s international policy office, Marcin Przydacz, was asked if the US was right to invite Putin. “We don’t like it,” he replied.
“But we were invited to the G20 summit as guests, and it’s not our role to tell the participants who should be part of it,” he added, noting that Russia is a founding member of the G20. However, “if it were up to us, Russia should be isolated in all international forums.”
Nevertheless, “President [Nawrocki] is going to Miami and doesn’t intend to change his plans at this stage”, confirmed Przydacz. “Poland will be at the G20 summit because it’s in our interest…This isn’t the only format in which we sit with countries we disagree with.”
However, he also added that, “if the Russian leader actually intends to come, and is not just invited, we will discuss this with our European and Euro-Atlantic allies”.
Putin has not attended a G20 summit in person since 2019, initially due to the COVID-19 pandemic and later amid the fallout from Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine and the International Criminal Court’s arrest warrant against him. The US is not a member of the ICC, so the arrest warrant does not apply on its territory.
Przydacz told Wirtualna Polska that Putin “should be held accountable for his crimes”. Asked if Nawrocki would shake hands with the Russian president at the G20, Przydacz said that he “doesn’t think any interactions will occur”.
The United States has expressed "strong support for Poland’s accession to the G20 as a permanent member" following talks in Warsaw, after which it also emphasised "strong and growing" Polish-American relations https://t.co/qTpCACnMfu
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 2, 2026
He also emphasised that Poland’s invitation to the summit was a “major success, demonstrating our growing role”. He said that Nawrocki would use the event to push its ambition to become a full member of the group.
He added that it would also seek to “bring a Central European perspective” to the event, representing its entire region, which has so far been excluded from the G20.
Earlier this week, Polish foreign minister Radosław Sikorski said that, in his opinion, the US should make Putin’s invitation to the G20 conditional upon Russia implementing a ceasefire in Ukraine, reported news website Interia.
However, he noted that, when a G20 meeting of finance ministers took place in the US earlier this year, Poland had attended alongside Russia.

Since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Poland has been one of Kyiv’s closest allies, providing extensive military, humanitarian and diplomatic support to its eastern neighbour.
Poland has also been one of the primary targets of Russia’s hybrid actions against European countries, including airspace violations, acts of sabotage, cyberattacks and disinformation.

articles.title: Iraqi Resistance threatens nationwide sit-ins over US-pushed Iran flight ban
articles.body:
Iraqi Resistance threatens nationwide sit-ins over US-pushed Iran flight ban
Mass rallies demand end to Iraqi compliance with US flight sanctions
TEHRAN — The United States expanded its economic warfare against Iran into Iraqi airspace this week. Baghdad complied. Resistance factions immediately pushed back.
Following a September 8 U.S. Treasury threat to impose secondary sanctions on any airport servicing 27 Iranian airlines, the Iraqi government ordered aviation authorities in Baghdad, Najaf, Erbil, Sulaymaniyah, and Kirkuk to suspend all Iranian flights. Najaf International Airport grounded operations in the early hours of Friday.
The closures have stranded thousands of religious pilgrims, students, and medical patients.
They have also sparked an immediate backlash from Islamic Resistance groups. Factions view the shutdown as a direct extension of the U.S.-Israeli military and economic campaign designed to weaken the Resistance Front.
Threatening sit-ins and seeking fatwas
Harakat Hezbollah al-Nujaba Secretary-General Akram al-Kaabi promised direct action on Friday. He vowed his group will organize sit-ins at airports across the country unless normal air traffic resumes.
“We will not wait long,” Kaabi warned, condemning political forces that tolerate American dominance.
Kata’ib Sayyid al-Shuhada leader Abu Ala al-Walai urged the Iraqi parliament to pass a resolution rejecting the U.S. dictates, citing Russia and China as models of state independence.
He described Baghdad’s compliance as a betrayal of religious heritage. “It is not fitting for the Iraq of [Imam] Hussein [AS] to be part of an unjust siege on Iran, the land of knowledge and jihad,” al-Walai stated.
Kata’ib Hezbollah escalated the pushback by requesting Shia religious authorities issue a fatwa determining whether it is religiously permissible to help an enemy besiege the Iranian people.
The group urged citizens to circumvent the embargo directly by purchasing Iranian commodities.
Hadi al-Amiri, Secretary-General of the Badr Organization, condemned the unjust siege and said the government must not submit, calling it the first test for achieving full and comprehensive sovereignty.
Street protests and the fallout
Public anger materialized quickly. Demonstrators in Basra gathered near the airport and surrounded a grounded Iranian passenger aircraft.
Crowds in central Baghdad chanted against the siege, directing their anger at Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi.
Lawmakers are rebelling against the executive order. First Deputy Speaker Adnan Faihan declared the flight ban unconstitutional on Saturday. He outlined the material risks of isolating an ally.
Faihan warned that if Tehran retaliates by cutting natural gas exports, Iraq will lose up to 40 percent of its national power grid capacity. Basra parliamentarians gave the government 48 hours to explain the decision, gathering signatures for an emergency legislative session.
Senior political figures joined the dissent. Former Prime Minister Adel Abdul Mahdi labeled the closure a major mistake against an allied neighbor.
The office of Marjaa Sayyed Mohammad Taqi al-Modarresi condemned the capitulation, while Sayyed Abdul Qader al-Hassani al-Alousi described the ban as a historic error striking at Iraq’s religious identity.
The al-Zaidi government is attempting to manage the fallout. The prime minister’s office claims it is holding direct talks with Washington to secure exemptions for medical and religious travel. Yet Baghdad’s submission has yielded no financial relief, according to a report by Tasnim News Agency.
The U.S. Federal Reserve continues to block regular dollar cash transfers to Iraq despite the government’s enforcement of the aviation ban.
Trump has repeatedly said he approves of the conduct of Iraq’s new head of state, declaring that al-Zaidi is “a fantastic man.”

articles.title: Bahrain commits to joining US-led Falcon Strike task force, buying more air defense systems
articles.body:
Rania R.a. Abushamala
25 September 2026•Update: 25 September 2026
Bahrain has committed to joining the US Central Command’s Task Force Falcon Strike and purchasing additional US munitions and air defense systems, the US Embassy in Manama said Friday.
The commitment was made during a Military Consultative Committee meeting held Wednesday and Thursday co-chaired by US Deputy Assistant Defense Secretary Michael DiMino and Bahraini Defense Minister Lt. Gen. Abdullah bin Hassan Al-Nuaimi, the embassy said on US social media company X.
“Bahrain committed to join USCENTCOM’S Task Force Falcon Strike and purchase more U.S. munitions and air defense systems,” the embassy said.
The steps would strengthen Bahrain’s efforts to become “stronger, more interoperable, and more capable of providing for its own defense,” it added.
The US military’s CENTCOM announced the creation of Falcon Strike in August, describing it as the first multinational, multidomain task force for attack drones. On Aug. 13, it said US and allied personnel would operate one-way attack drones and unmanned systems in the air, on the sea surface and underwater.
Bahrain’s commitment comes amid efforts by the US and regional partners to strengthen defense coordination in the Gulf as tensions in the region rise.
Manama hosted a security dialogue involving 12 countries in July that addressed defense cooperation and freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz.

articles.title: All operational British Rivet Joint spy planes near Russia
articles.body:
Britain deployed its entire operational RC-135W Rivet Joint intelligence fleet on missions around Russia on 25 September, with both aircraft currently available to the RAF flying separate sorties over the Baltic and Black Sea while the third British Rivet Joint remains in the United States for refit and maintenance work.
Open-source flight tracking identified the aircraft as ZZ664 and ZZ666, both operating from RAF Waddington. ZZ664 flew around the Baltic region and close to the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad, while ZZ666 operated over the Black Sea before both aircraft began their return towards the UK. Neither aircraft was shown entering Russian airspace.
The UK operates three RC-135W Rivet Joint aircraft, meaning the two sorties represented the RAF committing its entire immediately available Rivet Joint force to intelligence-gathering activity around Russia on the same day. The third aircraft is currently in the United States undergoing refit and maintenance work, leaving the two aircraft seen over eastern Europe as the complete operational British fleet at that point.
The visibility of the sorties is also part of the point before someone asks if this should be secret, civilian services such as Flightradar24 build their tracking picture from sources including ADS-B, where an aircraft broadcasts information such as identity, altitude and position, and multilateration, or MLAT, where a position is calculated from the timing of transponder signals received by several ground stations. Both British aircraft were readily visible on civilian tracking networks for substantial parts of their missions, meaning these were not flights whose broad presence was being concealed from public view. Military aircraft can reduce the information available to civilian trackers, although MLAT can still plot an aircraft transmitting suitable transponder signals, so public visibility does not necessarily reveal every element of the mission. Had there been a requirement to minimise that visibility, however, the tracking picture could have been considerably less complete.
The Baltic aircraft followed a route around eastern NATO territory and Kaliningrad, an area containing a concentration of Russian military facilities, while the second aircraft operated over international waters in the Black Sea.
The RC-135W Rivet Joint is the RAF’s principal signals intelligence aircraft and is designed to intercept, locate and analyse electromagnetic emissions generated by military activity. Rather than relying primarily on cameras, the aircraft carries an extensive suite of receivers and processing equipment used to collect communications and electronic signals, including radar emissions, allowing crews to build a picture of activity at considerable distance.
Mission specialists aboard the aircraft can detect and classify signals while the sortie is under way, helping identify radar systems, communications networks and other emitters. This allows Rivet Joint to collect intelligence while remaining in international or allied airspace rather than entering the territory being monitored.
The three British aircraft are operated by No. 51 Squadron from RAF Waddington and are closely related to the RC-135 fleet operated by the US Air Force. British Rivet Joints are regularly used for intelligence missions around NATO’s eastern flank, but the simultaneous appearance of both operationally available aircraft around Russia placed the whole immediately usable UK fleet on missions covering Russia’s western and southern approaches.

articles.title: Ukraine’s biggest steelmaker halts production
articles.body:
Ukraine’s biggest steelmaker halts production
Ukraine’s largest steel producer, ArcelorMittal Krivoy Rog, has halted production after repeated Russian missile strikes caused extensive damage to the plant, the company announced on Friday.
The Russian Defense Ministry has said that Moscow is targeting Ukrainian military and defense-related facilities and supporting infrastructure in response to Kiev’s escalating long-range attacks on Russian energy and industrial sites.
The steelworks, located in the central Ukrainian city of Krivoy Rog, also includes iron ore mining operations. Before the escalation of the conflict in 2022, it produced 4.9 million tons of steel annually.
ArcelorMittal said the facility had been hit four times over the past five weeks, most recently on September 21. The strikes caused extensive damage to production facilities, leaving the company unable to restart operations “in a safe and sustainable manner.”
CEO Mauro Longobardo said the company would focus on preserving the plant’s infrastructure so production could eventually resume. ArcelorMittal expects to take a charge of around $1 billion due to the reduced value of the facility and its equipment.
The shutdown follows stoppages at Zaporozhstal and Kamet Steel, both owned by Ukrainian metals giant Metinvest. Together with ArcelorMittal Krivoy Rog, the three plants accounted for about 90% of Ukraine’s steel output before Russian strikes brought production to a halt, according to the Financial Times. 
“As of today, [Ukraine] doesn’t have a steel industry anymore,” Aleksandr Vodoviz, head of the CEO’s office at Metinvest, told the FT, adding that repairs could take “days, weeks, months, or years.”
The Russian Defense Ministry said this week that it had struck the Krivoy Rog steelworks and other industrial facilities involved in Ukrainian military production. Other recent targets cited by the ministry include drone production and storage sites, power infrastructure, bridges, ports, warehouses, and logistics hubs.
A day before the latest strike on the steelworks, Ukraine launched its largest drone attack on Moscow, killing several people and hitting a major oil refinery.
Russia has condemned strikes on civilians as acts of terrorism, while maintaining that its forces only target military and defense-related facilities.

articles.title: IRGC: Iran will continue punishing US until its seven conditions are met
articles.body:
IRGC: Iran will continue punishing US until its seven conditions are met
TEHRAN— Brigadier General Hossein Mohebbi, spokesperson for Iran’s Islamic Revolution Guard Corps (IRGC), says Iran will continue its campaign to punish the United States until Washington meets seven conditions set by Tehran.
“We will not stop punishing the US until Iran’s seven conditions are met,” Mohebbi said on Friday, stressing that Iran’s missile capabilities are capable of penetrating and destroying multilayered US air-defense systems.
He said Washington had expected Iran to surrender after deploying military forces to the Persian Gulf, but instead encountered a different form of resistance from the Iranian side.
According to the IRGC spokesperson, the sacrifices of Iranian martyrs have strengthened national resolve and contributed to greater courage and security among the Iranian people.
“We are the victors of the war and are turning it into permanent strategic deterrence,” Mohebbi said.
US failed to secure Hormuz
Mohebbi also challenged Washington’s stated rationale for its military presence in the region, saying the United States had claimed that its objective was to safeguard maritime security but had failed to achieve that goal during the recent conflict.
“Despite having the world’s largest navy, the US could not keep the Strait of Hormuz open even for a few hours,” he said.
He said Washington had sought to portray the continued availability of the strategic waterway as necessary to prevent a surge in global oil prices, while arguing that effective control over maritime traffic in the strait remained with the IRGC’s naval forces.
Mohebbi said that before the war, daily traffic through the Strait of Hormuz ranged from dozens to more than 100 vessels, whereas the current situation was different, with oil shipments belonging to Iran’s trading partners passing through with Tehran’s permission.
The Strait of Hormuz, one of the world’s most strategically important maritime chokepoints, connects the Persian Gulf with the Gulf of Oman and the Arabian Sea and carries a significant share of global oil and gas shipments.
US military superiority failed to deter resistance
The IRGC spokesperson further rejected 'US efforts to project an image of overwhelming military and technological superiority.'
He said the United States had relied heavily on the capabilities of its advanced air, naval and ground forces, but that Iranian Armed Forces had demonstrated the ability to target such military assets during the recent war.
Mohebbi’s remarks portrayed Iran’s military response as part of a broader strategy aimed not only at countering the United States during the conflict but also at establishing a longer-term deterrent capability.
He said the sacrifices made during the war had transformed the nature of Iran’s national security environment, arguing that the country had emerged from the conflict with greater resolve and a stronger deterrent posture.
The comments came as Iranian officials continued to emphasize that Tehran’s approach to the confrontation with Washington combines military deterrence with political and diplomatic demands.

articles.title: Journalist Mariia Yizhvenko, 29, killed in Russian drone strike on Kyiv business centre
articles.body:
Journalist Mariia Yizhvenko, 29, killed in Russian drone strike on Kyiv business centre
Journalist Mariia Yizhvenko, 29, has been killed in a Russian strike on a business centre in Kyiv. She had only recently left NV Business, the business news section of a Ukrainian media holding company, and was planning to start a family with her husband.
Source: Mariia's husband and combat medic Danylo Yizhvenko; Mariia's former colleague Oleksandra Nekrashchuk
Details: Danylo reported Mariia's death and said they were actively planning their future. At the end of last year, they took out a loan to buy a flat and planned to have a child this winter.
Around two weeks ago, they bought Mariia a car so she could more easily travel around the city with their future child. She had taken two driving lessons to refresh her skills.
"The car burned down. Masha was killed. I lost my friend, my girlfriend, my wife and the mother of my future children, who will now never be born [...]
Masha was a wonderful, intelligent person who cared deeply about Ukraine. She was my voice of reason and the person who always showed me what true care looked like," Danylo wrote.
Oleksandra Nekrashchuk, deputy editor-in-chief of NV Business, said Mariia covered defence tech, Ukraine's IT sector and military technology. Several months ago, she left journalism to pursue a career in the corporate sector.
"She was not just a talented journalist but an incredible person – bright, intelligent and deeply thoughtful [...] She could explain the most complicated things simply and genuinely wanted to help her country. Her kindness and smile will remain in the memory of everyone who had the privilege of knowing her," Nekrashchuk added.
Danylo set up a fundraiser for Mariia's funeral. He said any remaining money will go to the Ukrainian military. Mariia's family will announce the time and place of the farewell later.
Russian forces have attacked Ukraine with almost 300 attack drones of various types since the evening of 24 September. Ukrainian air defences have destroyed 267 drones.
In Kyiv, a Russian drone struck an apartment block in the Pecherskyi district, killing a 14-year-old boy. Debris fell onto a 25-storey residential building in the Solomianskyi district, while another drone struck an office building.
Four people were killed in the strike on the business centre. Two were outside the building at the time. Another person was found dead in a car in the car park and one inside the building.
Daria Kulchytska, who owns a nearby flower shop, told Suspilne Kyiv, a branch of Ukraine's national broadcaster, that she arrived early that morning to inspect damage from the overnight attack. By the time the area was struck again, workers had cleared up and boarded the windows with plywood.
"We were relieved that we'd got off lightly. Then someone called me over to work out where to take the broken glass. I went outside, my partner arrived – and then [there was] this explosion," she said.
Daria was knocked to the ground and her partner was also injured.
"I don't know how I survived because there was a body lying next to me. I went up to a woman – she wasn't breathing. It was horrific on the other side of the road. The person in the car was dead and the guys were pulling her out," she said.
Another eyewitness, Nataliia Potiuk, said there was no information at the time about Russian aerial assets heading towards the district.
"I turned towards the window and saw a Shahed [drone] fly past. A few seconds later, there was already a column of smoke. A lot of people were injured. They were taking people away with shrapnel wounds," she said.
Subscribe on Patreon to back our journalism long-term.

articles.title: Putin says Russian interests will guide return to talks
articles.body:
Russian President Vladimir Putin said on Sept. 25 that proposals to resume negotiations with Ukraine remained under consideration, but Moscow would decide its next steps according to its own interests.
Speaking to reporters after the 12th St. Petersburg International United Cultures Forum, Putin accused Kyiv of disrupting plans to restart talks by launching attacks during Russia’s parliamentary elections.
“They are all on the table. It’s all possible,” he said of proposals for a settlement, adding that Moscow would carefully consider its response to the attacks.
Putin said Ukraine had expressed willingness to resume negotiations several weeks before the State Duma elections and that Russia had indicated it would be ready after the vote.
He accused Ukrainian forces of launching a mass drone attack on Moscow overnight on Sept. 19–20 and striking polling stations.
Putin claimed Russia’s retaliatory strikes had prompted Kyiv to raise the prospect of a ceasefire, including a reciprocal halt to attacks on oil and energy facilities. He also said Ukrainian forces were struggling to counter Russia’s Geran drones.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has described attacks inside Russia as a response to Russian strikes on his country’s civilians and infrastructure, while calling for direct talks to end the war.
Putin also rejected warnings that Russia was preparing to attack Europe and accused some European governments of using Ukraine against Moscow.
“We are not preparing for any military action against Europe,” he said, adding that Russia had no plans or grounds to escalate tensions.

articles.title: Why is the Swiss government opposing stricter neutrality rules?
articles.body:
Why is the Swiss government opposing stricter neutrality rules?
The Swiss government and parliament are urging voters to reject a proposal during an upcoming referendum that would strengthen the country’s neutrality policy by constraining Bern’s ability to impose unilateral sanctions.
The motion is being pushed by pro-sovereignty politicians, who have criticized the government’s decision to largely adopt EU sanctions against Russia following the escalation of the Ukraine conflict in 2022.
Under the current system that the Federal Council seeks to preserve, the seven-member ruling body decides on a case-by-case basis whether Switzerland should copy restrictions imposed by other Western nations.
The proposed amendment will be put to a nationwide vote on Sunday, September 27.
Why do sanctions matter?
Switzerland largely aligned itself with the EU sanctions regime targeting Russia after the escalation of the Ukraine conflict in February 2022.
As of July, Bern reported freezing 8.5 billion Swiss francs ($10.3 billion) in assets owned by Russian companies and individuals targeted by Brussels and another 6.8 billion francs ($8.2 billion) in funds owned by the Russian Central Bank. The Swiss Federal Council has rejected calls to confiscate the money.
Moscow has repeatedly accused Switzerland of abandoning its traditional neutrality by taking the sanctions path, arguing that it had lost its standing as a “trusted neutral mediator.”
Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov reiterated Moscow’s stance to Swiss Federal Councillor Ignazio Cassis personally, when the two met on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly session in New York in July 2025.
Russia as well as several other non-Western nations reject any sanctions not authorized by the UN as illegal under international law and consider them a form of economic warfare.
What is at stake in Sunday’s vote?
The “Safeguard Swiss neutrality” initiative was launched by the Pro Schweiz (For Switzerland) pro-sovereignty movement and figures associated with the conservative Swiss People’s Party (SVP), which strongly backs the proposal.
It would define Switzerland’s neutrality in the Constitution as “perpetual and armed.” Switzerland would be barred from joining or cooperating with military or defense alliances unless it was facing a direct military attack.
The country would also be prohibited from imposing sanctions against belligerent states, with exceptions for measures mandated by the UN and those intended to prevent sanctions circumvention.
A newly-strengthened neutrality policy would be used to “prevent and resolve conflicts” and “to act as a mediator,” if the proposal is passed.
Who is against it?
The Swiss Federal Council argues that the more rigid interpretation would restrict Switzerland’s freedom of action and could weaken its national security. Parliament has also recommended rejecting the initiative.
“Anyone who waits until the crisis is already here before they are willing to cooperate is too late,” Cassis has said.
The government is particularly opposed to surrendering its ability to decide whether to adopt sanctions.
“Neutrality does not require an automatic response,” the councillor said. “It requires us to take responsibility and weigh up our interests.”
Who backs it?
SVP President Marcel Dettling has accused Cassis and Swiss diplomats of seeking to erode neutrality and “play the big shot everywhere in the world.”
“Switzerland is neutral. This means we do not interfere in foreign affairs. Every individual is entitled to their own opinion, but official Switzerland is neutral and offers its good offices to all parties in conflict,” he said.
SVP member Christoph Blocher, who was a member of the Federal Council in the 2000s, rejected the notion that neutrality should be “flexible,” denouncing it as “dangerous nonsense.”
The SVP argues that fixed constitutional rules would make Swiss policy more predictable and enhance the country’s credibility as a mediator. It also contends that unilateral sanctions against parties to a conflict are incompatible with staying neutral on it.
What do the polls say?
Recent surveys show substantially more respondents opposing the neutrality initiative than supporting it.
A LeeWas survey for 20 Minuten and Tamedia, conducted earlier this month among 12,948 eligible voters, found 31% supported the initiative and 68% opposed it. Support had fallen by five percentage points compared with the previous survey wave.
Historically, Swiss voters have often sided with the Federal Council’s recommendations.
In June, they rejected the SVP-backed proposal to cap Switzerland’s population below 10 million through 2050, with 54.79% voting against and 45.21% in favor. The Federal Council had opposed the initiative.
On the same day, voters approved stricter rules governing access to alternative civilian service by 52.46% to 47.54%. That measure intended to preserve participation in the mandatory military service was backed by the Federal Council and parliament, with the SVP being among the supporting parties.
How does Swiss direct democracy work?
Switzerland has one of the world’s most extensive systems of direct democracy, with voters deciding national issues up to four times a year, often with several proposals on the ballot at once.
A popular initiative seeking to amend the Constitution requires 100,000 valid signatures collected within 18 months before it can proceed through the political process toward a nationwide vote. Constitutional amendments require a double majority – a majority of voters nationwide and a majority of the cantons – to pass.
Rules are less restrictive for optional referendums on laws passed by parliament.

articles.title: ‘Hands Off!’: European Leaders Reject Trump's Call to Quit the ICC
articles.body:
European leaders are rallying behind the International Criminal Court (ICC) after President Donald Trump called for countries to "immediately" resign from the organization, amid a broader push by the U.S. Administration to dismantle it.
Irish Taoiseach (Prime Minister) Micheál Martin pledged his support for the ICC and said Ireland “strongly opposes efforts to undermine the court,” during his speech at the United Nations General Assembly in New York on Thursday.
Referencing the Hague-based court as he discussed the conflict in Ukraine, Martin said Russia must be held “accountable” for its actions. “There can be no impunity for war crimes… that is why Ireland is a steadfast supporter of the International Criminal Court,” he said, stressing that all “measures against it should be immediately withdrawn.”
Netherlands Prime Minister Rob Jetten issued a similar defense of the ICC earlier in the day. Without directly mentioning Trump or the U.S., Jetten reflected on how the court has come “under attack” and asked how can anyone “possibly be opposed to prosecuting the very worst crimes?"
“I believe there can be only one response,” he continued. “To say: 'hands off' the ICC, and all those other institutions that protect the international legal order.” The remarks drew loud applause from attending delegates.
The ICC is recognized as the world’s highest criminal court. It draws its jurisdiction from the Rome Statute, a treaty that went into effect in 2002 and is ratified by 125 countries. Neither the U.S. nor Israel is a state party to the Rome Statute, and therefore they do not recognize the jurisdiction of the court.
Trump has long complained that the ICC oversteps its authority and should not claim jurisdiction over U.S. citizens. His calls against the organization culminated in a public appeal at the U.N. on Tuesday. During his 45-minute speech, Trump called “on all nations that are members of the ICC to officially resign from this rogue institution, immediately.”
He said the U.S. is “opposed to the out-of-control institution known as the ICC” and “will never allow U.S. service members or anyone else to be investigated or given show trials by an anti-American tribunal with no jurisdiction over us.”
His call to action was swiftly rejected by German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul.
"We will, of course, not be doing that," Wadephul told Germany's Deutschlandfunk radio station on Wednesday. He described the court as "an important institution” and said the issue is "one of the areas where we do indeed have to acknowledge a regrettable difference in policy from the U.S. Administration."
Similarly, European Council president Antonio Costa said the E.U. stands “firmly behind” the ICC and argued it’s “unacceptable to threaten or attack the International Criminal Court, its officials, and its staff.”
At the U.N. assembly, the only nation to follow Trump’s lead appeared to be Naoero, a microstate island country formerly known as Nauru.
Naoero President David Adeang said in his speech late Tuesday that he would formally withdraw his country from the Rome Statute, citing the ICC’s “increasing irrelevance.”
"Naoero joins a growing number of nations standing up for their sovereignty against the ICC’s illegitimate overreach,” said U.S. Assistant Secretary for East Asian and Pacific Affairs Michael DeSombre, after meeting with Naoero’s Deputy Foreign Minister.
Leaving the ICC is neither an immediate or clean break, experts tell TIME.
Withdrawal takes at least a year, and states remain bound to cooperate with proceedings opened before their departure, according to Sergey Vasiliev, a professor of international law at Open University Netherlands.
“The state that intends to withdraw has to file a notification of withdrawal from the statute, and it comes into effect only one year after such notification has been received by the depository of the treaty,” he says. “Those states are still obliged to provide full cooperation to the court for all the proceedings and cases that started while they were a state party and right until the moment when their withdrawal becomes effective.”
Five other states—Niger, Burkina Faso, Mali, Venezuela, and Chad—have recently moved to withdraw from the organization. Vasiliev calls their planned departures a “serious loss,” but says it is not “lethal to the existence of the ICC.”
Hungary formally moved to withdraw from the ICC last year under former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán, but his successor, Péter Magyar, reversed the decision, signaling its renewed commitment to the organization.
A timeline of Trump’s campaign against the ICC
Trump’s complaints with the ICC date back to his first term. In late 2017, the ICC requested to open an investigation into American actions overseas, looking into alleged war crimes committed by U.S. personnel in Afghanistan.
Trump pushed back and challenge the court’s authority. During his speech at the U.N. General Assembly in 2018, he claimed the ICC had “no jurisdiction, no legitimacy, and no authority” and vowed to “never surrender America’s sovereignty to an unelected, unaccountable, global bureaucracy.”
“The United States has always objected to the ICC's exercise of jurisdiction over its service members,” says Vasiliev, noting this has been an ongoing point of contention.
However, “the ICC has jurisdiction over crimes committed on the state party territory, even when those crimes are committed by non-state party nationals,” he adds.
In 2020, Trump signed an Executive Order issuing sanctions in response to the ICC’s Afghanistan investigation, calling the court’s actions “illegitimate assertions of jurisdiction.” The sanctions and visa restrictions against personnel of the ICC were later revoked by former President Joe Biden in 2021.
In more recent years, the Trump Administration’s arguments with the ICC have largely centered on the court’s investigation into possible Israeli war crimes in Gaza. The court issued arrest warrants for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, a Trump ally, and Israeli Defense Minister Yoav Gallant in November 2024.
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani had previously pledged to execute the ICC’s warrant and have Netanyahu arrested when he traveled to the city for the U.N. assembly. But in July, Mamdani conceded that his Administration had “reviewed every avenue available,” only to find they did not have the jurisdiction.
Shortly after returning to office in early 2025, Trump signed an Executive Order declaring a “national emergency” and imposing sanctions on the ICC over what he said was the court’s “illegitimate and baseless actions targeting America and our close ally Israel.”
Efforts were ramped up again in July, when U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced a “whole-of-government” effort “to systematically disable the ICC’s ability to operate, target American servicemen or officials, or otherwise threaten American sovereignty.”
A month later, the State Department imposed sanctions on the ICC’s president, Judge Tomoko Akane, and Abdoulaye Seye, a Senegalese senior trial lawyer for the Office of the Prosecutor. The ICC referred to the sanctions as "a flagrant attack against the independence of an impartial judicial institution which operates pursuant to the mandate conferred by its states parties."
The sanctions targeting the ICC personnel were imposed under the 2025 Executive Order issued by Trump. On Tuesday, 38 civil society groups jointly filed an amicus curiae ("friend of the court") brief with the U.S. District Court in support of a lawsuit challenging the legality of the sanctions imposed under that Executive Order.

articles.title: US sends Abrams tanks and crews back to Lithuania
articles.body:
Two US Army battalions are due to deploy to Lithuania in late October as part of a regular troop rotation, including a heavy unit equipped with Abrams tanks and an engineering battalion, according to Lithuanian officials.
Lithuanian Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas said preparations and logistical arrangements for the deployment were under way, with around 1,000 US personnel expected to arrive. The troops are due to remain in Lithuania for nine months, maintaining a US presence broadly similar in size to previous rotations.
Kaunas said: “The preparation process and logistical arrangements are currently underway, and two battalions will arrive in Lithuania at the end of October.”
One of the formations will be a heavy battalion equipped with Abrams main battle tanks and other heavy weaponry. The second will be an engineering battalion, which Lithuania says will support work connected with the development of its military division, border protection and other defence projects.
The Lithuanian Ministry of National Defence confirmed the deployment, saying: “US troops are returning to Lithuania. A US heavy battalion with Abrams tanks and an engineer battalion will deploy to Lithuania.”
Kaunas discussed the rotation during a visit to the Pentagon, where he met US Deputy Assistant Secretary of Defence Elbridge Colby. The Lithuanian minister also raised the possibility of establishing a permanent US military base in Lithuania, although he said no decision had been taken.
American forces have operated in Lithuania through successive rotational deployments, with the forthcoming nine-month rotation continuing that model rather than representing a newly announced permanent stationing arrangement.
The Lithuanian defence ministry said the presence of the two battalions would contribute to the country’s defence and NATO forces on the Alliance’s eastern flank.

articles.title: New Russian ambassador arrives in North Korea
articles.body:
Russia’s newly appointed ambassador to North Korea arrived in Pyongyang on Saturday, the diplomatic mission announced on social media, nearly a year after his predecessor died in the DPRK capital.
Ambassador Andrei Podelyshev arrived with his wife aboard a direct Nordwind flight from Moscow, the Embassy and TASS reported, before “immediately” heading to the World War II-era Liberation Monument to honor fallen Soviet soldiers.

articles.title: Urgent: Xi, Trump agree Iran should fulfill commitment not to develop nuclear weapons
articles.body:
WASHINGTON, Sept. 26 (Xinhua) -- Chinese President Xi Jinping and U.S. President Donald Trump have agreed that Iran should fulfill its commitment not to develop nuclear weapons, according to a release made public after Xi wrapped up his state visit to the United States on Friday.
The two leaders also agreed that no country or institution shall charge transit fees for passage through international waterways.
During the three-day visit, Xi and Trump exchanged in-depth views on bilateral relations as well as major international and regional issues. ■

articles.title: Germany stated that Putin's participation in the G20 summit could initiate negotiations on ending the war in Ukraine
articles.body:
Germany stated that Putin's participation in the G20 summit could initiate negotiations on ending the war in Ukraine
Kyiv • UNN
Minister Johann Wadephul considers Putin's participation in the G20 summit an opportunity to begin serious negotiations regarding the war in Ukraine. He emphasized the need for a ceasefire.
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said on Friday that Russian President Vladimir Putin’s participation in the G20 meeting could mark the beginning of "serious negotiations" on ending Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Politico reports, UNN writes.
Details
U.S. President Donald Trump invited the Russian president to the next G20 summit, scheduled for December in Miami.
Many leaders, including Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni and EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs Kaja Kallas, expressed serious reservations about the invitation.
However, Wadephul expressed a more optimistic position during a press conference with his Canadian counterpart in Ottawa.
This will indeed be a litmus test, including for Vladimir Putin, regarding his readiness to negotiate. Therefore, such opportunities must be used. We have repeatedly called on the Russian government and Putin to sit down at the negotiating table. And if such an opportunity arises, then perhaps this will at least become the beginning of serious negotiations
At the same time, he added that a necessary condition for meaningful dialogue should be a ceasefire for the duration of the negotiations.
Canadian Foreign Minister Anita Anand said she was surprised by Trump’s invitation to Putin, but added that Canada would participate in the summit nonetheless, since that, in her words, is "true diplomacy."
Wadephul’s statements differed from the official position of his government. Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s spokesman, Stefan Kornelius, said earlier this week that "the German government does not view relations with Russia as normal" and that Berlin was coordinating a joint response with its partners.
The German Foreign Ministry did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
As the publication notes, the White House invitation was the latest U.S. attempt to bring Moscow back into the international diplomatic arena and could lead to Putin’s first in-person participation in a G20 summit since 2019.

articles.title: Taiwan plans to procure 200 additional anti-ship missiles
articles.body:
TAIPEI (Taiwan News) – The Ministry of National Defense plans to procure an additional 200 anti-ship missiles from the National Chung-Shan Institute of Science and Technology, reports said Saturday.
A budget of NT$22 billion (US$693.38 million) will launch the project next year for an eight-year period, per Liberty Times. The contract will cover upgraded versions of the Hsiung Feng II and Hsiung Feng III missiles.
Taiwan was already planning a total of more than 1,400 anti-ship missiles, including US-made land-based Harpoon systems. However, the military reasoned that in the face of China’s rapidly expanding and modernizing navy, the original plan was not ambitious enough, Liberty Times reported.
The new missiles will include the latest semiconductors allowing the systems to counter electronic jamming by China’s newest ships and amphibious vehicles and reach their intended targets.
The extra missiles would also help avoid the risk of depletion as shown by the wars in Ukraine and Iran. The likelihood existed that some missiles would be destroyed by the enemy, while each enemy ship would need to be hit by two to four missiles to guarantee its sinking, the report said. In this scenario, the 200 new missiles could serve as a backup.

articles.title: Yemen releases latest statement on no. of Saudi aristrikes
articles.body:
According to local Yemeni Al-Masirah TV website, General Yahya Saree, the spokesman for the Yemeni Armed Forces, issued a statement on Saturday addressing the intensified attacks by the Saudi enemy against his country.
The spokesman stated that over the past 24 hours, the Saudi enemy carried out 27 airstrikes using F-15 and Typhoon fighter jets launched from the Khamis Mushait and Taif airbases. These Saudi airstrikes targeted civilian infrastructure—including bridges, roads, and other facilities—in the provinces of Taiz, Marib, Saada, Amran, Ibb, and Hajjah.
According to the report, Yahya Saree added that the total number of aggressive Saudi airstrikes and missile attacks has reached 1,059 since the escalation of hostilities began.
MNA/6959498
